records.text: We update our AI adoption tracker through September 2026. n AI-related investment growth remains strong, particularly for semiconductors, n where equity analysts expect global revenue to reach $868bn (ann.) by the end of 2026. 2026 gross profit forecast revisions since 2022Q3 for AI-exposed global public companies currently stands at $1.1tn. AI-related hardware investment in the US national accounts also continues to rise and now stands at $555bn (3-month annualized average; 1.7% of GDP) above its 2022 level. AI-related hardware shipments from Germany have recovered in recent months and US AI hardware net imports rose to $66.5bn in July. AI adoption by firms rose by 1.4pp to 23.8% among US establishments (with n adoption expected to rise to 27.6% in the next 6 months) according to the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS). Adoption is approaching 50% in the information, professional, and finance sectors. At a detailed subsector level, publishing, computing, and securities firms continue to lead adoption. Web search firms expect a nearly 20pp increase in adoption over the next six months Establishments with over 250 employees continue to lead in adoption (44%; latest six survey average) while adoption has grown more slowly recently among smaller firms. Other business surveys note that 44% of surveyed firms have adopted workplace AI tools, up from 10% a year ago. AI’s labor market impact remains visible but narrow. The results suggest that a diesel shock can be transmitted not only through the final delivery of goods, but also through freight-intensive supply chains that span multiple stages of production. Taken together, the two lenses suggest that the effect of a diesel shock extends beyond categories with visibly high transportation margins. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2% on the heels of a two-tenths rise in participation. We expected LFPR to rebound into year-end, reversing its summer downturn; that happened this month a nudged measure slack a touch higher. Wage growth also continues to decelerate. Wage growth in services sectors is a different story. Growth in average hourly earnings slipped further to 2.8% y/y in September, down from 3.9% a year ago. Page 22 A case for paying the belly Shoki Omori | Strategist | +81-3-6730-0835 This note looks at the 1y1y x 2y3y x 5y5y forward fly in yen OIS on three points: how to read its level, the regimes in which paying the belly is rewarded, and the shape of the recommendation. On Tuesday, 29 September the fly stood at -37bp (2 x 2y3y at 2.73% minus 1y1y at 2.27% minus 5y5y at 3.56%), which at first glance says the belly is rich. Against the chord joining the midpoints of the wings (1.5 and 7.5 years), however, the belly sits 3bp higher (+6bp in fly terms), so curvature is fair; the -37bp is the slope (-43bp) that a 1:2:1 structure with asymmetric wings carries mechanically. The question is whether to pay the belly. In spot terms that is a levered trade paying 4.6 units of 5y against 2y and 10y; it lost only about 4bp in September's front -led bear flattening, is rewarded by convergence to the house path (the house curve gives -27bp at end -2026 and +3bp at end -2027), and carries +3bp per three months, losing only in a super-long-led term-premium shock or if terminal repricing concentrates in the belly. Paying the belly looks like a trade: we add it at -37bp with a target of 0bp and a stop of -55bp. With refineries being impaired and the price of diesel, fertilizers, etc., still climbing higher, the upside risks to inflation remain intact despite the allegedly normalization in flows. As we approach the US midterm elections, we cannot rule out escalation of the conflict, which can only add insult to injury. How to respond to supply shocks? Central banks are supposed to react to infrequent supply shocks only if they threaten to de-anchor inflation expectations. But is that reaction function optimal to deal with a sequence of supply shocks which are becoming increasingly likely due to geopolitical dynamics? By not reacting to a sequence of supply-driven inflation shocks, the Fed is passively easing monetary conditions by validating lower real rates. Moreover, the volatility of supply shocks can also be inflationary. A good example is the volatility of oil prices driven by the Iran war. Yes, oil prices volatility can be inflationary Of course, inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon and real shocks can only alter relative prices, unless monetary (and fiscal) policy accommodates those shocks. In theory, an increase in oil prices need not be inflationary in the sense of increasing the overall level of prices. QT fine-tuning is unlikely, we think, at least in the very short run. Food, autos, household durables, recreational goods, airlines and delivery services emerge as the most freight-and fuel-exposed categories, making up 18% of total PCE prices and 20% of core PCE. The road from pump to prices is long and varied with several layers of attenuation between a diesel price increase and retail price increases for consumer goods and services. Transportation is only a small share of final costs, diesel is only one component of freight costs, and pass-through is often incomplete due to margins, inventories and sourcing adjustments. If sustained, the roughly 80% YTD increase in diesel prices could add 20-30bp to headline inflation and 15-20bp to core inflation. Ultimately, persistence is critical: a sustained increase is more likely to work its way through contracts, inventories and supply chains into consumer prices, while a short-lived spike may largely be absorbed along the way. Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy Cross-Currency Basis 4Q26 Outlook 01 October 2026 J P M O R G A N It has been an eventful few months for US rates markets, as the Fed delivered its first hike since July 2023 at its September meeting in a unanimous decision. The SEP skewed hawk- ishly as well, with the median participant now looking for one more hike this year and most of the committee seeing the Fed on hold or hiking more in 2027. The press conference fol- lowing the meeting was also hawkish: when asked about price stability, Chair Warsh said that they are “serious about this,” indicating that this is unlikely to be a one-and-done hiking cycle. The committee’s views on risks to growth are more heavily skewed to the upside than at any other time since the SEP was introduced, as economic data has continued to come in strong. The Middle East conflict has continued its escalation/descalation pattern, and oil prices have fluctuated accordingly. The resulting inflation pressure remains a concern. Giv- en this backdrop, markets have continued to price in more hikes: the implied distribution inferred from options on June 2027 3M SOFR futures has continued to shift further to the right (Figure 1T h e J u n e 2 0 2 7 3 M S O F R i m p l i e d d i s t r i b u t i o n h a s c o n t i n u e d t o s h i f t t o t h e r i g h t ), and the 1Yx1Y OIS rate has eclipsed the highs reached during the 2022- 2023 hiking cycle

records.text: ws – or accelerates. Service failures: Metros’ inability to secure a steady revenue stream has major implications for infrastructure and service delivery. The Auditor-General and Municipal Finance Management Act reports explicitly attribute lost municipal revenue to inadequate maintenance and illegal connections. Households with intermittent or unmetered services have a rational basis for withholding payment. Broken infrastructure means unread meters, estimated bills, and billing disputes – all of which the MFMA report confirms have increased in Buffalo City, eThekwini and Nelson Mandela Bay. Stats SA’s 2025 General Household Survey found highly unequal access to basic services across the eight metros, which maps directly onto the political risk gradient entering the LGE 2026. Cape Town sits at the favourable end of all three indicators. Mangaung, Buffalo City and eThekwini are underperformers on sanitation and water – the services most directly attributable to municipal governance quality. Smaller envelope, weaker governance: The AGSA MFMA 2023–24 shows metros lost ZAR8.64bn of revenue to water leakage and ZAR14.52bn to electricity losses in a single year. Only Cape Town maintained a clean audit in 2023–24. Service delivery failure also feeds state dependence, according to data. For each month in 1997, it is calculated as the average year-over-year change for the same month in the five preceding seasons (1991-95) and five subsequent seasons (1999-2003). For each month in 1998, the average uses 1992-96 and 2000-04. We added the 2015-16 El Niño for comparison too. Interestingly, both the 1997-98 and 2015-16 El Niño periods tended to be more disinflationary compared to the rolling 10-season average for the US-grown corn, soybeans, and wheat, as the charts above show. These products may have benefitted from more favorable growing conditions in some regions of the US, and of course other economic events could have been unfolding. In contrast, Colombian-grown coffee was more inflationary in the 1997-98 El Niño period compared to the rolling 10-season average, roughly lining up with the beginning of the El Niño event in the Southern Hemisphere. The dynamics may suggest that any El Niño-related impact on food prices might be uneven across regions, timing, and food categories, and not necessarily uniform. Commodity price growth in these categories also looked different across the two different El Niños, though in both cases neither appear uniformly inflationary. Where else in other prices? Did any El Niño-related commodity price fluctuations feed into consumer prices? In both the 1997-98 and 2015-16 episodes, El Niño impacts are fairly difficult to see in the inflation data, though perhaps related volatility was visible in some food PCE categories.

Second, we apply mode-specific estimates for diesel's contribution to trucking, rail, water transportation, and courier operating costs. Finally, we consider a range of pass- through assumptions, recognizing that higher freight costs may be only partially reflected in consumer prices because of various layers of attenuation, including margin compression, inventory management, sourcing decisions etc. One intuitive way to think about the framework is that diesel affects inflation through a series of progressively smaller channels. A rise in diesel prices increases freight operating costs, but only by the proportion of those costs attributable to fuel. Higher freight costs then affect only the transportation-intensive portion of a product's cost structure. Finally, firms may choose to pass through only part of those higher costs to consumers. As a result, even a large diesel shock typically translates into a much smaller increase in final consumer prices. 1 October 2026 6 Barclays | US Energy and Inflation

records.text: US Economics Weekly 02 October 2026 Citi Research 2 A substantial move higher in US Treasury yields over the last month took a pause this week, but despite numerous dovish developments, 2-year yields were less than 10bp lower over the week and 10-year yields were slightly higher. Yields remain sensitive to oil prices but were more reactive this week to global developments and dovish Fed speak. Yields were much less responsive to clearly dovish data, but we do not think Fed officials will be as dismissive. Most notably, both NY Fed President Williams and Fed Vice Chair Jefferson clearly pushed back on near-term market pricing for another rate hike. Pricing for the October meeting fell from ~16bp of a hike priced a week ago to about 5bp now. Data before each meeting will ultimately determine the path of policy rates, and our base case remains that this data will support leaving rates unchanged for the foreseeable future (until cuts resume in June 2027). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 Energy | Further up in September: Energy prices increased 3.8%M in September, pushing the year-on-year rate to 18.8%Y from 14.3%Y, a touch above our forecast (17.8%Y). We do not have details, but we expected that the strength would come from fuels (diesel), with also some upside from the progressive pass-through of TTF prices into retail electricity and natural gas tariffs. More upside to come: We also take on board the latest market-based forwards for oil and natural gas. Compared to mid-September, TTF prices have eased a touch, but brent is significantly higher in the short-term ( Exhibit 8 ). In addition, crack spreads between refined products (e.g., diesel and gasoline) and crude remain exceptionally high (see our analysis here), suggesting further upside retail fuel inflation. In the other direction, we also take on board the recently announced tax cuts in Germany, from October to December (see box below for more details). The SII revision allows an insurer-specific adjustment to the RCS capped at the lower of 1.05 and the ratio between RCS insurer portfolio (using the insurer’s own weights and average durations)and RCSreference portfolio, such that if the insurer portfolio produces a materially lower-risk corrected spread than the reference portfolio, the VA is scaled down accordingly: Crucially, the 1.05 cap is designed such that insurers very high-spread portfolios cannot massively increase their VA. What about the Macro VA? This is a mechanism designed for scenarios where spreads in one jurisdiction become materially more stressed than the EA-spreads overall – and it is the successor of the old country-specific enhancement. The key Macro VA trigger is whether the country-specific risk-corrected spread exceeds 130% of the EUR corrected spread. Crucially, the country 𝑅𝐶𝑆 is not simply equal to that country’s sovereign spread, but it’s rather built on a representative portfolio from debt instruments held to hedge the €-denominated insurance products sold in that country. records.text: 2 October 2026 Europe Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 8 Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) In response to the market pressures in 2022, the ECB announced a two -part policy. The first was flexible PEPP reinvestments. The second was the creation of the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI). In 2022, the maturing principal from the PEPP portfolio was being reinvested. When PEPP was created in 2020, a key feature/innovation relative to the APP was the flexibility to deviate from the capital key. In 2022 , the ECB viewed the pandemic as having left lasting vulnerabilities on the economy and these were judged to be contributing to the uneven transmission of monetary policy. This gave the ECB the basis to introduce flexible PEPP reinvestments as a stabilisation device. With PEPP reinvestments having now ended and it being perhaps legally difficult to justify re -opening a pandemic -era facility (at least without a very significant shock), the focus for any future action by the ECB is likely to be the Transmission Protection Instrument. TPI deployment: three-step process First, the ECB would conduct an analysis of what is driving the market pressure and identify whether it is country-specific fundamentals or not. Second, the ECB would determine whether a member state suffering pressures is eligible for TPI. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 12 The extreme weather conditions brought on by the 1997-98 El Niño caused significant disruptions to global agriculture, livestock, and fisheries. In western South America, particularly Peru and Ecuador, flooding destroyed cropland, damaged irrigation infrastructure, and disrupted harvests. Link here. At the same time, Indonesia and other parts of Southeast Asia experienced severe drought, which reduced agricultural yields, strained water supplies for irrigation, and contributed to widespread forest fires that further damaged farmland. Link here. East Africa also suffered extensive flooding that harmed crops and livestock, and flooding also triggered outbreaks of Rift Valley fever, a disease that affected both livestock and humans. Link here. High ocean temperatures off the South American coast also harmed fisheries. Weather-sensitive categories such as fresh fruits and vegetables, coffee, seafood, and livestock products can be particularly sensitive to El Niño disruptions. This drove Bund yields lower and saw G4 front-ends reduce hike premium alongside dovish policy communication from the Fed and ECB. The key test for the Fed path will be the next inflation print, but we still think there is an asymmetry towards lower yields as fundamental support for duration builds. In Europe, tightening financial conditions due to wider sovereign credit spreads warrants the slower hike path priced into the front-end, but elevated energy prices continue to complicate the choices for the ECB. records.text: ar). The envelope's bridge bonds would extend the latter, possibly to a different order of magnitude. Ranking the seven precedents by the legal character of their redemption source gives a clear order. Strongest is a tax: the Gulf bonds were repaid in four years from temporary corporate and oil surtaxes, the tax-cut bonds legislated the 5% consumption tax first and were repaid over 20 years, and the pension bonds draw on consumption- tax revenue from FY2014, interest included. Next is a levy: the GX fossil-fuel levy and emissions-trading payments and the child-support contributions have their payers and start dates fixed in law. Next is an inter-account transfer: the semiconductor/AI bonds depend on transfers from the FILP investment account, that is, on investment returns. The envelope's "mainly additional non-tax revenue" sits beyond even that lowest rung. Non-tax revenue is an expectation rather than a source and counting twice items already transferred to the general account up to a 70% cap, such as the foreign-exchange special account's surplus (a record JPY5,360.3bn in FY2024), would leave the redemption source nominal. EUR 54bn? EUR 43bn? 6½%? Unpacking the government’s arithmetic . On an unchanged-policy basis , the government estimates that the deficit would deteriorate by 1.1pp in 2027 (EUR 32-34bn), towards 6½% of GDP. The EUR 54bn of tightening the government has communicated overstates effective tightening in 2027 in two respects: • Around EUR 11bn reflects measures decided in 2025-26 whose effects carry into 2027. The EUR 43bn balance is the quantum of measures in the budget required to achieve the 5.0% deficit from the government’s unchanged-policy baseline. • More importantly, th is EUR 43 bn is measured against a deteriorating counterfactual, not against 2026. EUR 33bn is needed to simply prevent the deficit from drifting above its 2026 level. The nominal deficit itself falls by only EUR 6.8bn between 2026 and 2027. A more meaningful measure of the fiscal stance from an economic perspective is the cyclically-adjusted budget balance, which is set to improve by around 0.5pp (EUR 15bn) in 2027, despite a 0.3pp headwind from rising debt-service costs. This dynamic limits opportunities for younger, lower-income workers, who tend to switch jobs more often, including college-educated workers seeking employment, even when aggregate employment remains relatively stable and layoffs remain subdued. In addition, AI-related efficiency gains in sectors such as professional and business services may have reduced demand for some junior roles, further constraining employment prospects at the lower end of the wage distribution. The unemployment rate for 20-to-24-year-olds reached a decade high of 9.2% in 2H 2025 (Exhibit 14). The good news is that the unemployment rate for this group now appears to be past its peak. The unemployment rate among 20-to-24-year-olds with a bachelor’s degree or higher has also eased from recent highs (Exhibit 14), suggesting that the worst of the pressure associated with post-pandemic overhiring normalization and a low-hiring labor market may have passed. In our view, AI was not the sole driver of the rise in unemployment among younger workers last year. Had it been, we likely would have seen labor market outcomes for young college-educated workers deteriorate progressively this year as new AI models were adopted in the workplace. We expect AI’s labor market impact to remain relatively limited through 2026, with broader reallocation more likely in 2027. The stop condition is an allocation to super- longs, and for a fiscal-dominance regime in which the source stays at non-tax revenue, the size reaches several trillion yen and a super-long dedicated issue materializes, a 30y payer tail remains the insurance, as it has been since August. There are four touchstones: the Fiscal System Council's discussion of the envelope and the special account in October and November, the meeting of JGB Market Special Participants in late November on the FY2027 issuance plan, the budget proposal, issuance plan and tax reform outline in late December, and the dedicated bridge-bond bill submitted to the ordinary Diet session. The order in which the market should read them puts the redemption-source clause before the size. If a tax or levy is legislated the bridge becomes shorter and stronger; if it stays at non-tax revenue it remains long and weak. Either way the maturities that receive the supply are the same 2y to 10y and the direction of the core trade does not change. The largest metro municipalities that run major cities are geared to generate more than 80% of their own revenues through electricity, water, refuse and sanitation charges as well as property rates and other taxes. In sharp contrast, rural municipal entities’ revenue streams rely heavily (>70%) on government grants, subsidies and donations. In between are numerous towns, large and small. Grave going concern issues in local government finances: The bulk of party campaigns centre around improving collapsed service delivery and fixing broken municipal finance models. Overall, our assessment of Italy's medium-term fiscal outlook reveals both strengths and vulnerabilities. The process of fiscal consolidation needs to continue and could become more challenging politically as economic growth slows. The very constructive market view on Italy observed in recent years, reflected in several sovereign rating upgrades and a significant compression in risk premia, is probably approaching its limits. The upcoming electoral cycle is likely to introduce an additional layer of uncertainty. That said, a return to the levels of market stress witnessed in 2018 appears unlikely. There is now broad political recognition of the benefits associated with fiscal discipline and maintaining market confidence. Italy has tested investors' tolerance in the past and is well aware of the economic costs of a confrontation with markets and European institutions. Moreover, as discussed above, a number of structural buffers continue to make Italy more resilient than is often perceived. While public finances remain vulnerable and require continued discipline, other factors suggest Italian fundamentals are in a better shape than over past years. The final envelope and loan take-up fell short of the original ambition, while implementation delays and missed milestones left some funds undisbursed, especially in Eastern Europe. Relatively high final Recovery Fund disbursements should leave 2026 EU-Bond n issuance above the Commission’s EUR 180bn target. Issuance would reach a record high this year, above our forecast earlier in the year and the Commission’s plan. Even if we believe that the OAT-Bund spread is overshooting, a meaningful correction needs a catalyst. There is little the French politicians are likely to do to bring relief given the electoral calendar. That creates the conditions for a turbulent 6-8 months for OATs. The ECB, however, has options. The TPI backstop was introduced in 2022 to guard against spread volatility during the post-Covid hiking cycle. The concern then was BTPs with the 10yr spread to Bunds trading around 200-250bp. The current OAT-Bund spread is nowhere near that, although it is likely more about the speed of moves rather than the level per se. T o use TPI, the ECB would have to judge that the widening is not warranted by country-specific fundamentals, which we’d argue there is an element of in the micro sense, but less so in the macro (see discussion above). However, there is clearly a very high bar for usage including all the eligibility criteria. As we discussed last week, a much easier option for the ECB to bring some relief to OATs – should it wish to do so – is to push back on hike pricing given that was part of the catalyst for the widening (see above). records.text: European Rates Weekly 01 October 2026 Citi Research 11 EU’s liquidity surplus at the end of 2026 is expected to be around €28bn. As of 30 September, the EC has raised €701bn of long-term funding since the start of the SURE/NGEU programmes. It has disbursed €606bn under various programmes receiving EU funding (including the disbursements made on 1 October) meaning it has raised €96bn more in funding than it has disbursed so far. Accounting for the €106bn of submitted but not yet disbursed payment requests, its liquidity deficit (excluding Bills) is €10bn. However, The EU has a further €38bn to issue under its H2 26 funding plan, after which (if fully completed, as we expect) it should end the year with a liquidity surplus of around €28bn (Figure 10). Also worth noting that the EU has significantly increased its Bills issuance – which it uses for the temporary liquidity needs – of which it currently has €48.1bn outstanding (Figure 11). Figure 10. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 5 All three input indexes are not seasonally adjusted, and the BEA does not appear to seasonally adjust the resulting PCE software series. The new PCE software index can therefore be replicated as the weighted average of these three inputs. What does the change imply for inflation going forward? The clearest effect is on potential seasonality. In the last few years, CPI software has exhibited a pronounced acceleration during the first few months of the year. Because the CPI series previously drove the PCE component but now receives only a 60% weight, that seasonal pattern should have a smaller effect on PCE software inflation. As a result, we expect the usual early-year acceleration in software inflation—and therefore its contribution to core PCE—to be somewhat more modest in early 2027 than it would have been under the previous methodology. Beyond that seasonal effect, however, the directional implication for the inflation trend is less clear. Prior to 2026, the relevant PPI software indexes generally ran above CPI software inflation. That relationship reversed in 2026, with CPI running stronger than the PPI measures. If the earlier relationship reasserts itself, incorporating the PPI series would not necessarily lower PCE software inflation over time. Second-round polling indicates that it is also likely to win in the second round, most clearly against the far-left LFI candidate. The RN’s position on fiscal policy has evolved over the past few years. It recently proposed a golden fiscal rule to be submitted to a referendum if it wins the presidency. The RN has indicated its opposition to the current budget, but , more crucially, has signalled that it does not seek to force a censure of the government (de facto opening the door to the adoption of the budget, as happened last year). EA and UK inflation All eyes on gas prices We expect that the pass-through of the sizable increase in gas prices to consumers' utility bills will remain gradual. However, gas shocks tend to be more pervasive than oil, and the latest moves pose upside risks to EA and UK core inflation. • We use EA and UK price data, ending in 2024 and disaggregated at a very detailed level, to estimate the pass-through of gas prices to core inflation, which we currently forecast 0.6pp higher in the euro area and 0.4pp higher in the UK in Q4 27 than we had before the Iran conflict, respectively at 2.5% y/y and 2.4% y/y. • Our analysis shows that the transmission of gas supply shocks appears more widespread than oil supply shocks, with effects reaching a larger range of inflation subcomponents across food, non-energy industrial goods, and services. In our estimates, a gas shock that raises energy inflation by 1% after six months increases core inflation by around 0.1pp in the euro area and 0.2pp in the UK over a two-year horizon, almost twice the pass-through of an oil shock of equivalent magnitude. • This reflects differences in how oil and gas are used across the economy. In our previous note , we outlined what the budget might look like. Italy has signalled its intention to make use of the budget flexibility available for energy expenditure under the National Escape Clause. The new fiscal documents should provide further details. • Our analysis suggests that Italy could move from fiscal tightening of around 0.25–0.30% of GDP, as envisaged in the latest fiscal plan, to a broadly neutral fiscal stance in 2027 while remaining compliant with EU fiscal rules, thanks to the newly available flexibility. Based on the information currently available, the 2026 deficit could be lower than the current fiscal target of 2.9% of GDP, largely due to a higher-than-previously projected growth rate. We estimate that a 2027 deficit target of 2.7–2.8% of GDP, incorporating the full flexibility for energy expenditure, could be considered consistent with EU fiscal rules. Even deploying the precautionary ESM facilities would require a unanimous agreement among euro area mem ber states. The centre ground in European politics is narrowing, and politics is drifting to the right. Unanimity on burden-sharing policies could be more difficult to achieve. The third element of effective resolution is market confidence in the availability of the ECB balance sheet. Having risen from EUR1.2 trillion in 2007 to EUR8.8 trillion at the peak in 2022, the ECB balance sheet has now contracted by 33% as the TLTRO3 bank liquidity mature d and the QE asset portfolios passively roll off. Investors find it easier to re-engage in the market when the official sector is on the same side. No quick fix: While a DA-led coalition returned after LGE 2026 probably could not turn around Johannesburg quickly, we believe it could materially change the direction of travel (not to mention boost animal spirits). The most plausible first- term gains would likely be better senior appointments, tighter financial and procurement controls, stronger utility governance and a shift back towards infrastructure investment – the basics of the DA election manifesto (page 7). The appropriate benchmark would therefore be stabilisation and institutional repair, rather than turning Johannesburg into Cape Town within five years. Therefore, the real test in our view is not whether the DA can ‘replicate’ Cape Town in Johannesburg, but whether a DA-led coalition can create enough political stability to allow competent institutions to function. If it can, Johannesburg's trajectory could improve meaningfully within one term – though repairing its infrastructure and finances would be likely to take considerably longer. NEW

records.text: 2 October 2026 UK Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 4 Whatever can’t be explained by a typical MPC surprise can also shed some light on recent curve movements. For example, if front -end rates have risen by less than would typically be expected following a policy surprise, it may suggest that markets are placing more weight on tightening over f uture meetings rather than on an immediate move. We highlight one caveat: t his method tells us how much the market move resembles policy tightening . I t does not mean its economic effects will match those of an actual Bank Rate change, because the two can have different drivers and work through different channels. What do our estimates show? First, we find that the market has delivered the equivalent of about 40bp of surprise tightening. That is close to the cumulative insurance hikes we expect the MPC to deliver in the upcoming meetings. Second, as seen in Figure 4, the fit isn’t perfect . However, it tells us something interesting. Compared with a typical MPC surprise, short-term rates have risen by less, and ten -year yields have risen by more, suggesting that markets may be pricing hikes for upcoming meetings rather than an immediate move. In other words, much of this tightening depends on the MPC eventually delivering, a point we come back to in the conclusion. But with significant risk premium now embedded on both fronts, relief in energy prices and yield pressures are also now the clearest path to immediate relief. The tail scenarios of oil sharply lower or higher are outcomes that could pose n risks or opportunities for many investors, and we are often asked where leverage might be best for those oil-driven scenarios using our cross-asset frameworks. Compared to options pricing, oil higher or lower screens well for both tail n scenarios because oil implied volatilities have not risen to their old highs. High implied volatility in rates combined with the offsetting effects of growth and policy for rates in an oil shock mean that they do not screen as the best exposure to a move in oil prices. Europe’s energy exposures mean that Europe-linked assets across asset classes screen well. Low FX implied volatilities mean that European FX screens as well as, or better than, equities as an expression of either scenario. records.text: 14 Global Economic Weekly | 02 October 2026 Closer EU/UK relationship: Potential growth dividends but slow progress The government opened the door to a much closer relationship with the EU. A much closer EU/UK relationship can deliver growth dividends, but progress is likely to be slow. The government plans to use a UK-EU summit this year to lay out the different options for the UK’s long-term relationship with EU to find consensus around one. These options include customs union, single market membership or full re-joining. The economic gains would depend heavily on the degree of integration. The date of the EU- UK Summit is unclear, though there is some speculation that it could be on Nov. 20. There seems to be a twin approach on EU-UK relationship- the first to implement the limited reset already underway and the second to explore different options to getting closer to the EU. But it is unlikely that the EU would engage in serious negotiations on the EU- UK relationship until after the next election. We think the EU is likely to want the government to win a durable and fresh mandate from the public on a new EU/UK relationship before negotiating a fundamental change. Moreover, the debate on trade- offs or costs is unlikely to be easy. Meanwhile we can expect to hear positive noises from both sides. The downside error in our payroll forecast in September came from professional and business services payrolls. After downward revisions, they have fallen in each of the past three months. Along with weakness in hours worked and softer payroll incomes, they raise a question about softening labor demand—or supply. We have expected the breakeven pace for payrolls — the pace consistent with a flat unemployment rate — to be about 50k per month this year. Through June, the observed breakeven was close to our estimate; but it has fallen since then to average near zero over the past 12 months. July provided a firm start to the third quarter, while consumer confidence and services activity have also improved. The UK is no longer trading simply as an economy avoiding recession. It is showing genuine, if uneven, resilience. The complication is that resilience has not brought monetary relief just as the energy shock has lifted headline inflation. CPI reached 3.1% in August, although core CPI held at 2.6% and services inflation eased to 3.4%, suggesting that the shock has not yet become a generalised domestic inflation problem. Underlying services inflation was unchanged at 3.8%, but higher energy prices have pushed the expected CPI peak to 3.8% in early 2027. The Bank held rates at 3.75% with a 6–3 vote, with three members preferring an increase to 4%, but the change extends beyond the vote split. Our economists now expect 25bp hikes in November 2026 and February 2027, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%, before cuts begin in Q4 2027. records.text: European Rates Weekly 01 October 2026 Citi Research 6 The upcoming changes to the SII regulation have the potential to change the way insurers allocate to assets hedging their long-term liabilities. T o us, the biggest change is the revision of the Volatility Adjustment, making government bonds considerably more palatable than swaps from an ALM perspective. Solvency II is fundamentally a framework addressing how much economic risk can an insurer run relative to the capital available to absorb it. Assets 𝐴 are (broadly) marked to market; liabilities are valued as best estimate cash flows (BEL) plus a risk margin (RM); eligible own funds are the difference between the two (OF). Against them sits the capital requirement SCR, calibrated to a one-year 99.5% confidence standard. Interest rates change the present value of liabilities. Credit spreads impact asset values, but through the Volatility Adjustment (VA) or Matching Adjustment (MA) can also affect liability values. Broadly speaking, duration mismatches infer capital consumption, while diversification translates into capital relief. And assumptions about what happens beyond the observable yield curve can move both solvency and hedging requirements today. So, Solvency II does more than measure insurance risk: it validates a transmission mechanism from markets into insurers’ balance sheets, and from balance sheets back into markets. Catalyst.Metric: Diesel prices pass-through to headline and core inflation

records.text: On this basis, we estimate that the roughly 80% YTD increase in diesel prices, if it proves sufficiently persistent, could ultimately raise headline inflation by 20-30bp and core inflation by roughly 15-23bp, with the effects likely to emerge gradually as higher costs work through inventories, contracts and pricing decisions. If diesel prices instead reverse, realized pass- through could be materially smaller. Bottom line The exposure analysis and pass-through estimates point to a common conclusion. Diesel-price shocks are unlikely to remain confined to the energy components of the price indices, given diesel's central role in freight transportation and distribution networks. However, neither are they likely to generate a broad-based, one-for-one increase in inflation. Instead, the effects are likely to be concentrated in freight-intensive categories such as food, motor vehicles and parts, household furnishings, apparel, recreational goods, airlines, and delivery services, while the aggregate inflation impact is moderated by the relatively small transportation share of final prices, diesel's limited contribution to total freight costs, and incomplete pass-through to consumers. Ultimately, persistence is critical: a sustained increase is more likely to work its way through contracts, inventories and supply chains into consumer prices, while a short- lived spike may largely be absorbed along the way. UK | Fiscal & MPC speak: This week, Prime Minister Burnham announced the reform of the pension triple lock, from April 2030. The government's plan is to uprate pensions by the higher of inflation and 2.5%, while ensuring that the state pension keeps up with average earnings growth over time. Near-term savings are negligible - the OBR already assumes the triple lock guarantor is 2.5% into 2030 - and even the long-run savings depend on inflation and earnings growth. Any potential savings, it is important to stress, exist in relation to the counterfactual, where with the current triple lock, any major price shock boosts the state pension in a 2-step process, first as spot inflation rises, and then as wage growth adjusts with a lag. The level of French spreads has outstripped what can be explained by fundamentals, and moreover, is hard to justify even with the potential for a shift in forward expectations of French fundamentals. We have previously estimated the sensitivity of OAT-Bund spread to 1y ahead deficit expectations at around 10bp/1pt. Our economists have revised their expectations by 0.4% and 0.5% of GDP for 2026 and 2027 respectively, which by this measure only explains a small fraction of recent spread widening. Another possibility is that the market has revised its long-term expectation on French debt-to-GDP amid higher funding costs. The cross-country relationship between spread to OIS and debt-to-GDP , suggests a beta of about 1bp/1ppt of debt increase. This cross-country sensitivity has oscillated between 1 and 3bp/ppt since 2013, which suggests that even at the highest sensitivity the 50bp widening in September alone would represent an increase in the debt-to-GDP ratio of around 15ppts of GDP . Given that we haven’t seen incoming macro information consistent with such a shift in expectations, this suggests the latest leg of widening is increasingly driven by uncertainty and risk premium beyond fundamentals. The price index for business investment in GDP has been rising faster than consumer inflation, and some of these price pressures are directly boosting PCE inflation. Further escalation in energy prices and higher yields remain among the main risks to a more constructive market view from here. But with the market having now embedded significant risk premium in both energy prices and global front ends, relief in energy prices and yield pressures are also now the clearest path to immediate relief. Our baseline forecasts are for moderate relief in oil prices. But given the tails in both directions, we think it is helpful to think about where leverage might be best for those tail scenarios using our cross-asset frameworks. Those are among the outcomes that could pose the biggest risks or opportunities for many investors, depending on how they are currently positioned. We use our oil team’s price upside and downside scenarios as starting points. We benchmark an “oil relief” scenario as a ~25% fall in average short- and long-dated oil prices, and an “oil higher” scenario as a ~20% rise in average short- and long-dated oil prices. We assume that in the adverse “oil higher” scenario, longer-dated oil moves higher by more versus spot than in a “relief” scenario, as the market potentially prices more persistence in the supply shock. records.text: Global Strategy1 October 2026 ab 3 Having added long USD/PHP last month, we are now further adding long USD exposure via an equal weighted long USD/ZAR and long MXN/ZAR basket. USDZAR is up just 0.8% this year, outperforming the Euro, despite a sharp deterioration in its terms of trade, which we estimate at close to 3%/GDP . Historically this magnitude of trade balance deterioration may be offset by a 10% REER depreciation. We do not forecast such a move in the context of South Africa's improving fiscal credibility (we remain received 10y ZAR rates vs the US) and with potential for South African credit rating upgrades ahead, but we do believe that current valuations leave little room to absorb potential further widening in global credit spreads at a time of weak domestic growth. Elsewhere, we maintain our long-held shorts in CLP , PLN, IDR and PHP - currencies where real yields and external balances are mediocre, CBs look likely to disappoint tightening expectations and debt flows typically anchor external funding. We continue to target 64/18,500/1000/4.45 respectively into YE. We note that the latter three have external imbalances comparable to their 2022 lows. The repricing in real rates reflects expectations of both a higher neutral rate and more restrictive Fed policy. Higher neutral is consistent with signals from equity markets, as the S&P is only 1% off its all-time high. The key question at this point is, how much further could the moves go? In the front-end, things are cloudy but arguably well priced. The spread of 2y over 5y5y real SOFR – a measure of expected Fed policy restraint – has risen in line with the curve bear-flattening, but is not especially high, even after adjusting for term premia. As the June supplementary budget showed, JPY3.1tn of additional deficit bonds were absorbed by drawing down front-loaded refunding bonds with the JPY168.5tn calendar unchanged; the label does not set market prices. What distinguishes the envelope's bridge bonds from the seven precedents is that their redemption source is described as "mainly additional non-tax revenue", with no tax or levy written into law. Both the length and the strength of the bridge are weaker than in any precedent. Even outside the fiscal metrics, the supply lands on the curve. Under our assumptions (a continued third super-long cut and a calendar held at JPY168.5tn) it lands in 2s, 5s and 10s, the same zone the policy rate raised to 1.25% on Friday (Sep 18) and our path to 1.75% in January and April 2027 are pushing up. Morgan Securities LLC Global Markets Strategy FX Markets Weekly 03 October 2026 J P M O R G A N JPY FXO: Betting on 160 Yen price action of late has been at odds with the strong policy rhetoric. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 9 FOMC decisions ahead of elections While it is sometimes argued that the Federal Reserve may avoid policy moves immediately ahead of elections, the historical record does not show clear evidence. Looking at FOMC meetings held within 14 days of US presidential or midterm elections since the early 1980s, the FOMC has delivered rate hikes, rate cuts, and held rates, with decisions generally appearing consistent with underlying macroeconomic conditions and the prevailing policy cycle. Notably, there are several examples of the FOMC taking significant policy actions despite proximity to an election. One such case is November 1, 1988, when the FOMC raised the federal funds rate 25 bp just one week before that year's presidential election. A hiking cycle was already underway at the time, amidst core PCE inflation that exceeded 4%, and the November 1988 meeting was the fifth time the FOMC tightened that year. The Committee subsequently continued tightening in the months that followed. More recently, the FOMC delivered a 75 bp rate hike only six days before the November 2022 midterm elections amid elevated inflation and an ongoing tightening cycle. These episodes suggest that when economic conditions warranted policy tightening, the FOMC was willing to act, regardless of the political calendar. records.text: . One explanation argues that real rates are driven by a combination of fiscal deficits and the AI investment boom, coupled with QE unwinding. Some others suggest that monetary policy is the driver. The front end is the anchor that drives the long end, under the assumption that risk premium stays roughly constant. Can the two stories be true at the same time? Yes, and the best way to think about this is to ask what happens when private savings at a global level are not enough to finance an increase in global investment at the prevailing interest rate. What should happen in equilibrium is that the new market clearing real rate should be higher. This is effectively an increase in r*. Next, the connection with monetary policy. If r* is higher, an unchanged monetary policy stance represents, effectively, a loosening of financial conditions. This is what we have been witnessing over the last few quarters. Therefore, independently of the Fed’s resolve to bring inflation back to target, the equilibrium interest rate forces the market to reprice, and forces the Fed to acknowledge that a tighter policy stance is needed to keep financial conditions constant, let alone to tighten financial conditions at the margin. In other words, fundamentals are not driving the long end of the curve more or less than the expectations of what the central bank will do. LLC Global Economics Comment: Who Would Be Exposed to a Ban on US Diesel Exports? 2 October 2026 | 2:06AM BST Refined product margins have widened significantly since March, and the threat n of a US diesel export ban has raised concerns around further price increases. In this Global Economics Comment, we analyze how a ban on US diesel exports could impact growth and inflation across global economies. Our commodities team estimates that a US diesel ban would lower retail diesel n prices by $0.25/gallon per week of export bans, implying a modest 2-3bp drag on headline US inflation after a month. But this small decline in inflation would likely reverse and ultimately turn inflationary for consumers after roughly two months, since our commodity strategists estimate that each week of a diesel export ban would raise US retail gasoline prices by $0.3/gallon once diesel storage capacity is exhausted. A US diesel export ban could theoretically pose downside growth risks in Latin n America in the very near term. Using global input-output tables, we estimate that a sudden cutoff of US supply could lower GDP by around 1% in Latin America, although these effects would be dampened by inventory buffers and increased exports from the rest of the world. The labor force participation retraced more of the sharp drop earlier this year, though at 61.8%, LFPR is back to where it was in April and May and still down from 62.1% at the start of the year. LFPR increased 0.15 pp from 61.64% to 61.79%. The labor force increase of 485K in September also undoes some of the shift from employment to out of the labor force that has occurred, with employment rising 406K in September. But the 78K increase in the unemployed increase in the total labor force was enough to push the unemployment rate back up to 4.2%. Employment increased by 406k in September, bringing the 6-month moving average to 51K. Employment rose by 433k for prime-age workers, and by 162k for teenagers, but employment declined for 20- to 24-year-olds and for older workers. Within the other measures we watch closely to assess the degree of slack in the economy, the teenage unemployment rate rose 0.4 pp to 14.5% in September, hanging on to the gains over the last few years, and 1.2 pp higher compared to September of last year. The unemployment rate of Black or African Americans rose 1.0 pp to 7.0% in September, though that is down -0.6 pp from a year earlier. records.text: US Economic Weekly | 02 October 2026 3 AI demand Hyperscalers have dramatically accelerated capital spending, with capex projected to rise roughly 90% y/y this year and by a further 36% next year. This investment boom represents a sizeable demand shock that is already affecting portions of the price basket and could generate broader second-round effects over time. While this is an upside risk, the direct inflationary impact is likely to remain limited, absent meaningful supply constraints akin to those seen in 2020-23. Electrical equipment, computers, and electronic products account for a relatively small share of aggregate consumption (Exhibit 4), limiting the pass-through to overall inflation. Energy Geopolitical disruptions associated with the conflicts involving Iran and Russia-Ukraine have contributed to persistent shortages in energy and refined petroleum products. These shortages have already lifted headline inflation through higher gasoline prices and have contributed to stronger core inflation through categories such as airfares. If sustained, higher diesel and fuel costs could gradually feed into a broader range of consumer prices via transportation and logistics costs. Though this too is likely a limited upside risk since transportation services account for roughly 0.7% of consumption, while petroleum and coal products comprise an additional 1.2%. records.text: US Economics Weekly 02 October 2026 Citi Research 8 University of Michigan consumer sentiment could improve very modestly in early October data, to a still-low level of 48.5. We expect inflation expectations to fall slightly, reflecting stable and modestly declining gasoline prices over the last few weeks. Of course, as the level of prices remains high, sentiment could remain weak as the University of Michigan survey questions focus heavily on perceived purchasing power. We are also particularly interested in details of the survey that describe how consumers are responding to higher prices. While soft sentiment overall has not necessarily translated to weaker spending the last few years, actions around buying plans could be a better indicator of purchasing behavior. While we would not forecast hard data based on these survey details, more people saying it is a bad time to buy because of affordability issues this year compared to last year could be a reason that passthrough of higher input/energy costs to final selling prices has been more limited than the tariff passthrough in 2025. Some slippage looks likely. We see two main risks to the government’s 5% of GDP target. The first is political. Parliament is likely to amend some measures, particularly around pensions, benefits and taxation. If recent budget negotiations are any guide, this could push the deficit target towards 5.2 -5.3% by the end of the parliamentary process. The second is macroeconomic. The government assumes 1% growth in 2027, only slightly above our own projection, consensus, and the BoF ’s forecast (0.9%). But these projections predate the latest tightening in financial conditions and renewed increase in energy prices (the government assumptions were set as of August 24 – see here our note on recent developments). Those risks would affect execution rather than necessarily the budget voted by Parliament. We therefore distinguish the budget outcome from the eventual outturn: parliamentary changes could leave the target around 5.2 -5.3%; including further macroeconomic and execution slippage, we maintain our 5.4% deficit forecast for 2027. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 17 Investment Grade Reverse Yankee: Hyperscalers Continue to Tap Non-USD Markets Hyperscalers Diversified Their Funding Base And Tapped Numerous Currencies This Year While September saw a lull in AI-debt supply overall, non-USD hyperscaler issuance has continued to broaden. This month saw a £4.25bn four-part GBP deal from AMZN, only a few weeks after GOOGL's debut A$5.5bn six-parter in August. The recent deals bring total non-USD hyperscaler supply to $72bn: nearly a third of global hyperscaler supply this year. We maintain our expectations for further non-USD issuance from hyperscalers, with recent media reporting also pointing to potential EUR deals in the pipeline for 4Q. In contrast to 2025 when hyperscalers only tapped USD and EUR markets, less than 40% of non-USD supply this year has come in EUR. So far, issuers have diversified their funding towards five other currencies, including CAD, GBP, CHF, AUD, and JPY ( Exhibit 43 ). Given their relatively large deal sizes ( Exhibit 45 and Exhibit 46 ), these issuers have already become some of the largest issuers in many of the local IG benchmarks (Exhibit 44 ). However, since only two issuers (GOOGL and AMZN) have utilised the non-USD markets so far this year, sector concentration remains less pronounced in other markets, particularly EUR, AUD and GBP. The prospect of a plunging vote share for the ANC has become a widespread consensus, supported by polling (see page 6). The ANC’s national vote share in LGEs dropped from 54% in 2016 to 46% in 2021, and it is polling in the low 30s for November’s elections. As electoral decline intensifies existing divisions – and shrinks the pool of patronage and power available to hold the party together – the ANC has become increasingly disjointed, in our view. The lead-up to the LGE has revealed an ANC in an even more fragmented and factionalised state than we had previously presumed. We consider infighting to be both a partial cause and a symptom of the party’s failure to submit its full candidate list to the Independent Electoral Commission (see, for example, Daily Maverick, 14 September 2026). Declining support for the ANC and growing numbers of smaller parties and independents also increase the likelihood of coalition governments across metropolitan municipalities, secondary cities and local municipalities. Financial conditions have tightened considerably since the expiry of the US -Iran memorandum in mid-August. Two-year gilt yields have risen by around 45bp, with no change in Bank Rate. The move has already fed through to borrowing costs, including mortgages, consumer credit and corporate debt. This raises an obvious question for the MPC: if markets have already tightened on its behalf, does the Committee still need to hike? In this weekly, we look at three key questions: • What has driven the recent tightening in UK financial conditions? • How much Bank Rate tightening have markets effectively delivered? • Can the MPC rely on market pricing, or will they eventually need to hike? Since then, J.P. Morgan has continually adapted the framework to reflect changes in the global trading landscape. Over time, the methodology has expanded beyond the major developed economies to encompass emerging mar- kets, incorporated real exchange rate measures, and evolved toward annually updated trade weights that better capture changing patterns of global commerce (Figure 2). As we not- ed in our last major overhaul in 2015, maintaining our own EER framework allows us to apply a consistent methodology across a broad set of countries while retaining the flexibility to develop specialized measures that support our research on global and regional economic trends at daily frequency in both nominal and real terms. This report presents the latest update to the J.P. Morgan EER system. As we have done annually since 2015, the trade weights have been refreshed using the most recent UN Comtrade data available. This extends the underlying trade information through 2024 and updates the weights used in our indices through 2027. This year's update, however, goes beyond the routine annual revision. t post-pandemic energy inflation, we can see that annual gas and electricity inflation is slower to react to an energy shock in the UK (Figure 18). However, a recent change in the UK CPI basket will increase the speed of pass-through from an energy shock to inflation. Since February 2025, fixed energy bills are now being incorporated in the gas and electricity CPI baskets. Unlike the variable cap that changes every quarter, fixed bills allow consumers to fix the price of their electricity and gas for a period of 1-2 years. The weight of fixed bills in electricity inflation increased from 16% in 2025, to 32% in 2026, while for gas inflation, the fixed bill share increased 18pp to 34% in 2026. These shares have scope to increase further, as fixed energy bills become more popular with higher energy price volatility. A key feature of fixed bills is that prices offered by energy companies are allowed to change more frequently and not at set intervals. When we compare months without changes in the variable cap (non-Ofgem) in 2022 and 2026, increases can now occur monthly as energy companies adjust their fixed prices to the higher wholesale energy price outlook (Figure 19). 2 October 2026 9 Barclays | EA and UK inflation

Even before the recent market turbulence, we had documented that sovereign bonds in Europe were instead trading at their most ‘inconvenient’ range (Exhibit 8), likely a consequence of both high government supply and ECB QT. The acute market stress we’ve been witnessing in recent sessions adds to such concerns. It suggests that even if money market volatility is contained (Exhibit 10), broader market conditions tightening – in particular through EGB cheapening – represents another route to adjust ECB QT. We note that QT currently represents about 40% of net bond supply to the public (Exhibit 9). Market implications Taken together, we think the above can motivate a cautious stance on extending QT for the ECB. Excess liquidity may already be below the upper end of the plausible range of reserve demand and reserve demand can itself vary with time and market conditions. Further, even if the operational framework suggested liquidity injections through structural asset purchases should come last, we believe the change in convenience yields and subsequently the more acute stress on EGBs are signals worth considering. We treat the intervention threat seriously, and continue to think that the 160 line-in-the-sand in USD/JPY that BoJ/MoF has defended since July will hold. Three considerations are in order for JPY FXO structur- ing to benefit from intervention: • First, the proximity of spot to the well-policed 160 level, alongside generally higher Yen vols since the July inter- vention episode, means that a healthy amount of premium can be collected at present by selling the 160+ segment of the option-implied spot distribution, despite unfavorable forward points. • Second, currency markets continue to be staunchly USD- centric, which implies that selling JPY puts in low-beta Yen-crosses (e.g. CHF/JPY , SEK/JPY , SGD/JPY etc.) is both safer than doing so in USD/JPY in a stronger dollar environment, and also more premium-friendly due to less punitive forward points. • Third, collecting option premium by selling JPY puts with strikes north of 160 is less rewarding for its own sake, but considerably more for funding potential intervention ben- eficiaries (i.e. buying JPY calls) in the current Yen FX policy climate. records.text: US Economic Viewpoint | 01 October 2026 13 Maybe there is enough wealth for a rainy day for everyone However, aggregate household balance sheets remain far healthier than headline delinquency data or age- / income-based dynamics might suggest. Surging equity wealth pushed household assets above 10x of liabilities in 2Q 2026 (Exhibit 23). We see this as a continued tailwind for spending. But what would happen if there were a hiccup in stocks? In our view, balance sheets have plenty of buffer. If stocks were to fall 20%, the asset/liability ratio would only drop to 9.5, which is still higher than levels seen before 2H 2025. Additionally, liquid assets, including checking accounts, savings accounts and money market mutual funds, which should be more evenly distributed across the population, also remain elevated relative to liabilities by historical standards. Bottom line, the balance sheet picture is not one of broad-based household deterioration. Rather, aggregate household finances remain healthy even as pockets of stress persist among lower-income households that are more dependent on labor income and consumer credit. While this remains an important risk to monitor, aggregate consumption is still disproportionately driven by higher-income households, suggesting the macro implications are likely limited unless credit stress broadens materially. Page 25 Swap spreads defy the sell-off Steven Zeng, CFA | Strategist | +1-212-250-9373 Note: This note was originally published on 30 September 2026. Swap spreads have been resilient in the recent sell -off, with 5y through 30y spreads sitting near their recent highs. This stands in contrast to past sell -offs, when sharp increases in yields have typically pushed swap spreads lower, particularly at the long end. There are a few likely reasons for this. First, equity markets have also been resilient to the rise in yields, and as we’ve noted previously, long -dated swap spreads exhibit similar behaviors as a risk asset. Second, Treasury’s intervention last month, together with the prospect of further actions, has helped put a floor under spreads. The impact has been more notable at the long end, particularly in 20y , which has disproportionately benefited from larger buybacks. Finally, market technicals, including mortgage convexity flows and corporate rate locks, have also contributed to wider spreads. The front end has behaved somewhat differently. 2y spreads have underperformed since the September FOMC meeting. Front-end spreads are less sensitive to Treasury debt-management decisions and more closely influenced by funding conditions and T-bill valuations. As the market has repriced the expected Fed path sharply higher, bills have cheapened both outright and relative to SOFR, with that weakness spilling over

In a disorderly slowdown, markets might also anticipate policy support and public spending to cushion the adjustment, further limiting the long-end rally. The result would likely be a bull steepener, as lower r* and flight -to-quality demand pull long-end yields lower, but elevated term premia limit the extent of the rally. records.text: US Economic Presentation2 October 2026 ab 39 Source: BEA, BLS, Haver, UBS What next? More bumps in the road? The expansion rests on AI and the related wealth gains. We are now passing peak fiscal support to growth, and monetary policy tightening and fiscal policy turning to drag means the two will be working in the same direction for the first time in years. In contrast, we are past peak tariff impact on inflation and potentially peak energy shock inflation. Will energy prices fall back, or supply constraints rise? The labor market has been resilient, but details suggest more vulnerability than appreciated. If the AI investment or support for equities falters, the expansion itself would be at risk. The FOMC now appears headed toward further restraining the ex-AI economy. As a base case, we expect the FOMC to raise the Fed funds rate twice in 2026. We doubt that dampens the AI investment momentum, within which much of the investment is imported and not payments to domestic workers or income. Rate hikes will work to slow the rest of the economy. Plus: Can the geopolitical disruptions, policy uncertainty and volatility get out of the way? records.text: erall level of prices. If the price of oil goes up and triggers increases in other prices, the price of other goods and services not impacted by the shock can go down to compensate for the initial shock. In other words, only relative prices are affected. However, in practice, inflation measures go up when oil prices increase because prices are sticky, in particular to the downside. The change in relative prices to restore equilibrium occurs, at least in the short run, with some oil-related prices going up and other prices staying at the pre-shock level. Measured inflation goes up. If we apply the same argument to oil prices that go up and down without necessarily changing on average, that is, if oil prices become more volatile, the same effect takes place. It can be argued that the analogy is not good because gasoline prices, which capture the main direct effect of oil shocks, are very flexible, going up and down with oil prices. However, other indirect effects of oil prices, which impact other goods and services, can create more persistent inflation if oil prices become more volatile and contaminate core measures of inflation more persistently. These are prices that are impacted by oil prices but downwardly rigid: going up with oil prices but not reversing when oil prices fall.

records.text: ntegrated as the same financial instrument". What the market should track is therefore not the table by issuing law but the table by absorption channel and the calendar by maturity. The FY2026 issuance plan teaches the relationship between the two tables (Figure 7). The initial total of JPY180.7tn breaks down by accounting label into new bonds JPY29.6tn, the four bridge bonds JPY2.35tn, FILP bonds JPY13.0tn and refunding bonds JPY135.8tn, while toward the market it is absorbed as calendar-based market issuance JPY168.5tn, non-price auctions II JPY5.0tn, inter-year adjustment JPY1.2tn and retail JPY5.9tn. The supplementary budget approved on Wednesday (Jun 3) added JPY3.1tn of deficit bonds and lifted the total to JPY183.8tn, but the whole increase was absorbed in the inter-year adjustment (JPY1.2tn to JPY4.4tn), the cap on front-loaded bonds fell from JPY50tn to about JPY47tn, and the calendar stayed at JPY168.5tn. As the Finance Minister put it, the bonds were "deficit bonds in form, but the annual issuance plan was left untouched". New issuance rose JPY3.1tn on the books and market supply did not. Conversely, even if bridge bonds keep the headline for new bonds from rising, supply rises if they go on the calendar. The label does not set market prices; the calendar and the maturity mix do. As in previous years, we think passage of the budget through a parliamentary vote is likely to prove out of reach. As a result, in our view the government would effectively be left with three options: • Roll over the existing fiscal framework through a loi spéciale (special law). Such a solution is intended as a temporary stopgap rather than a fully-fledged budget framework and would therefore be ill-suited to operating for more than a few months. • Invoke, as in previous years, article 49-3 of the Constitution to force the passage of the budget bills without a vote in the National Assembly2 . In this case, adoption of the legislation would remain contingent on the failure of any subsequent motion of no confidence. This means that the government would likely need to secure either the support or the abstention of the Socialist Party or RN to ensure passage of the budget. Importantly, article 49-3 could be applied to an amended version of the government's initial draft. • Resort to budgetary ordinances (executive orders under article 47 of the Constitution) on the grounds that Parliament failed to complete its examination of the bills within the constitutional deadlines. According to NOAA and the BOM, the current El Niño has already reached the peak strength of the 2015-16 episode. That puts South and Southeast Asia at risk, especially production of paddy and rice, since the region accounts for ~58% of global rice production and ~80% of exports. Historically, strong El Niño events have had a significant impact on rice yields across the region, while policy interventions to curb rice trade have played a bigger role in driving prices. This year, water reservoir levels at the start of the season have been high, limiting the damage so far. However, weak rainfall is expected to cut rice output by 3.9% yoy in Thailand (to 20.3mn tons) and 4.6% yoy in India (to 147mn tons) in 2026. records.text: Alexandre Stott +33(1)4212-1108 | alexandre.stott@gs.com Goldman Sachs Bank Europe SE - Paris Branch European Daily: France—Tighter Financial Conditions, Slower Growth 2 October 2026 | 8:41PM CEST The surge in France’s borrowing costs (and accompanying decline in equities) has n led to a significant tightening in financial conditions. Our financial conditions index—which weighs financial variables by their effects on GDP—has tightened 50bp since August 1st, making it one of the 3% largest two-months move since 2000. The effect of tighter financial conditions on growth tends to be less acute in n France than elsewhere in Europe, because of longer debt maturities for households and corporates. That said, the tightening in financial conditions partly reflects the renewed increase in policy and political uncertainty, which is likely to be a headwind of its own. Moreover, the increase in interest payments hides the fact that fiscal policy will likely be contractionary next year, too, despite our forecast for the deficit to remain above 5% of GDP . As a result, we forecast little growth in France this year and next. Our tracking n estimate for Q3 stands at 0.09% qoq (non-annualised). We then look for growth to run below trend until after the elections, and are lowering our forecast by 0.2pp over 2027. The AI boom and bearish case for duration The economic impact of AI is generally understood as a demand shock and a supply shock that arrive at different speeds. The IMF described the buildout as “a positive demand shock today and a positive supply shock tomorrow, rolled into one”. Fed Vice Chair Jefferson made a similar point about the timing of these shocks and inflation, noting that if demand arrives first, inflation rises, while if supply-driven cost reductions arrive first, inflation falls. The current buildout phase is primarily a demand shock, lifting rates through both real yields and short -term inflation expectations while also increasing term premia. The most direct channel is aggregate demand. We wrote recently that the competition to win the AI race is pushing firms to invest aggressively and potentially overinvest. Chair Warsh noted at Jackson Hole that business capex is growing at its fastest pace since 2021, with more than half attributed to the AI buildout. Competition for electricity, construction labor, computer equipment and other finite inputs is creating price pressures in those sectors. Another key channel is the equity market. Earnings have grown significantly across many AI -related companies, while equities of others are discounting expected future payoffs in the form of higher valuations today. Hard data The initial release of August hard data presented a mixed outlook for the euro area. In Germany, retail sales staged a partial recovery following July’s sharp contraction (driven by an 8.0% m/m decline in automotive fuel sales ). While German fuel sales recorded flat growth (0.0% m/m) in August, overall turnover also included growth in food sales and an acceleration in non -food purchases. In contrast, French consumer spending disappointed, contracting by 0.5% m/m on the back of lower energy consumption and reduced food expenditure — a weakness reflected in French retail sales too, which fell by 1.1% m/m in August. While consumption has remained surprisingly resilient so far, the full effects of the recent energy and inflation shock may not have been fully transmitted to household spending decisions yet. In this respect, the sharp decline in consumer confidence recorded in September, a variable historically highly sensitive to inflation developments, is another signal suggesting that consumption growth could soften in the quarters ahead. records.text: mber ar our own estimates Will the budget pass? Likely, but risks remain: It is very clear that having a 2027 Budget Law in place before the election would benefit the next government (however it is made up): it could amend the initial budget in just a few weeks in summer 2027, while it would otherwise have to devote the first months of its term (maybe up until November-27) to pass an initial budget law for 2027. This is well understood, and the reason why we think the budget is likely to be adopted. To get there, the current government may need to resort to article 49.3 of the Constitution to pass the text without a vote each time this is needed in the National Assembly (see Exhibit 6 ). While doing that, the government risks facing a vote of no confidence which it can survive only if part of the opposition abstains (ie implicitly agreeing that the government remains in place). An alternative route would be parliament failing to reach a final decision on the budget and the government then implementing it by ordinances (in line with article 47.3 of the constitution). In that context, we attach a low probability to a scenario in which the budget would not adopted or implemented. We flag that in that case, the deficit would likely be on a path towards 6% next year (see more details here).

A 45bp rise in two-year rates – as implied by market rate expectations - is not the same as a 45bp hike in Bank Rate. Different parts of the curve move by different amounts when policy expectations change. So, we need to make a like -for-like comparison. We approach this by asking a simple question: what kind of MPC surprise would have historically produced a curve movement similar to the one we have seen since the 60-day memorandum expiry? To answer this, we use the UK Monetary Policy Event -Study Database (UKMPD), which identifies monetary policy surprises from market movements in a narrow window around MPC announcements. We extend the database with the latest data and our own calculations. For each maturity along the OIS curve , we regress its move around each MPC announcement on the identified policy surprise. Across more than a decade of announcements, this tells us how much each part of the curve typically moves in response to a 100bp policy surprise. These estimates give us a benchmark for how the curve normally reacts to a policy surprise. records.text: ly to be limited given its brief duration, but risks to growth and inflation have clearly risen. While near-term shortages and damage to crops are to be expected, it worth noting that the rain-reliant agricultural regions have been less affected, with rainfall pacing 7% below the long-run norm owing to El Niño. Reservoir levels have also surged as a result of higher rainfall, increasing buf- fers against an extended El Niño affecting next year’s crop. Inflationary effects remain a risk, particularly with ongoing supply shocks to energy, but are likely to be short-lived. The impact on growth could be more pronounced, with the histori- cal analogy of the 4Q11 flooding suggesting a ~6% q/q hit to activity. This analog remains imperfect, however, given the prior episode occurred in a period of strong activity and affected the central industrial basin, which accounted for 45% of GDP at the time. This year’s episode has thus far been more dispersed, in agricultural areas that represent a smaller share of GDP. A key area of concern is greenfield FDI regions in the east, given investment has been a major driver of growth. Tourist arrivals are also a source of vulnerability, rep- resenting a much larger share of the economy than before. In particular, arrivals from China are worth watching as golden week kicks off in the mainland, though these arrivals have already been hampered by weak incomes onshore and higher costs of travel this year. For now, we retain our UWs in THB and ThaiGBs

601/10/2026 Metropolitan municipalities the main battleground; turnout will matter Support for major political parties in Gauteng province metro municipalities Gauteng in focus: The province’s three metros – Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni – will be the focal point of the elections. Home to more than 12 million people and around one-third of South Africa's GDP, these metros have become increasingly fragmented, with no party commanding an outright majority. The election will test whether the ANC can arrest its decline, whether the DA can consolidate coalition support, and whether smaller parties can continue to play kingmaker in coalition formation (see page 10). Polling points to ANC weakness: Reliable political polling in South Africa is sparse, but the recent polls above indicate a continued loss of support for the once dominant ANC in key economic hubs of the country. Polling conducted July 2026, for instance, shows support for the DA in Johannesburg outstripping that of the ANC for the first time, and the DA looks within striking distance of a majority in Tshwane in the SRF poll, which we consider more authoritative. Recent polling for Ekurhuleni is sparse, but the political ‘newcomer’ to the LGE fray, MK, outperformed the EFF in the 2024 national and provincial election, indicating that it might be building up momentum beyond KwaZulu-Natal, where its support is rooted (see page 10).
