The week began with positive news on the inflation front, albeit mainly from revisions. The BEA released its methodological changes for three components of PCE inflation, revising prior inflation readings in the process. Revisions to portfolio management and advice, software and accessories, and legal services were larger-than-expected, reducing the year-on-year rate of core PCE inflation in July by 36bp, from 3.34% to 2.98%. Portfolio management and advice was the primary driver of the downward revision, accounting for 30 of the 36bp of the total revision. Revisions to software contributed another 6bp. Elsewhere, core goods inflation continues to reflect tariff payback and AI-related price pressures. At 0.03% m/m, readings on core goods continue to be roughly flat, in line with their pre-Liberation Day trend. In the other direction, computers and peripherals added to goods inflation again in August. Core services remained elevated, boosted by airfares and communication services. Following the larger-than-expected downward revisions, we nudged our inflation outlook lower. We expect headline and core PCE inflation to reach 3.4% and 2.9%, respectively, in December, versus 3.6% and 3.2% previously. This does not preclude renewed convergence in spending if lower-income real incomes and purchasing power improve, but it creates structural support for the upper arm of the K, especially in the face of other shocks in the labor market or affordability space. Could the equity wealth effect be broadening? One candidate explanation for the recent convergence in spending growth is that equity market gains may be reaching a broader set of households than in previous cycles. As housing affordability has become more challenging, some lower- and middle-income households may be increasingly turning to equity markets as an alternative vehicle for wealth accumulation. Consistent with this possibility, Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) data show that stock ownership has increased across nearly every income group since 2010, including among lower- income households. However, the available evidence remains suggestive rather than conclusive, and the latest SCF data are only available through 2022.

records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 15 The experience of cereals, fresh fruit and vegetable prices were a little more mixed. 12- month PCE inflation for cereals gently trended up in the 1997-98 period, but trended down in the 2015-16 period. 12-month PCE inflation for fresh fruits and vegetables generally moved sideways in both El Niño periods, albeit with some noise in the 1997-98 period. Looking across the individual components, inflation either fell over the period, or across the two periods the component inflation experience mixed at most. The coming 12 months could be different (there is a lot going on) but all told, the 1997-98 and 2015-16 experiences don't suggest that El Niño risks adding another upside inflation risk to the FOMC's plate. Is that counterintuitive? Perhaps not, given the lack of negative impact on domestic US growing. Also, economists at the FRB of Kansas City find that the effect of commodity prices on retail food prices has declined in recent decades, and that food-at-home prices are driven more by packaging, processing, and transportation dynamics, rather than direct agricultural production costs and other associated costs (link here). That could dampen the extent to which any El Niño-driven changes in commodity prices work their way into the consumer price index. records.text: pe On Tuesday, 29 September the OIS forwards were 2.27% for 1y1y, 2.73% for 2y3y and 3.56% for 5y5y, so the 1:2:1 fly was -37bp. Reading that as "the belly is rich" ignores the asymmetric spacing of the wings: the midpoints of the three forwards are 1.5, 3.5 and 7.5 years, so the belly is two years from the front wing and four years from the back wing. On a straightforward curve the fly equals minus two times the slope per year. With the slope at 22bp per year (129bp from 1y1y to 5y5y over six years) the straight-line value is -43bp, and the +6bp difference from the actual -37bp is the curvature: the belly sits 3bp above the chord joining the wing midpoints (2.70% at 3.5 years), or 6bp cheap in fly terms (Figure 26). There is no valley, only slope. records.text: US Economic Presentation2 October 2026 ab 39 Source: BEA, BLS, Haver, UBS What next? More bumps in the road? The expansion rests on AI and the related wealth gains. We are now passing peak fiscal support to growth, and monetary policy tightening and fiscal policy turning to drag means the two will be working in the same direction for the first time in years. In contrast, we are past peak tariff impact on inflation and potentially peak energy shock inflation. Will energy prices fall back, or supply constraints rise? The labor market has been resilient, but details suggest more vulnerability than appreciated. If the AI investment or support for equities falters, the expansion itself would be at risk. The FOMC now appears headed toward further restraining the ex-AI economy. As a base case, we expect the FOMC to raise the Fed funds rate twice in 2026. We doubt that dampens the AI investment momentum, within which much of the investment is imported and not payments to domestic workers or income. Rate hikes will work to slow the rest of the economy. Plus: Can the geopolitical disruptions, policy uncertainty and volatility get out of the way? records.text: MK: Registered as a party for the first time in December 2023, MK won 14.6% nationally in 2024 and 45.9% in the province of KwaZulu-Natal. Its defining metro battleground in KZN is eThekwini, where it won about 48% of votes in 2024. Outside KZN, Gauteng provides spoiler capacity (MK took 13.2% in Johannesburg in 2024). MK’s main weakness in the 2026 LGE is that it has zero council governance track record. The party’s ward-level organisation is the key unknown. EFF: The Economic Freedom Fighters have weakened nationally, from a vote share of 10.8% in 2019 to 9.5% in 2024, as MK has cannibalised its anti-ANC base in KZN. It remains a kingmaker in the three metros in the province of Gauteng (12–14% in 2024). The EFF has indicated it will not align with GNU partners and prefers a tactical bloc with MK to deny either DA control or ANC confidence-and-supply (see MISTRA Barometer II). If the EFF and MK combine in Johannesburg and Ekurhuleni, a DA-led coalition would become arithmetically very difficult. Patriotic Alliance: The GNU-aligned PA (its leader Gayton McKenzie is a government minister) won 2.06% nationally in 2024 and is contesting all 257 municipalities this year versus 80 in 2021. The PA currently holds seats in four metros, and it has been peeling votes from the ANC and the DA in Coloured and working-class Black townships. records.text: M Update 2 September ISM Manufacturing: Continued solid growth, continued supply constraint The manufacturing ISM slipped a tenth to 54.5 vs our forecast of 54.8 and consensus of 55.0. This was a solid reading, little changed from 54.6 a month earlier. The ISM index swung above 50 at the start of the year, indicating broadening activity, and the broadening persisted into September. The most direct measures of activity remained about as positive as they had: slightly slower growth in production but slightly faster in new orders and in employment. However, input pressures remain a source of strain. In September alone, the prices paid index jumped to 77.9 from 71.1, though still below the April high of 84.6. And supplier deliveries continued to slow, at about the same pace as in the prior month. (The supplier deliveries index has averaged 59.3 over the past six months and was 59.0 in September.) These are both probably the result of higher input prices. Energy is the obvious culprit, but manufacturers' commentary in the ISM release showed strains also in AI-related areas and in tariff-affected areas. From the computers and electronics industry, "Finding alternate sources of supply outside of China, local pushback on data centers in the U.S. and continuing material/component shortages are affecting business." records.text: rough audit of our trade weights back to 1970, and extended coverage to 11 frontier economies. Improvements include 1) a more rigorous approach to miss- ing data, 2) more accurate, concurrent manufacturing GDP data used in the export weights, 3) more precise handling of Euro area accession for individual exchange rates, and 4) extending our suite of EERs to include the broader set of frontier economies we have begun tracking in our EDGE publication. What seems on the surface like a straightforward exercise is made challenging because of missing (or in some cases, cor- rupted) data. There are different flavors of missing trade data (Figure 3). Russia last reported in 2021, Vietnam appears to have delayed reporting for 2024, Ghana skipped a single year, and Venezuela hasn’t reported since 2009. The US is shown as an example of a country reporting every year. When a country does not report, we have two options: fill-forward the prior year, or apply a “mirror” methodology. In cases like Vietnam for 2024, we simply fill-forward the prior year’s data, on the assumption their trade patterns did not change much year-to-year. For Russia, however, the war with Ukraine and subsequent sanctions have led to a major shift in trade partners, so filling-forward would be misleading. The “mirror” approach is to take the data reported by Russia’s trade partners and use that instead. This has led to a major shift in trade weights for Russia since 2022 (Figure 4). 0 20 40 60 10 12 14 16 18 20 22

Can Chair Warsh handle to communicate to the market that despite core PCE remains persistently high around 3% there is room to wait without paying a credibility cost? It seems too early to interrupt the hiking cycle, and it is unlikely that, relative to October, much can be learned to have more confidence by December that the economy needs higher rates. With the credibility game still alive and kicking, inflation that despite the soft surprise remains persistently high and energy prices still represent a relevant upside risk to inflation, the Fed should carefully weigh the pros and cons of skipping October. Can we ignore the dynamics of energy prices? The dynamics of the Middle East war is leaving market participants scratching their heads. On the one hand, there are reports signalling normalization of oil flows form the Middle East. Transportation costs are much higher but according to some sources oil is flowing. However, the price of a barrel of oil remains above $100. Moreover, every time there is a de-escalation of the conflict, the price of oil falls towards a higher floor, likely due to inventory depletion and less credible de-escalation attempts. records.text: As ECB QT drains excess reserves towards EUR2tn, and both the Fed and BoE n recalibrate their balance sheet policy, we take a fresh view of the liquidity outlook for the Euro area. The recent bout of acute widening in sovereign spreads creates renewed interest in the limits to ECB QT, as it relates to money market functioning and broader market health. ECB surveys, as well as revealed bank behavior over recent years, suggest that n excess reserves are likely already within the plausible range of equilibrium demand. We also argue that given reserve demand is state-contingent – increasing with uncertainty/volatility – there is a case for erring on the side of caution when assessing surveyed preferred levels of system-wide liquidity. Although money markets volatility has been contained, we show that ECB QT has n amplified the bond cheapening effect of government issuance over recent years across all EGB markets. In that sense, bond underperformance vs swaps thus overlaps with the risk from reserve availability, including for Bunds. This suggests that reserve stabilisation may not be so far off, in which case a n recalibration of ECB balance sheet policy – even as structural bond purchases were supposed to come last in its balance sheet normalisation process – is a possibility. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 21 OIG finds "deficiencies" but no misconduct or criminality The Federal Reserve's Office of Inspector General (OIG) released a report (link here) finding no evidence of criminal wrongdoing in the Federal Reserve's renovation of its Washington, DC headquarters. The report assessed the Board's oversight of the Eccles Building renovation project and its costs, which it stated " more than doubled from $921 million in the Board's February 2020 renovation budget to $2.018 billion in the Board's 2024 renovation budget (its most recently revised budget)." While the OIG's report outlined " deficiencies" in the management of the renovation projection and recommended corrective actions, the report noted, "We did not identify administrative misconduct during our evaluation." In addition, the OIG stated, "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the US Attorney General in accordance with the Inspector General Act." The renovation project and its cost overruns led the Trump administration's Department of Justice to issue grand jury subpoenas to the Federal Reserve and former Chair Powell in January. The stated focus was whether Powell had misrepresented aspects of the project in testimony to Congress. records.text: M Idea 2 Headline and Core Up What happened | Headline jumps (3.8%Y) and core increases a touch (2.5%Y): EA headline inflation increased to 3.8%Y in September, from 3.2%Y the previous month. The print was 10bp above consensus but in line with our updated forecast after the countries releases earlier this week (here). Core inflation increased to 2.5%Y from 2.4%Y, in line with consensus, but a touch less than we thought. The uptick in headline came primarily from energy (18.8% from 14.3%) with a jump of 3.9%M on the month. Food inflation rebounded to 1.4%Y from 1.1%Y, with a sharp increase of non-processed food inflation (4.0%Y from 2.7%Y). We suspect this reflects adverse weather conditions this summer. Services inflation increased to 3.2%Y from 3.0%Y, we think mostly because of the correction of a soft August print for tourism. Goods inflation eased a touch (1.1%Y from 1.2%Y). This is a surprise, as we thought it would continue to be lifted by IT products and lubricants. All in all, we continue to stress that EA inflation does not show strong evidence of a broad- based transmission from higher energy costs to core or food inflation. What drives the deficit down in nominal terms? We now move to a more conventional decomposition, setting aside deviations from trend, and us ing figures published by the High Council of Public Finances (the government's economic and budgetary report – RESF – was not available as we went to press). Viewed in nominal terms, the adjustment looks much smaller than the headline measures suggest. Public expenditure is projected to rise by around EUR 41bn (1.3% of GDP) in 2027, while compulsory levies increase by around EUR 48bn (1.5%), including EUR 17bn (0.6%) from discretionary measures. This also illustrates the limits of measuring savings against a counterfactual trend. Healthcare spending, for example, still rises by EUR 5.5bn despite EUR 5bn (0.2% of GDP) of savings relative to trend. The restraint comes from a mix of under - indexation and outright policy measures: around EUR 3bn from the pension freeze on the social security perimeter, healthcare savings, a freeze in the civil -service point d’indice, and tighter transfers to local authorities. On revenues, the largest measures concern employer social-contribution exemptions. The same macro development can therefore help the index and hurt the median UK company. This is where cash conversion becomes more than a quality screen. The FTSE 250’s sharp free-cash-flow improvement strengthens the funded mid-cap opportunity, but higher floating-rate exposure and domestic duration still argue against buying the cohort indiscriminately. The preferred combination is earnings upgrades, cash conversion and financing resilience. Aggregate EPS growth without those attributes remains vulnerable to the higher hurdle rate. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 19 Reverse Yankee Spread Performance The performance of hyperscaler new issues this year has been mixed, with many deals seeing spread widening in the first 20 days of trading (Exhibit 47 ). Since July, hyperscaler new issue performance has been relatively more benign, mirroring the better relative performance of these issuers' secondary bonds. Even so, hyperscaler EUR bonds still trade wide to the AA benchmark, with AMZN trading closer to the A-rated index (Exhibit 48 ). The underperformance remains particularly pronounced in the long-end, with these issuers' curves screening steep compared to the overall market (Exhibit 49 ). In the APAC LC space, GOOGL's AUD bonds spreads were tighter post issuance in August, outperforming the AUD LC corp bond market (Exhibit 51 ). In contrast, GOOGL's JPY bonds saw spread widening in the past two months, significantly underperforming the JPY LC corp bond market ( Exhibit 52 ). On a cross-currency adjusted spread basis, EUR hyperscaler bonds still trade modestly tight to their USD bonds, though the differential has narrowed since late August (Exhibit 50 ). As we have discussed elsewhere, this repricing has been sup- ported by elevated energy prices, resilient growth, sticky inflation, higher perceived neutral rates, and some position unwinds. While we think current pricing is generally excessive versus our forecast (Japan aside), we are not keen to fade it aggressively. records.text: 2 October 2026 Fixed Income Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 Circuit breakers To sum up, OATs are now cheap under the same valuation framework that identified them as being very expensive post -GFC. There is also evidence of positioning dynamics that could lead to a self -reinforcing widening of OAT spreads, especially at the front end of the curve. Finally, the RN, which is currently leading in the polls, has shifted towards a more conservative fiscal stance and opened the door to the adoption of the current budget. Taken together, the evidence points towards an overshoot in OAT spreads. What are th e possible circuit breakers? The ECB has developed a post -GFC toolbox to enable it to deal with unwarranted tightening of financial conditions. It has demonstrated its flexibility on numerous occasions in engineering credit easing via the TLTROs (which are a way of decentralising liquidity provision) and the PEPP (which all owed bond purchases away from capital keys). It has since enshrined some of these tools in the TPI. Ultimately, any ECB intervention is predicated on its assessment of unwarranted and disorderly market dynamics. The flattening of the spread curve was a key element that triggered Draghi’s “whatever it takes” moment and the OMT. Thus, the ECB could justify at least a verbal intervention by pointing to evidence that changes in the market structure have amplified the recent moves and led to a significant flattening of spread curves that is unwarranted by fundamentals

Fiscal policy flips to a drag in 2027, working in the same direction as monetary policy. That has not happened since both fiscal and monetary policy supported growth during the pandemic. • Bond markets have lost their anchors amidst less FOMC transparency, a new voice and reaction function. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 49 FOMC meeting minutes preview: the shift We expect the September FOMC meeting minutes to reflect the hawkish shift underway among FOMC participants which culminated in a unanimous decision for the first rate hike since 2023. The meeting discussion as captured in the somewhat sparser Warsh-era minutes likely reflects the general assessment among participants that inflation remains too high and has failed to display progress toward the Committee's 2.0% objective. The strong retail sales report released during the meeting likely only highlighted the resilience of the expansion, the perception of little risk to raising rates, and the narrative that domestic demand remains strong. We also expect that almost all participants will say further monetary policy tightening is needed. Discussion: resilience, too-high inflation, no longer all supply shocks The FOMC statement was expectedly brief but offered a template for phrases expected to occur in the minutes discussion. "Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little. Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."

Headline PCE inflation started January 2015 at 0.0% and rose to 1.7% by December 2016, while core PCE inflation rose from 1.2% to 1.6% in that period, still below the FOMC's 2 percent target. Naturally, a lot else is going on in inflation dynamics than weather effects. Looking at specific categories, El Niño fingerprints are difficult to discern in the detailed PCE price data. In many related categories, the components' inflation drifted lower through the El Niño period. Both El Niño episodes suggest that the most visible effects were category-specific and temporary, rather than a sustained source of inflation. For example, in both the 1997-98 and 2015-16 El Niño periods, PCE prices for food for off- premises consumption (groceries) decelerated on a 12-month basis, and in the 2015-16 period, was also outright deflationary. For purchased meals and beverages, the categories' inflation peaked before El Niño began, and both trended down (disinflation) over the period. Similarly, considering feed costs, on a 12-month basis, beef and veal PCE inflation also declined over both El Niño periods. Warming ocean temperatures could pose a risk to fisheries, but 12-month fish and seafood PCE inflation still moved sideways in the 1997- 98 period. Public expenditure is projected to rise by around EUR 41bn (1.3% of GDP) in 2027, while compulsory levies increase by around EUR 48bn (1.5%), including EUR 17bn (0.6%) from discretionary measures. This also illustrates the limits of measuring savings against a counterfactual trend. Healthcare spending, for example, still rises by EUR 5.5bn despite EUR 5bn (0.2% of GDP) of savings relative to trend. The restraint comes from a mix of under - indexation and outright policy measures: around EUR 3bn from the pension freeze on the social security perimeter, healthcare savings, a freeze in the civil -service point d’indice, and tighter transfers to local authorities. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 10 El Niño — here we go again? The probability of a very strong, or "super," El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) event during fall and winter 2026-27 has now risen above 90%, according to NOAA's Climate Prediction Center last week (link here). This natural cycle, which can interrupt climate and precipitation patterns around the world, has been strengthening since it was first declared an El Niño in June, according to NOAA data as of early September (see the chart at the link here). This year's El Niño has been tied to warmer-than-average water temperatures along the equator in the Pacific Ocean, an active Pacific hurricane season, an Atlantic hurricane season without any named hurricanes to date, wildfires in Indonesia and low water levels in the Panama Canal (link here). A comparable very strong "super" El Niño with sustained strength was in 1997-98. Will history repeat itself? Based on that experience, what might we expect for US weather, crops, or inflation? What is El Niño? El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern characterized by a weakening of the easterly trade winds over the tropical Pacific Ocean, allowing warm surface water that is normally concentrated near Indonesia and Australia to spread eastward across the central and eastern Pacific. records.text: The Q3 2026 earnings season will kick off during the week of October 12. By n the end of October, roughly 70% of S&P 500 market cap will have reported. Most of the hyperscalers are scheduled to report during the last week of October. Consensus expects S&P 500 year/year EPS growth of 27% in Q3. This n compares with realized growth of 33% in Q2, excluding some accounting distortions. Analyst estimates show the beneficiaries of AI infrastructure spending accounting for over 50% of S&P 500 EPS growth this quarter alongside hyperscaler capex growth of 116%. We expect most companies will once again surpass consensus earnings n estimates this quarter. For the median S&P 500 stock, consensus estimates show year/year EPS growth slowing from 14% in Q2 to 9% in Q3. Input cost pressures will likely limit the magnitude of sequential margin expansion in Q3, and the dollar should provide a modestly smaller tailwind to S&P 500 revenue growth this quarter than last quarter. However, recent economic growth data have been strong and S&P 500 earnings revision breadth has remained positive. AI monetization and productivity will remain key themes during the Q3 n earnings season. Last quarter, hyperscaler cloud revenue growth accelerated to 48% alongside surging revenue backlogs, boosting investor confidence in the likely return on AI investments. records.text: Jiuk Choi 1 October 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Emerging Markets Weekly: Find an Idea from UST Yield The stronger US dollar following the resumption of Fed rate hike expectations has weighed on EM FX. Flows into EM assets are differentiated, as we see increased inflows into bonds, while inflows into equit ies remain somewhat muted. Investors have increased their allocations to short-tenor EM sovereign bonds, while reducing flows at the long end. This reflects tactical carry demand rather than broad conviction in EM duration. Also, we expect the current oversold conditions in USTs to ease in October given how much the market has already priced into the curve. Similar historical episodes suggest that high-carry currencies with favorable terms of trade, such as MXN and BRL, would benefit from an easing of monetary policy repricing. By contrast, IDR and ZAR depreciated the most based on historical price actions. Given this, we initiate a short ZAR position with selecting MXN as the long leg of the cross. We believe that resilient terms of trade and an expanding trade surplus driven by stronger US growth should support MXN, although a potential US diesel export ban remains a risk. Our model of the wholesale costs component as of this writing expects an increase of 11% q/q in Q1 27, which would be implemented in January. Energy companies also forecast the Ofgem cap, and have much better visibility on projected changes in non-wholesale costs. In recent quarters, we have underestimated the cap change when forecasting solely non- wholesale costs, while energy companies have correctly been able to predict the non-wholesale part of the cap. For example, EDF forecast the Q1 cap increasing 20% q/q, which we reconcile with our own model forecast by assuming it forecast increases in non-wholesale costs. Prior to the conflict, energy companies had flagged that increases in investment costs would drive up energy bills, even if wholesale costs fell. These tensions create a structurally higher outlook for UK energy inflation even if wholesale costs were to subside with a resolution to the Middle East conflict. At the time of our last inflation forecast update, our model expectation for wholesale cost changes was 15% q/q, and we added 5pp to the quarterly increase to account for increases in non-wholesale costs, reaching a 20% q/q assumption for the Q1 2027 cap. records.text: Cayla Seder 30 September 2026 1 Insights Classification: General, Complimentary Material DM FX Weekly : It’s a higher - for - longer world Key themes this week: Markets are not getting any reprieve from yields. Every day seems to bring fresh headlines about long- end yields reaching new multi-decade highs. In many ways, this environment makes sense. The war in Iran remains ongoing, keeping upward pressure on commodity prices and reinforcing expectations for higher interest rates. At the same time, growth, at least in the US, has become less sensitive to higher rates as AI-driven investment is increasingly supported by cash-rich semiconductor companies and hyperscalers. As a result, rising rate expectations are not yet translating into broad concerns about economic growth. Importantly, real-money investors have not shown meaningful demand for Treasury duration, suggesting they are not stepping in to buy the dip. This points to a genuinely "higher-for-longer" environment rather than a temporary rate shock. Our data show this dynamic influencing investor behaviour. While outright risk aversion remains limited, our Behavioural Risk Score has oscillated between -2 and +2 in recent weeks, signalling growing hesitation to add risk from current levels. This environment has proven a tailwind for the USD, pushing USDNOK through our stop/loss levels. Instead of reupping our USD short though, we have opted to keep our position neutral for now. records.text: we trust, dated 10 September, we project external financing of USD20bn in 2027 (an increase from USD12.3bn in 2026). Specifically, we expect a notable rise in multilateral borrowing. Market expectations are high for potential agreements with multilateral institutions (including the IMF) to provide significant financing support, which would alleviate supply pressure in both Coltes and hard-currency bonds. Despite current uncertainties, we are increasing our multilateral lending forecast for 2027 to USD10bn, up from USD4.9bn in 2026. The government's potential to swap multilateral loans into COP-denominated debt to cover its FX risk, by paying the long-end COP basis could drive the long-end basis upward. Historically, there is a positive correlation between the government's multilateral financing inventory and the COP basis (Figure 1). ECB Commentary The most important ECB commentary this week came from President Lagarde’s interaction with MEPs at the ECON committee. • Lagarde said, “we do not react to energy prices”; instead, the ECB reacts to the risk of higher energy prices becoming embedded in inflation. This is an attempt to break the 1:1 link between terminal rate pricing and energy prices. • There are “no signs yet that inflation is becoming embedded”. Th is suggests the ECB is not overly worried by the recent rise in CES household inflation expectations , and the absence of embedded inflation remains significant for the path of monetary policy. • “Since our last meeting long-term interest rates have risen notably”. This will “slow growth and reduce pass through by more than projected in our September forecasts”. This comment suggests longer-term rates are helping the ECB push back against inflation risks, reducing the likelihood the ECB will need to hike as far as markets are pricing. • Lagarde mentioned “a measured response as appropriate”. Our interpretation of “measured” is (1) a quarterly pace of hikes and (2) hiking to no more than a mildly restrictive stance. Lagarde mentioned in the summer that the ECB was delivering a “measured” response but failed to say this again at the September press conference. Although yields remain elevated, market expectations for the October FOMC meeting fell substantially with just ~5bp of hikes priced for later this month. Revisions lowered core PCE inflation by close to 40bp, with the 3-month pace now at 2%. Job growth in September slowed and was revised lower in previous months, while the unemployment rate rose modestly to 4.2%. Growth remains resilient, but strength is heavily focused in AI-related parts of the economy. Consumer/household data is much more modest. We do not see signs that pockets of strength are leading to any retightening in the broader economy as wage growth continues to slow. We think Fed officials will be increasingly uncomfortable weakening the broader economy further as the labor market is already not a source of inflationary pressure. The more volatile phase of the rates selloff over n recent weeks marked a departure from the more fundamentally driven move through much of the summer. Micro factors related to de-risking and managing negative convexity/CTD switch risks have potentially played supporting roles, but we think the magnitude of flows directly attributable to these factors should have diminished given mortgages have become less negatively convex and how actively asset managers appear to have managed their duration risk in recent months. After the recent vol pickup, we now see the level of implied vol at the upper end of fair value given macro risks, reducing the risk of further spikes. How quickly vol can retrace from here though depends on the path for yields—even after the initial spike following a large rates selloff, unless yields stabilize, implied vol typically remains close to the highs (Exhibit 1), especially on shorter tails. Only following the local peak in yields does vol typically mean revert and retrace the spike. In that vein, we think implied vol for now can remain elevated until the macro picture provides some broader, gradual relief. From current levels of policy pricing, we also are beginning to see risks associated with the left-tail becoming a more meaningful source of realized vol, although our base case remains for any relief rally to be grinding. records.text: iew: Minutes to show degree of hawkishness The minutes should provide greater insight into the Fed’s decision to raise rates in Sep. While the committee voted unanimously, investors will be looking for clues on whether there is meaningful disagreement over how much additional tightening may be needed. Does the FOMC view the move as a midcycle adjustment, or are there broader concerns that could warrant a full-blown hiking cycle? We also expect the minutes to shed more light on how policymakers interpreted the latest inflation data. Data review: Economic growth even better after revisions 2Q GDP growth was revised up by 70bp to 2.2% in its final estimate. Revisions were also positive elsewhere, with 1Q GDP growth raised by 40bp to 2.5% and annual growth in 2024/25 revised higher. Incorporating these revisions, we have marked our 2026 GDP forecast up by 20bp to 2.3% on a Q4/Q4 basis. The broader implication is that underlying economic momentum was even firmer than previously estimated, which, in our view, points to stronger productivity growth and a higher neutral rate. Viewpoint: Midterms are not a gamechanger Our base case remains a divided Congress. The key message is simple: this is not 2024. We see very little chance of the midterms producing policy changes large enough to materially alter the growth, earnings, or AI investment backdrop over the next two years. As mentioned above, the UK is reliant on gas generators to meet the marginal demand for electricity, and therefore the two exhibit a strong correlation (Figure 10). However, the UK has an idiosyncratic component due to the Ofgem cap, which regulates changes by energy providers in variable gas and electricity bills to a specific model of wholesale costs (for more details on the cap, see here). The cap for each quarter is calculated in a conditioning period of around three months, which begins roughly four months before the cap is to be introduced. As the cap is regulated to only change in the first month of each quarter, and energy moves affect the cap with a lag due to the conditioning period, traditionally the Ofgem cap has sheltered consumers from price changes in gas and electricity markets with a long delay. For example, looking at post-pandemic energy inflation, we can see that annual gas and electricity inflation is slower to react to an energy shock in the UK (Figure 18). records.text: vely, gains in these relatively blue-collar industries matter because labor income, rather than wealth, remains the primary driver of spending decisions for most lower- income households. Consumers have more cushion than previously thought Recent GDP and income data revisions from the BEA suggest households accumulated substantially more savings than previously estimated. Personal saving since mid-2021 was revised up sharply, with savings over the past 12 months marked higher by roughly $320bn (39%), mainly due to higher estimates for private wage & salary income, and downward revisions to tax payments and nominal spending. As a result, the July 2026 saving rate was revised up to 4.6% from 3.0% previously. We’d also note that the nominal spending revision was mostly due to the methodological changes for inflation, rather than weaker real spending. The latter was minimally affected by the revisions and came in at a strong 2.6% y/y in Aug ’26. More recently, the personal saving rate fell to 4.1% in August, its lowest level since 2022. This coincided with strong consumer spending and flat real disposable income. Together, these data suggest households have a larger financial cushion than previously believed, potentially providing an additional buffer for consumer spending.

records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 As previously announced by the BEA, three PCE components were revised as part of the annual national accounts revisions: portfolio management and advice, software and accessories, and legal services. Ahead of the release, the broad expectation was that these changes would lower the year-over-year rate of core PCE inflation through July by roughly 10–20bp. The actual revision was considerably larger. July core PCE inflation was revised down 36bp, from 3.34% to 2.98% y/y. Portfolio management and advice was by far the largest contributor, accounting for 30bp of the total revision, while software accounted for the remaining 6bp. Following the revisions and the August release, core PCE inflation is running at a 2.05% three-month annualized pace, down from 2.30% in July, and at a 2.74% six-month annualized pace, down from 2.93%. On a 12-month basis, core PCE inflation stands at 3.01% in August, following a revised 2.98% in July. The revisions were therefore a meaningful dovish surprise. But the more important questions for the outlook are different: What exactly changed in the BEA’s methodology? How should we modify our forecasting models? EU Debt Supply in 2026 and Beyond Uncertainty around the scale of EU debt issuance has remained elevated throughout 2026. The European Commission’s funding plan set a EUR 180bn EU-Bond issuance target for the year, equivalent to around 1% of EU GDP , of which approximately EUR 140bn has already been issued. We estimate that funding needs related to the Recovery Fund and other existing programmes, including Macro-Financial Assistance for Ukraine, SAFE and smaller facilities, could total EUR 242bn. Adding EUR 43bn of redemptions and assuming no programme-loan repayments produces gross funding needs of around EUR 280bn. However, after accounting for the EU debt-management office’s pre-funding and the stock of EU-Bills already issued, we expect around EUR 60-70bn of additional EU-Bond issuance before year-end. This would leave full-year issuance above the Commission’s target of EUR 180bn, marking a record annual total (Exhibit 5). The uni-grid shouldn’t change the risk profile of the loans issued by the GSEs, however, and so the lost revenue seems like an issue if they aim to maintain the same ROE. It’s not obvious to us that a backdoor cut in g-fees is the end goal here; the Administration probably would have gotten a clearer headline if they’d just lowered base g-fees or reduced LLPAs across the board. So, we lean towards thinking that annual g-fees will need to be raised to offset the reduction in LLPAs. That means that, while the grid is now effectively flatter and today’s weaker credit borrowers may have less of an elbow shift, the overall impact could be some- what muted. This will be hard to observe in real time, as we typically rely on the quarterly GSE disclosures to try to tease out the LLPA vs. annual g-fee mix. But of course, we’ll also be monitoring X for any updates indicating an intentional policy shift on this point. records.text: North America Economic Research 02 October 2026 J P M O R G A N www.jpmorganmarkets.com Economic and Policy Research Michael Feroli (1-212) 834-5523 michael.e.feroli@jpmorgan.com JPMorgan Chase Bank NA The September employment report came in a little bit softer than expected but overall wasn’t too worrying. Nonfarm employment increased only 29,000 last month, and the gains for the prior two months were revised down by a net 60,000. That left the 3-month average gain at 51,000 last month, which is close to most estimates of trend monthly growth in the labor supply, i.e. breakeven job growth. The unemployment rate rose from 4.1% in August to 4.2% last month but at higher precision was up only 3 basis points. However, this occurred alongside a welcome 0.2pp increase in the labor force participation rate to 61.8%, bringing with it an increase in unemployed new and reentrants to the labor pool. The average workweek held onto the August increase and was unchanged in September at 34.4 hours, a positive signal about labor demand that should mollify concerns caused by the miss on headline jobs. Wage growth has been decelerating, a trend which continued last month as average hourly earnings were up only 0.1% for the month and 3.0% over a year ago. That deceleration should give comfort to Fed policymakers that the economy is not overheating in a way that calls for a hurried rate hike cycle. records.text: M Idea 6 Oil Tracker: Running out of buffers Our baseline outlook for the US economy assumes a permanent oil risk premium. The renewed pressure on energy prices has dragged the world into the seventh month of this prolonged energy price shock. Historically, episodes of acute geopolitical or physical supply disruption have mostly lasted 3–6 months, with the notable exception of the 1978–79 oil shock and its aftermath. As buffers such as higher U.S. exports, weaker Chinese imports, and ample inventories begin to fade, we update our oil tracker to highlight developments and trends that matter for U.S. economic growth. The latest data suggest that crude oil inventories in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) have fallen further, while both U.S. crude oil imports and exports have remained on an upward trend. Crude oil prices have continued to rise, while diesel margins have widened further. We convert diesel and gasoline prices to a per-barrel basis for a better comparison: diesel was at $216.13 per barrel, while gasoline was at $190.06 per barrel. The gap between gasoline and crude oil prices has remained broadly unchanged, whereas the gap between diesel and crude oil prices has continued to widen since early July. Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT) OMT was created as a policy tool in the wake of Mario Draghi’s “whatever it takes” verbal intervention in July 2012. OMT is the ECB’s ultimate sovereign backstop, for when a euro area member state has been cut off from market financing. OMT is conditional on the member state in question being under a full ESM bailout programme or a precautionary financial assistance programme (with primary market purchase agreement). OMT is not relevant in the case of France today. records.text: We have made mark-to-market changes to our labor outlook. We expect job growth to average 77k/mo in ‘26, comfortably above breakeven, allowing the u-rate to edge down to 4.2% in 3Q26. The labor market remains stable, and we expect that to persist, with only modest effects from policy tightening in ‘27. Job growth is likely to average around 60k in ’27 and ‘28, with the u-rate falling to 4.1% by 1Q27. While immigration-related constraints should keep labor supply growth subdued, easing tariff uncertainty has reduced downside risks to demand. AI's labor market impact is likely to remain limited through ‘26, with broader reallocation more likely in ‘27. Fed: Hike first, ask questions later • As expected, the Fed hiked by 25bp at the Sep meeting, with a strongly hawkish message. The statement dropped language linking inflation to supply shocks (I.e., no more excuses), while the SEP showed stronger growth, higher inflation and a lower u- rate despite two hikes this year. Chair Warsh reinforced the message, making it clear that the job is not done. In our view, growth is solid, the labor market is roughly in balance, inflation is too high for comfort, and monetary policy has been too easy. Hence, we maintain our out of consensus call that the Fed will hike two more times this year by 25bps each in Oct and Dec.

Unlike hurricanes and other weather events that typically affect economic activity over a relatively short, discrete period, El Niño is a more sustained climate phenomenon. El Niño typically develops in the tropical Pacific Ocean during the Northern Hemisphere spring and summer, with weather impacts appearing first in many regions outside the US during the Southern Hemisphere winter (June-August). These early effects can vary widely, ranging from warmer or cooler conditions to wetter or drier weather, depending on the location. The current El Niño is tracking very closely to the 1997-98 El Niño. Of the three other NOAA-recorded "super" El Niño events (including 1982-83 and 2015-16), 1997-98 had the most sustained strength. GOVERNANCE INSTABILITY AND SYSTEMIC WEAKNESS How local incumbents have survived – until now: Despite steadily deteriorating service quality, three mechanisms have protected the ANC in local government, in our view. ▪ Patronage dependency: When the governing coalition in a local government controls resource distribution even when it has failed on service delivery, continued support is rational for vulnerable households. ▪ Political identity: The ANC's liberation legacy had previously created an accountability asymmetry, whereby voters ‘punish’ individual ANC ward councillors while continuing to vote for the party in the proportional representation vote. ▪ Disengagement: Turnout fell to a record-low 46% in the LGE 2021. With 35% of a shrinking pool, a party can govern with fewer absolute votes than before. As all three of the above mechanisms have continued to weaken simultaneously, several smaller parties have threatened ANC administrative control in key metros, shifting the patronage calculation for grant-dependent voters. For example, the historical legitimacy premium is generationally declining – 2026 first-time voters were born in 2007–08, long after the first democratic elections in 1994. From service failure to ballot: Voter dissatisfaction with municipal failure has been a core driver of the almost 30pp collapse in the ANC’s vote share over 2004–24, in our view. EUR 54bn? EUR 43bn? 6½%? Unpacking the government’s arithmetic . On an unchanged-policy basis , the government estimates that the deficit would deteriorate by 1.1pp in 2027 (EUR 32-34bn), towards 6½% of GDP. The EUR 54bn of tightening the government has communicated overstates effective tightening in 2027 in two respects: • Around EUR 11bn reflects measures decided in 2025-26 whose effects carry into 2027. The EUR 43bn balance is the quantum of measures in the budget required to achieve the 5.0% deficit from the government’s unchanged-policy baseline. • More importantly, th is EUR 43 bn is measured against a deteriorating counterfactual, not against 2026. EUR 33bn is needed to simply prevent the deficit from drifting above its 2026 level. The nominal deficit itself falls by only EUR 6.8bn between 2026 and 2027. A more meaningful measure of the fiscal stance from an economic perspective is the cyclically-adjusted budget balance, which is set to improve by around 0.5pp (EUR 15bn) in 2027, despite a 0.3pp headwind from rising debt-service costs. records.text: 2 October 2026 Euro Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 There are, however, some factors of concern . First, costs are rising. The input prices index was raised by 0.7 pts relative to the flash estimate and increased by 4.3 p ts over the month. Interestingly, firms have been sharply increasing their purchases of materials. It is unclear whether this reflects concerns about future price increases or confidence in stronger demand ahead, although the new orders index was revised slightly higher (+0.15 pts). Output prices were also revised up, albeit only marginally (+0.1 pts), and are 1 pt higher than in August. September confidence surveys The European Commission’s Economic Sentiment Indicator retreated by 0.5 pts to 97.9 in September, ending a four-month streak of improvements. The headline index was dragged down by a sharp deterioration in consumer confidence (-1pp), while the industrial and services sectors remained broadly stable . Details reveal that the decline in consumer confidence was driven by worsening expectations regarding household financial conditions over the next 12 months, with persistent price pressures remaining a primary concern. Conversely, anxiety regarding the labour market appeared to ease, as consumer unemployment concern sub-index moderated during the month. Still, sentiment should be underpinned by the solid employment and income climate. n Monthly Labor Survey for August (7 October): We expect total cash earnings growth (same-sample basis) to pick up to 3.6% YoY (July: +2.9%). The August data should largely reflect the results of this year’s wage revisions. The rise in scheduled earnings, an indicator of underlying wage trends, looks to stabilize at around 3.0%, setting the baseline for nominal growth this fiscal year. Moreover, with summer bonus payments nearly complete, we believe special cash earnings will settle at an average gain of roughly 4% during June-August. n Consumption Activity Index for August (7 October): We project a modest drop of 0.2% MoM. We believe the figures will be dragged down by the inclement weather during the summer holidays, particularly in spending on services such as travel. Durable goods should experience a backlash from the recent surge in spending driven by fast-forwarded purchasing. n Economy Watchers Survey for September (8 August): The key will be the effect of August’s poor weather on sentiment. Furthermore, prices have been revised for a broad array of products since September, so the impact of inflation fears on sentiment will also be a key factor in assessing the results. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 9 Financial conditions: The Fed awakens Following the 25bp rate hike in September and the shift into an "oil risk premium" baseline, we reset our financial conditions index to September 15 2026, the day prior to the September FOMC meeting, to track our FRB/US-based measure of financial conditions in this new hiking cycle. As of the morning of October 2, following the jobs report, financial conditions were about one rate hike tighter than they were before the September FOMC meeting. The index aims to capture how changes in asset prices weigh on future economic activity. It includes five daily variables: the 10-year Treasury yield, S&P 500 returns, the corporate BBB credit spread, the valuation of the U.S. dollar, and the price of oil. These are aggregated based on their estimated growth elasticities relative to the federal funds rate using the Federal Reserve's FRB/US model. As a result, the index can be interpreted as the equivalent change in the federal funds rate, expressed in basis points, required to generate a similar effect on economic activity. Since the day before the September FOMC meeting, the easing in financial conditions has been equivalent to about a 29bp hike in the federal funds rate, driven primarily by a higher 10-year Treasury yield and USD appreciation. records.text: ? The USD has performed strongly over the past month, with the DXY approaching ytd highs and the greenback outperforming every G10 currency except the JPY (Figure 1). At the same time, US growth remains resilient, the Fed is among the most hawkish central banks in our MKTMedia dataset, and inflation continues to prove sticky. That said, having missed the initial leg of USD strength, we believe patience is warranted. As the USD has pushed many currency pairs toward the edges of recent ranges, we want greater confidence that demand is sufficient to drive a sustained breakout rather than another move that ultimately fades. While real-money investors have been net buyers since mid-September, those purchases have been modest relative to the surge in demand seen during the onset of the Iran conflict, suggesting that neither safe-haven flows nor oil-related concerns are generating compelling USD demand (Figure 2). We are no longer willing to run an underweight USD position, but if this is truly the beginning of a durable dollar upswing, we believe there will be ample time to participate rather than chasing the move and getting caught in any mean-reversion. Moreover, relative UST underperformance indicates that the term premia-driven concerns that correlate with underweight real money USD exposure could still weigh heavier on the USD than other G10 peers (Figure 1). On the one hand, the transmission to France’s economy tends to be dampened by the maturity structure of household and corporate debt, which have among the lowest share of variable rate debt in the Euro area (Exhibit 2, left). This is the reason why our statistical estimates point to a more muted effect from tighter financial conditions on growth in France than elsewhere (Exhibit 2, right). On the other hand, the ongoing tightening in financial conditions partly reflects other factors which have additionally negative implications for growth. First, we see a renewed increase in policy and political uncertainty relating to the budget negotiations and next year’s elections, which could delay consumption and investment decisions by households and firms (Exhibit 3, left). As a result, the final transportation margin could understate the economy's true dependence on freight services. To capture broader supply-chain exposure, we construct an upstream freight-intensity measure using the Leontief inverse from the BEA input-output accounts. For each PCE category, we calculate the direct and indirect requirements from truck, rail, water, and courier transportation as a share of producer value. A freight intensity of 5%, for example, implies that producing one dollar of output ultimately requires roughly five cents of freight inputs somewhere along the production network. While the measure captures transportation services embodied throughout domestic supply chains, it may not fully reflect freight services provided overseas before goods enter the United States. Some of this international freight exposure may nevertheless be embedded in import prices for raw materials, intermediate goods, and finished products, rather than appearing explicitly as transportation inputs. Consequently, freight exposure for highly import-dependent categories may be somewhat different from that implied by our estimates alone. At the major-category level, food and beverages purchased for off-premises consumption emerge as the most freight-intensive component of consumer spending, with upstream freight inputs accounting for nearly 7% of producer value. From here, we continue to see an asymmetry to lower Bund yields, either via a reduction of energy prices and hike risk, or via ongoing spread widening and safe-haven flows. We continue to forecast 10y Bund yields at 3.25% at end-2026. What’s causing the OAT widening? OATs remain the centre of the sovereign spread n widening, even as we began to see broader spillovers into other EGB markets this week. 10y OAT-Bund spreads widened beyond 150bp, before retracing to 140bp (Exhibit 3), levels only seen in the most acute phase of the European sovereign crisis in late 2011. Both domestic and global factors are contributing to the move. In general, the rise in the level and volatility of global rates and ECB hikes are a headwind to sovereign credit as a factor. Domestic macro and fiscal fundamentals – while not obviously deteriorating – remain unfavourable for OATs. Both the RBA and RBNZ raised rates at their most recent meetings, with further tightening expected, albeit at a faster pace and to a higher terminal rate in New Zealand. That said, inflation dynamics in New Zealand appear considerably less concerning than in many other developed markets. Online prices rose just 37bps q/q in September, below seasonal norms and suggesting underlying price pressures remain relatively contained. In Australia, by contrast, online prices rose an average of 122bps q/q in September, well above seasonal norms and indicative of more persistent inflationary pressures. Even so, the RBA retains a credible case for patience. Real wage growth remains negativ e, household incomes continue to be squeezed, and labor market conditions have begun to soften. As a result, while additional rate hikes are likely, the economic backdrop argues against an overly aggressive tightening path through the remainder of the year. In contrast, regional differences in durable goods prices appear limited, while higher accommodation charges should also feed through to nationwide CPI. However, accommodation charges are highly volatile from month to month. While they contributed positively in September, the outlook from October onward remains uncertain. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 43 Technology led all sectors in job cuts in September, with seasonally-adjusted cuts up 4K to 14K and not-seasonally-adjusted cuts up 5K to 11K. The sector has announced 166K cuts this year, up 54% from the 108K announced through September 2025. The tech sector has accounted for 29% of all job cuts announced in 2026, more than any other industry. In September, market and economic conditions led all reasons for job cuts, with 9K cuts or 20% of the total. Artificial intelligence was the fifth-most cited reason with 4K cuts in September, about 9% of the month's total. So far this year, AI has been cited in 120K job cut announcements, approximately 21% of all cuts, and it remains the leading reason. Employers announced plans to hire 91K workers in September (not seasonally adjusted), up from the 12K plans announced in August, as seasonal hiring announcements have begun, according to Challenger. However, that is down 23% from the 117K hiring plans announced in September 2025, and the lowest September total since 2011, when 77K hiring plans were recorded. ADP estimates private employment rose 90K in September ADP estimates private employment rose 90K in September, up from the 36K estimated in August. Goods-producing employment rose 31K in September, as natural resources and mining employment fell -1K, construction employment rose 15K, and manufacturing employment rose 17K. But in the September report (second figure), that momentum has been lopped off by revisions, with the temp services category switching from gains to losses in the past three months. records.text: 30 September 2026 Europe Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 appointment as ECB president in 2019 formed part of a broader bargain between France and Germany: Ursula von der Leyen, a German national, became European Commission president, while Christine Lagarde, a French national, became ECB president. There are three Executive Board seats to allocate next year: Schnabel’s (now in January, almost a year ear lier than expected ), Lane’s (May) and Lagarde’s (October). France and Germany have always held an Executive Board seat (Figure 1), and there is an informal agreement that no country should hold more than one Executive Board seat. A sequential process would therefore be difficult: France and Germany could be reluctant to accept one of the other vacancies before the presidency is settled, because doing so would effectively surrender their option to nominate a candidate for president later in the process. Schnabel’s early departure creates an opportunity to bring the succession decisions together. If Lagarde also left early, France and Germany could negotiate the ECB presidency alongside the other vacant Executive Board seat (Lane’s chief economist position ) rather than decide each appointment sequentially. A package agreement would resemble the EU’s previous grand bargains and may be more politically feasible than asking either country to accept another Board seat before the presidency is settled. While real money investors have reduced flows into the long end, it is worth noting that they have increased allocations to short-tenor EM sovereign bonds following the Fed hike. This contrasts with UST flow s, which have weakened across the curve. While it remains too early to draw a firm conclusion about post -FOMC flow trends , this chart suggests that real -money investors may prefer short- tenor EM bonds over comparable USTs , as some EM central banks have done their tightening cycle and could stay independent to the Fed . Short-tenor EM sovereign bond inflows should provide some support for EM FX, but they appear to reflect tactical carry demand rather than broad conviction in EM duration. The final action also preserves several key carve-outs, including goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs, USMCA-compliant imports, and a range of general and country-specific product exemptions. One grid to rule them all: FHFA tells the GSE to feed VS4 into the classic FICO grid On Monday afternoon, the FHFA Director reshaped the credit score saga once again, declar- ing that VS4 and classic FICO would now use the same LLPA grid—specifically, the grid that classic FICO has always had. A few quick thoughts: Given that VS4 scores, very roughly speaking, tend to be around 20 points higher than clas- sic FICO, this naturally means that VS4 is going to produce the lower score in many scenari- os. The average borrower is going to shift up the LLPA grid (down in dollars charged) simply by using a VS4 score, and we estimate that pulling FICO is only going to help borrowers in perhaps 15-20% of cases now. Moreover, around half of purchase borrowers won’t even have to consider pulling another score—they’ll already be at the lowest LLPA for their LTV . Originators now have even more incentive to speed up their transition to VS4; they’re clear- ly leaving money on the table now by not offering the other score. We see some upside to the growth hit implied by our gross value added calculations, however, since diesel has limited substitutes in many industrial applications. To assess this risk, we leverage our model of bottlenecks/supply shortages. In the model, we assume that there are no substitutes for these products or inventory buffers, but that supply is reallocated towards its most productive uses within a country. Under this assumption, the growth hit falls close to zero in most economies but remains sizable in Mexico and Latin America more broadly (right chart, Exhibit 4), although these effects would likely be dampened by inventory buffers and increased exports from the rest of the world. Any outright supply disruptions will likely be short-lived given the global nature of diesel markets and supply, so in practice the main economic impacts on other countries will come from rising diesel prices. Deadline for final RRF payment requests has passed. The deadline for the final RRF payment requests passed on 30 September and all 27 EU member states submitted their last requests. The European Commission (EC) received 15 payment requests for €92.2bn in September (€81.7bn in the last two days of the month). Including the previously submitted but not yet disbursed payment requests it now has €106bn of payment requests to assess and to disburse before the end of the year. Three quarters of initially available RRF funds will be utilized. While overseas credit and CLO investments often involve the use of cross-currency swaps, elevated rates volatility and tight credit spreads limit carry opportunities, making a sharp increase in positions unlikely. Attention will also turn to life insurers’ FY26 second-half investment plans, scheduled for release after October. However, at the beginning of the fiscal year, there were no indications of plans to materially increase allocations to FX-hedged foreign bonds through FX forwards or cross-currency basis swaps (Link). Research 1Clemente De Lucia | +39 -02 402-43012 | clem ente.delucia@db.com | September 2026 Main findings (1) Over the past few weeks, we have published two related notes. The first focused on the 2027 Budget Law, assessing its potential contours and the limits imposed by the EU fiscal framework. The second examined the timing of the next general election, the main political contenders and the market implications of different electoral outcomes. In this third note, we turn our attention on debt sustainability. Over recent years, markets adopted a constructive view on the country, reflected in several sovereign rating upgrades. However, both the international and domestic environment are becoming more challenging. Italy remains particularly exposed to the ongoing energy shock, given its greater dependence on imported energy relative to most of its major European peers. At the same time, financing conditions are tightening, with the yield on 10-year BTP up by more than 100bp since the start of the year, and, given Italy's high public debt burden, higher borrowing costs will gradually place additional pressure on public finances. Finaly, after an unusually long period of government stability by Italian standards, the upcoming election cycle could reintroduce a degree of uncertainty and potentially lead to less cohesive governing majorities. We expect inflation expectations to fall slightly, reflecting stable and modestly declining gasoline prices over the last few weeks. Of course, as the level of prices remains high, sentiment could remain weak as the University of Michigan survey questions focus heavily on perceived purchasing power. We are also particularly interested in details of the survey that describe how consumers are responding to higher prices. While soft sentiment overall has not necessarily translated to weaker spending the last few years, actions around buying plans could be a better indicator of purchasing behavior. While we would not forecast hard data based on these survey details, more people saying it is a bad time to buy because of affordability issues this year compared to last year could be a reason that passthrough of higher input/energy costs to final selling prices has been more limited than the tariff passthrough in 2025. Implications for the inflation path Our baseline forecast is for core CPI inflation to slow to 2.7% y/y in December (2.7% Q4/Q4) and further to 2.4% y/y by next December (2.4% Q4/Q4 in 2027). The corresponding core PCE inflation forecast after folding-in the BEA revisions released this week, is 3.0% Q4/Q4 for 2026, and 2.3% in 2027. While our analysis points to upside risks of around 15-20bp to core inflation, particularly in 2027 given the lagged nature of pass-through, we have not incorporated a markup into our forecast. The reason is straightforward: pass-through depends critically on the persistence of elevated diesel prices. Temporary fuel shocks can lift transportation costs fairly quickly, as we are already seeing, but sustained inflation effects typically require energy prices to remain elevated long enough for firms to adjust their pricing decisions. The other US inflation index Diesel & CPI pass-through While the primary focus of diesel pass-through into US inflation rightfully should be on the PCE index, for inflation markets, the focal point instead is CPI. records.text: 10 US Economic Viewpoint | 01 October 2026 Balance sheets: a “perfect 10” Surging equity wealth pushed household assets above 10x of liabilities in 2Q 2026. We see this as a continued strong tailwind for consumer spending. While equity ownership remains highly concentrated among higher-income households, balance sheet gains may not be as narrow as they first appear. Liquid assets, including checking accounts, savings accounts and money market mutual funds, which are likely more evenly distributed across the population, also remain elevated relative to liabilities by historical standards. Although there are persistent signs of credit stress among lower-income and younger households, who have thinner financial cushions, aggregate household balance sheets remain remarkably healthy. Liquidity positions remain well above pre-pandemic norms, credit utilization has generally improved relative to 2019, and household assets continue to provide substantial buffers against potential shocks. In our view, balance sheets remain supportive of consumer spending overall. While rising equity values and the associated wealth effects continue to disproportionately benefit higher-income households, healthy liquidity positions and strong aggregate household finances suggest the balance sheet tailwind extends beyond the top of the income distribution. records.text: M Global Idea 8 US Investment Grade Credit: Macro Poses a Bigger Test Than Elevated Supply There was no AI-related issuance in the US IG market during the month of September. Following a busy summer, we were expecting a slowdown in near-term supply, considering how much had been done already and issuers' efforts to better establish cadence. Importantly, we think it's now fairly well understood that higher capex next year will likely come with higher issuance. On the other hand, the macro backdrop has become more challenging, with rates selling off sharply and a more hawkish Fed path priced in. Therefore, thinking through the upcoming weeks, the macro environment will likely be the bigger test for corporate credit markets, while issuance might take a backseat. In our view, the credit market at large should be able to handle the sell-off in yields. With nominal growth running at an impressive 6%+ and earnings growth even better, the rate move has a strong fundamental underpinning and as such, we expect credit quality to hold up really well. Importantly, AI-related capex has been a large anchor for US growth, and our economists see it being relatively insensitive to the level of yields, at least locally. Notably, our economists' rate path is more dovish than consensus, calling for two more rate hikes (vs. market pricing that is closer to four). We see this in Figure 5, where the three-to-ten-year maturity change in gilt yields (decomposing changes using breakeven yields) was roughly equally driven by higher inflation compensation and the real yield. The one-year on the other hand has real yields falling. This matters for our headline estimate in a couple of ways. First, the effective real tightening is smaller than the 40bp estimate suggests . Second, and less comfortably for the MPC, the reason yields have risen is itself a warning sign . Rising inflation compensation suggests a growing risk of inflation broadening. This is exactly what insurance hikes are meant to guard against. Can the MPC hike without hiking? Not really. The markets have done some of the heavy lifting , but there are two findings that suggest the MPC still needs to deliver: 1. First, the tightening is borrowed against future hikes . There should be no further impact in November and December and an upward impact of the same magnitude in January when the measure is phased out. In August, after-tax wage growth for lower-income households reached 4.7% YoY, compared with 3.5% YoY for higher- income households (Exhibit 7). Similarly, Atlanta Fed wage data suggest the gap between higher- and lower-income wage growth has narrowed meaningfully (Exhibit 6). Part of the recent improvement reflects lower tax withholding following the implementation of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). However, the more important and sustainable story appears to be improving labor market conditions for lower-income workers. Job growth has broadened The more durable development is a labor market that is becoming increasingly balanced. Throughout much of 2025, labor markets were characterized by a low-hiring, low-firing environment. While layoffs remained subdued, hiring activity was also weak. That dynamic likely disproportionately affected younger workers, who are more likely to fall into lower-income cohorts and are typically more reliant on job mobility and new hiring opportunities than higher-income workers with stronger job attachment. This year, the picture has improved. Hiring activity has picked up more consistently while layoffs have remained low. The three-month average pace of payroll growth is now running near 70k, comfortably above estimates of labor-market breakeven. One reason may be reduced policy uncertainty. records.text: ECB Reserves Entering the Grey Zone ECB liquidity started to decline at end-22 as banks repaid TLTRO loans. Reserves are now draining largely through PEPP and PSPP QT plans, at a pace of EUR40bn/month. With the Fed now re-accumulating US Treasuries as part of its reserve management purchases, the BoE’s repo facility stabilising GBP liquidity and amending its QT plan, it was already natural to ask about the outlook for liquidity in the Euro area. We have argued that ECB liquidity was approaching crunch time into 2027. Renewed stress in EGBs creates urgency to re-examine the outlook for ECB QT, based on liquidity availability and broader market functioning. How much of a liquidity buffer? Like the BoE, and unlike the Fed, the ECB is pursuing a demand-driven system for reserve provision. This means that instead of creating the desired quantity of reserves in the system by buying assets (i.e. sovereign bonds), the ECB will allow the banking system to determine the desired level of reserves via its lending facilities – namely the MRO and LTROs. This will eventually mean that the MRO rate (15bp above the DF rate) will act as a soft ceiling on money market rates, in contrast to the current system of reserve abundance in which overnight rates are forced down to the deposit facility rate (DFR). The recent BofA Global Fund Manager Survey (see report: Global Fund Manager Survey: Racing the Frontier) continues to identify AI hyperscaler capex as one of the leading potential sources of a future systemic credit event. That said, we are nowhere close to this scenario yet. Large technology firms generally remain lightly levered, and our credit strategists do not view borrowing costs as a binding constraint on investment. In other words, the AI story appears more dependent on eventual monetization than financing risk. A broader AI-related correction, if it does happen, could affect consumers through two channels. First, it would weaken equity market wealth effects, which have disproportionately supported higher-income households. Second, a reassessment of AI investment plans could weigh on hiring and labor demand in sectors currently benefiting from the AI investment cycle, creating headwinds for lower-income consumption through weaker labor-income growth. The Summary of Opinions from that meeting was released on October 1. While many Board members reiterated their willingness to continue raising rates, the document contained little that could be interpreted as support for consecu- tive rate hikes. In addition, comments from the Cabinet Office appeared to reflect some concerns regarding continued tightening, which markets interpreted as modestly dovish. As a result, pricing for a consecutive 25bp rate hike in October declined to below 20%. • Economic Conditions: Four comments related to economic conditions were included, all suggesting that the economy remains on an improving trend. That said, one comment noted that, while external demand was positive, domestic demand remained negative and GDP growth was being supported by a decline in imports reflecting supply-side constraints, implying that the economy was not growing in a particularly healthy man- ner. • Inflation: Eight comments focused on inflation. Reduction in 5-11Y Liquidity-Enhancement Auctions At the September 28 meeting between the Ministry of Finance and primary dealers, partici- pants supported a proposal to reduce issuance through 5-11Y liquidity-enhancement auc- tions by JPY150bn per month from October, lowering the monthly auction size to JPY500bn (Link, Japanese only). Our estimates previously suggested that market-held balances in the 6-10Y sector would increase by roughly JPY30tn over the next twelve months before taking into account any reduction in liquidity-enhancement auctions. Incorporating the proposed reduction lowers the increase only marginally, to around JPY28tn (Figure 3O u t l o o k f o r C h a n g e s i n M a r k e t - H e l d J G B B a l a n c e s ). As such, the impact appears limited, and we continue to view the 10-year sector as one of the most challenging parts of the curve from a supply-demand perspective. We believe the reduction in liquidity-enhancement auctions is being funded largely through stronger-than-expected sales of JGBs for households. Demand for retail JGBs has remained robust, with issuance during April-September already reaching JPY5.1tn, close to the origi- nal FY issuance target of JPY5.9tn. At the current pace, annual issuance could reach JPY10tn, implying roughly JPY4-5tn of additional funding capacity (Figure 4R e t a i l J G B I s s u a n c e P a c e ). records.text: form: Limited near-term savings The government announced an ambition to create a National Care Service- a social care system which would be free at the point of use at the next Parliament. To fund the new social care system, the government proposed to reform the pension triple-lock system. The state pension could be adjusted to rise by the higher of inflation or 2.5% in April 2030, while state pension will also hold its value relative to earnings over time. The current pension triple lock adjusts the state pension to the larger of 2.5%, inflation or earnings. The pension triple lock is an expensive policy, and the IFS has noted that the government has spent an additional £9bn per year by 2026-27 on state pensions since 2010 as a result of the triple lock vs this new modified triple-lock system. The government noted that this pension change can save £15bn per year by 2040 (£11bn in today’s money), while IFS estimates it could be anywhere between £4-20bn per year by 2040. Overall, modifying the pension triple lock would be a welcome step to reduce long-term fiscal pressures which would have built up otherwise. But these savings are likely to build gradually rather than appearing immediately. Near-term savings are likely to be small from this change – the IFS estimates that this pension reform would save around £4bn a year in today’s number by 2035.
