records.text: 12 US Economic Viewpoint | 01 October 2026 That said, the predominance of fixed-rate mortgages in the U.S. housing market has helped insulate many households from higher interest rates in the mortgage side of the balance sheet. A large share of homeowners refinanced during the pandemic at historically low mortgage rates and therefore remain largely shielded from the post pandemic increase in policy rates. Because higher-income households are disproportionately homeowners, this has likely been an important factor supporting higher-income consumption and, by extension, overall consumer resilience. The same dynamic should continue to provide support even as interest rates move higher from here. However, that protection does not extend to all forms of consumer credit. As the Fed resumes hiking, financing conditions could become more challenging for households that rely on variable-rate borrowing. Credit card interest rates move closely with the federal funds rate and rose sharply during the last tightening cycle. A recent Boston Fed note showed that a 1pp increase in credit card APRs reduced aggregate card spending by almost 9% in the following month. The reduction in spending was about twice as large among account holders who carry a balance on their card & with low credit scores, likely lower-income consumers. records.text: US Economic Viewpoint | 01 October 2026 17 AI-related equity market risks bear watching Finally, much of the consumer's resilience over the past year has occurred alongside an equity market that has continued to grind higher despite repeated macro shocks. Oil prices moved above $100 per barrel, the 10-year Treasury yield approached 5%, and trade and geopolitical uncertainty remained elevated. Yet equity markets continued to advance, helped in large part by optimism surrounding AI-related investment and productivity gains. For consumption, that matters because equity wealth remains heavily concentrated among higher-income households. Strong market performance has therefore provided an important spending tailwind for the upper arm of the K. If that tailwind were to weaken materially, the impact would likely be felt first through higher-income consumer spending. So, one potential risk in our view is not necessarily higher interest rates themselves, but rather a reassessment of expectations surrounding AI investment. Investor enthusiasm around AI has supported both equity valuations and an extraordinary wave of capital spending by hyperscalers. If expected returns on those investments were called into question sooner than anticipated, or if evidence of monetization failed to keep pace with spending, market sentiment could shift. Morgan has been at the forefront in developing and main- taining Effective Exchange Rates (EER), dating back to the fall of Bretton Woods in 1971. In 2015, we conducted a large- scale overhaul of our methodology (see here). This report updates the trade weights to the EERs and also conducts a deep audit to streamline the methodology. The update chang- es the history of the EER across currencies, but the impact is minimal. International trade remains one of the primary channels through which exchange rate movements affect economic activity, inflation, and competitiveness. As global supply chains, production networks, and trading relationships contin- ue to evolve, measuring currency movements against a coun- try’s full set of trading partners has become increasingly important. records.text: it labor costs stay contained The revisions imply slightly stronger productivity growth in 2024 and 2025, but little changed recently: the revised 2.3% year-over-year pace in Q2 2026 is only 0.1 pp above the prior estimate. Compensation growth was revised slightly lower in 2024 and 2025 but higher in H1 2026. Together, the output and compensation revisions imply slower unit labor cost growth in 2024 and 2025, followed by stronger growth in 2026. Even so, the implied 2.2% year-over-year pace in Q2 2026 remains within its recent range and consistent with 2% inflation. The other thing that has not been completely revised away, was the rather lackluster productivity growth from 2025Q4 through 2026Q2, which was just 1.3% annualized over the last three quarters and now looks closer to 1.6%. That is consistent with a low- productivity regime in the US, not the lift we were expecting this year.

records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 47 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Data in the week ahead Monday, October 5 ISM services composite (Sep), 10:00 AM We project the ISM services composite fell -0.9 points to 54.5 in September, moderating but still indicating expansion. Most regional services surveys softened in September (see table below). The details of the regional reports sent mixed signals, however, with some showing softening demand while others were steadier. More consistent was commentary from respondents pointing to elevated input costs, economic uncertainty, and interest rates weighing on capital spending and interest-sensitive activity. The 2.2 index-point increase in the S&P Global services PMI flags upside risk to our forecast for the ISM gauge, but that may well revise lower next week. The S&P Global services headline index also measures business activity alone, whereas the ISM services index is a composite of business activity, new orders, employment, and supplier deliveries.  Upside: Strength in demand and business activity exceeded the seasonal norm throughout the summer, and was evident in industry-level survey responses. An upside surprise in September would suggest that momentum in the services sector is continuing into the early autumn.  Downside: A downside surprise due to softening orders and employment would carry more weight with us and would suggest moderating services- sector activity more than drag caused by an decline in the supplier deliverie

The 10Y French spread is now trading around 40bp too wide on this relative sovereign risk framework, which in our view reflects a mix of political uncertainty risk premia and residual mispricing. Historically, Italian spreads have traded quite cheap on our sovereign risk index, on average around 60bp cheap over a long history and around 50bp since 2014 (Figure 9I t a l y h a s h i s t o r i c a l l y t r a d e d q u i t e c h e a p o n o u r s o v e r e i g n r i s k f r a m e w o r k b u t h a s r i c h e n e d s i n c e M e l o n i b e c a m e P M ), likely reflect- ing political risk premia, in addition to other factors. Under PM Meloni, that cheapness has largely corrected, which we attribute to improved political stability and fiscal discipline. We are not arguing that the current political/fiscal landscape in France is directly comparable to Italy’s earlier regimes. However, it is plausible that French spreads could continue to screen cheap on this framework until there is greater evidence of political stability and fiscal discipline. To what extent does the VA revision make riskier Euro government bonds easier to hold? Consider an Italian lifer with substantially higher BTP exposure than the EUR insurance industry reference portfolio. The new framework allows such insurer to benefit from the 𝑉𝐴 more than it currently does: (i) through the CSSR, its BTP holdings contribute to the spread sensitivity of the insurer-specific actual fixed-income assets; (ii) through the optional RCS adjustment addresses the quality overshooting, (iii) for €-denominated assets, country-level spread stress can generate the Macro VA, based on the country’s RCSItaly relative to RCSEur. How does the VA differ from the MA? Is the latter changing? Similar to the VA, the MA adjusts the liability discount curve for wider credit spreads, after removing a fundamental spread representing risks retained by the insurer. Unlike the VA, where the insurer’s own portfolio matters mostly via the CSSR channel, with the RCS remaining anchored to the regulatory reference portfolio, in an 𝑀𝐴 portfolio the level and composition of spread on the actual assets directly feed the adjustment. In countries where internet retailing is a small share of transactions, retailers tend to tie their online prices to offline prices in order to minimise costs associated with making pricing decisions. A significant structural fiscal adjustment: The text confirms the target to reduce the budget deficit to 5% of GDP in 2027, from 5.4% this year. Given that without an adjustment the budget deficit would have been on track to reach 6.5% next year – as previously indicated by the government – this target implies a required EUR54bn of fiscal consolidation, with new measures (i.e accounting for the EUR11n which has already been voted on) accounting for EUR43bn of that. As a result, the structural primary budget balance is expected to improve by 0.8% of GDP, up from 0.4% in 2026. Out of the EUR43bn , 60% is slated to come from reduced spending (EUR26bn) and 40% from increased revenue (EUR17bn). As a result, spending-to-GDP is expected to be slightly lower in 2027 (at 56.9% of GDP versus 57.1% for 2026). We think this stronger focus on spending is likely intended to demonstrate a commitment to the EU’s expectations for budget consolidation, while tacitly admitting that the 3% deficit target for 2029, intended to stabili se the debt-to-GDP ratio, might not be reached. This is also the position of most presidential candidates, who rather target a return to 3% by 2032, at the end of the five -year presidential term. Labor supply remains volatile Labor supply in the US remains volatile. Despite solid top-line payroll growth estimates, September's unemployment rate increased 3bp, to 4.175%, now showing a rounded 4.2%, a tenth above where it stood in the prior two months (Figure 4). This is because the jump in household employment (+406k) was exceeded by a stronger gain in the labor force (+485k). After adjusting for differences in scope between the payroll and household surveys, the "payroll- consistent" measure of household employment rose 107k, above the payroll measure. Nonetheless, we maintain our view that the "breakeven" pace of job gains is modest, at best, given reduced immigration inflows and the aging of the domestic labor force. The labor force participation rate (LFPR) increased 0.2pp, to 61.8%, led by a strong jump (+0.9pp) in the participation of 16-24 year-olds and a gain in the 25-54 year-old cohort (+0.3pp). These moves more than offset a decline in the 55+ year-old cohort (-0.3pp). The price index for business investment in GDP has been rising faster than consumer inflation, and some of these price pressures are directly boosting PCE inflation. Core CPI inflation – reflecting prices that consumers are paying directly out of pocket – has slowed to 2.4%, only 20bp higher than its pre-pandemic average. In our view, September's supply slowdown is due to a combination of 1) significant front-loading of issuance that happened in previous months, especially over the summer, 2) emerging signs of regulatory/political challenges to new data center construction, and 3) the rates sell-off possibly requiring project-level renegotiations for data-center deals. In US IG, we think the macro backdrop - and not elevated supply - is the biggest test between now and year-end, with outflows expected on the back of a sharp drawdown in returns. We expect at least one more deal in the US market, and note that HQ hyperscalers continue to tap non-USD currencies in between their larger US deals earlier this year. HQ hyperscalers should remain largely insensitive to higher rates, and we expect another wave of volatility into the fall, especially around 3Q26 earnings and likely further upward capex revisions. Lev Fin was active in September, but we expect 4Q26 to look more like 1Q/3Q, with a slower pace of deals given higher rates and regulatory/political limitations. Lower-quality issuers and project-level debt are more sensitive to the current rate environment, in our view, but issuers might be able to negotiate better lease economics with tenants to improve their returns. Market technicals leading to overshoot: the evidence As discussed in this note, market structure and positioning have arguably amplified this week’s move. Hedge fund participation in bond markets and market leverage have both increased since Covid. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 8 Core PCE inflation revised down The annual revision materially lowered core PCE price inflation. Published 12-month inflation through August is now 3.01%, versus 3.34% through July in last month’s release; July was revised to 2.98% in the latest data. We expected a downward revision, but the result was below our 3.18% August projection and likely surprised the Fed: Chairman Warsh cited 3.2% through August after the FOMC meeting, while Governor Cook cited 3.4% on Monday this week. Incorporating the latest data lowers our Q4/Q4 forecast to 2.95%, just rounding to 2.9%, although that could change when we finalize our September CPI projection over the next week. While market-held balances in the super-long sector are not expected to increase materially over the next year, reflecting previous issuance reductions, ongoing BoJ QT (currently run- ning at an annual pace of JPY45tn) is still projected to increase market-held balances in the 6-10Y sector by roughly JPY28tn over the next twelve months (see below). At Monday's PD meeting, the Ministry of Finance and primary dealers also supported a proposal to reduce issuance through 5-11Y liquidity-enhancement auctions by roughly JPY1.8tn per year. However, we expect the impact on overall supply-demand conditions to be limited. With duration demand remaining subdued, the 10-year sector is likely to remain one of the most supply-demand-challenged parts of the curve. Against this backdrop, we continue to favor a 2s10s JGB curve steepener as our preferred trade recommendation. Below, we review (1) the Summary of Opinions from the September BoJ meeting, (2) the reduction in 5-11Y liquidity-enhancement auctions, (3) key fiscal issues to watch going forward, (4) why we continue to favor a 2s10s JGB curve steepener, and (5) an update on the USD/JPY basis market. These have been common questions this week. An interven- tion through TPI is far from straightforward and the ECB will not consider this lightly. This is not only due to legal issues but also because these legal considerations reflect the region’s institutional setup, which matters for the effectiveness of an intervention. What is more feasible is that the ECB takes steps to insulate banks and other countries that are seeing unwarranted contagion in their bond markets. The most straightforward policy implication is for the policy rate. Long-term bond yields and spreads have increased and are a substitute for some increases in the policy rate. Due to the recent starting point, however, and assuming no new surprises to the inflation outlook, a total of four hikes could still be quite easily justified based on current market levels. records.text: 10 Europe Economic Weekly | 02 October 2026 Closer EU/UK relationship: Potential growth dividends but slow progress The government opened the door to a much closer relationship with the EU. A much closer EU/UK relationship can deliver growth dividends, but progress is likely to be slow. The government plans to use a UK-EU summit this year to lay out the different options for the UK’s long-term relationship with EU to find consensus around one. These options include customs union, single market membership or full re-joining. The economic gains would depend heavily on the degree of integration. The date of the EU- UK Summit is unclear, though there is some speculation that it could be on Nov. 20. There seems to be a twin approach on EU-UK relationship- the first to implement the limited reset already underway and the second to explore different options to getting closer to the EU. But it is unlikely that the EU would engage in serious negotiations on the EU- UK relationship until after the next election. We think the EU is likely to want the government to win a durable and fresh mandate from the public on a new EU/UK relationship before negotiating a fundamental change. Moreover, the debate on trade- offs or costs is unlikely to be easy. Meanwhile we can expect to hear positive noises from both sides. records.text: h by Isabel Schnabel here). However, asset purchasing can still be a powerful financial stability or transmission tool at times of market stress. A good example is the BoE purchases to quash the LDI crisis in 2023 and their quick reversal (see speech by Isabel Schnabel here). A clear exit strategy is what differentiates asset purchases for market stabilisation purposes from regular quantitative easing (QE). Schnabel referred to the BOE LDI response as how an exit strategy “can be designed successfully”. For an inflation targeting central bank, “there can be no trade off between market stabilisation and price stability”. In other words, despite a higher bar for asset purchasing relative to a decade ago, even the hawks at the ECB have not ruled them out, in certain circumstances and with sufficient exit provisions to ensure monetary policy agility. Bottom line As long as the market pressures are “country specific” and rational and contagion is limited, the ECB will likely continue to watch rather than act. Market discipline could help ensure the 2027 Budget is agreed wi th minimal slippage relative to the initial proposal and could see RN move towards a clearer stability-oriented fiscal policy. The greater the sense of irrational pricing, the market overshooting fundamentals and spillover /contagion effects, the lower the bar for ECB intervention. records.text: 2 October 2026 Europe Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 9 Second, to the extent that other member states suffering from contagion and contagion is by definition not a "country -specific fundamental" risk premium, then contagion could give rise to TPI for other member states. The knowledge that TPI is available to lean against contagion should help reduce the likelihood of contagion. Possible conditions under which TPI could be used for France Above, we mentioned the possibility of TPI being used in case of : (1) irrational pricing of risk or (2) material contagion. Exactly what would trigger the conditions for TPI is inevitably (an d in some ways deliberately) ambiguous. Here , we offer a few indicative scenarios in which TPI deployment could potentially occur. Scenario 1: Pragmatic reform Spiralling yields pushes the French government towards a large-scale debt crisis. Unlike article 49-3, ordinances would remain in force even in the event of a successful motion of no confidence against the government. However, ordinances could only be based on the government's initial draft and would not incorporate subsequent parliamentary amendments. As highlighted above, a loi spéciale is intended to serve as a temporary stopgap rather than a durable budgetary framework. Relying on such a mechanism for more than a few months would be challenging, as it combines two major drawbacks: it offers limited scope to reallocate spending priorities, for example to accommodate higher defence spending, and, as recently highlighted in a report by the General Inspectorate of Finance, it would not allow for any meaningful reduction in the headline deficit ratio. Against this backdrop, if the government is determined to secure the adoption of a full budget ahead of the presidential election in April 2027, we think it will ultimately have to rely either on article 49-3 or on budgetary ordinances. Given that budgetary ordinances have never been used in this context and would likely be perceived as a more forceful circumvention of Parliament, we think the use of article 49-3 is more likely. That said, ordinances could emerge as a credible alternative later in the parliamentary process, particularly if no agreement appears within reach with the opposition by late November or early December. Positioning is still relatively light, but flows have yet to recover as geopolitical tensions and higher oil prices weigh on investor sentiment. records.text: Dwyfor Evans 30 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Hungary : Domestic Strength Meets External Headwinds The Hungarian forint (HUF) has experienced a year of two halves. In the first half of 2026, the HUF outperformed regional peers, supported by high real interest rates, strong investor demand for emerging market (EM) carry trades, and a sharp compression in political risk following the April election that ended the Orbán era. Expectations that EU funds could eventually be unlocked also improved sentiment. Recent months have been less favourable. Falling inflation encouraged expectations of monetary easing, reducing the HUF’s carry advantage, while investor positioning became increasingly crowded. At the same time, higher energy prices, rising global bond yields and broad USD strength weighed on one of the region’s more beta-sensitive currencies. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 3 US Economics Weekly UBS Research Economic Comment: on track for on hold The information this week lowered market pricing for an October rate hike down to 5 basis points of a hike priced, or roughly 22%. That followed a fair amount of FOMC speakers, alongside data that broke that way. Following the PMIs last week, odds of an October hike were over 70%. Then FOMC speakers seemed largely ignored as FRB of New York President John Williams and FRB of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson sounded patient. However, after Williams' more direct remarks this week, using "late" this year language, as a sign of his timing, market implied odds of an October rate hike fell below 50-50, or 47% at the end of Tuesday, before the inflation data was released. In reaction to Chairman Warsh's Jackson Hole speech we pencilled 0.25 pp rate hikes in September and another in December, after which we expect the FOMC goes on prolonged hold. Our reasoning for skipping October was threefold. First, not raising rates avoids action only six days ahead of the mid-term elections. Second, the FOMC could better limit how steep the front end pricing might become if they signalled a potential every meeting pace. Third, the inflation problem the FOMC faces is not one of rising inflation at the moment, but one of not declining inflation, raising questions how much the interest rate sensitive sectors need weight. Isabel Schnabel has announced her intention to leave the ECB Executive Board on 3 January 2027 and take a senior position at the IMF. By leaving almost a year before her term was due to end, Schnabel’s move triggers a political process to select her successor. It also lowers the hurdle for President Christine Lagarde to depart before her term ends on 31 October 2027. Schnabel’s resignation creates an opportunity for EU leaders to negotiate the ECB’s three upcoming Executive Board vacancies — president, chief economist, and head of markets – as a package. A package deal that solves all three positions at once is arguably politically easier than a sequence of separate decisions over the next year. Lagarde’s increasingly non-committal language and potential interest in playing a role in the French presidential campaign add to the case for an earlier exit. A 45bp rise in two-year rates – as implied by market rate expectations - is not the same as a 45bp hike in Bank Rate. Different parts of the curve move by different amounts when policy expectations change. So, we need to make a like -for-like comparison. We approach this by asking a simple question: what kind of MPC surprise would have historically produced a curve movement similar to the one we have seen since the 60-day memorandum expiry? To answer this, we use the UK Monetary Policy Event -Study Database (UKMPD), which identifies monetary policy surprises from market movements in a narrow window around MPC announcements. We extend the database with the latest data and our own calculations. For each maturity along the OIS curve , we regress its move around each MPC announcement on the identified policy surprise. Across more than a decade of announcements, this tells us how much each part of the curve typically moves in response to a 100bp policy surprise. On an unchanged -policy basis, the government estimates that the deficit would drift from 5.4% of GDP in 2026 towards 6½% in 2027. Around EUR 43bn of measures (1.4% of GDP) are required to bring it back to the 5% target, but much of that offsets underlying fiscal deterioration rather than reducing spending outright. Public expenditure is still projected to rise by around EUR 41bn in nominal terms, reflecting in particular higher interest costs, pensions, defence and healthcare, while compulsory levies increase by around €48bn (1.6% of GDP). We think the 5% target is likely to slip. How does the new risk margin calculation reduce the need to receive long-end swaps while freeing up capital? After-tax wage growth for lower-income households reached 4.7% y/y in Aug, exceeding the 3.5% pace for higher-income, extending the reversal of the wage-growth “K” that had persisted since late ‘24. Job growth increased and broadened in 2026. Job-switching activity and associated pay gains improved most among lower-income HHs. Also, recent GDP and income revisions suggest a larger HH savings cushion than previously thought. Balance sheets: a “perfect 10” Surging equity wealth pushed HH assets above 10x of liabilities in 2Q26, providing a continued tailwind for spending. While equity ownership is highly concentrated among higher-income HHs, balance sheet gains may not be as narrow as widely believed. Liquid assets (checking / savings accounts & MMMFs), which should be more evenly distributed across the population, are also very elevated relative to liabilities, by historical standards. Gas prices temper our optimism So, what’s holding us back from going all in on a consumer boom? Three things. First, the latest surge in gas prices could weigh on discretionary spending, particularly with the fiscal impulse fading. Specifically, it could “make secondary market purchases of securities issued in jurisdictions experiencing a deterioration in financing condi- tions not warranted by country-specific fundamentals”. The scale of TPI purchases “would depend on the severity of the risks facing monetary policy transmission” without any ex ante restrictions. Hence, both the context and scale of the market moves matter for whether TPI would be activated. In terms of the context, the ECB spells out a number of eligi- bility conditions that a country must meet. First, it must be in compliance with the EU fiscal framework: not subject to an excessive deficit procedure (EDP) or not assessed as having failed to take effective action to correct the excessive deficit. Second, it must not have severe macroeconomic imbalances: not subject to an excessive imbalance procedure (EIP) or not being assessed as having failed to take the recommended cor- rective action. Third, its debt trajectory must be assessed as sustainable (based on analysis by institutions such as the European Commission, the European Stability Mechanism and the IMF, and based on the ECB’s internal analysis. records.text: osed to diesel-specific volatility to better understand how the CPI fixings and market-implied path might respond to diesel-specific volatility. Our prior holding is that diesel shocks show up in the CPI largely through specific energy components, but, because diesel moves most of the goods in the economy, it's reasonable to expect correlations with food/core goods/transport prices over time. However, as described below, the data offer little support for that view once crude, gasoline and supply-chain conditions are accounted for. For this analysis, we separately regressed monthly changes in every NSA CPI component on changes in diesel prices, including up to three months of lags. Diesel, crude and gasoline tend to move together, so a naive regression of CPI subcomponents m/m on diesel m/m would find widespread statistical significance, but in reality mostly be picking up oil volatility, not diesel- specific impulses. We therefore attempted to remove the portion of diesel price changes explained by crude and gasoline; what remains is our proxy for a diesel-specific shock. Each regression also controls for crude, gasoline, seasonal patterns and the NY Fed's Global Supply Chain Pressure Index. 1 October 2026 9 Barclays | US Energy and Inflation

Against this backdrop, in this follow-up note we focus on public finance sustainability. Our main findings are as follows ❑ Our Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA) suggests that, under our baseline scenario, Italy's debt-to-GDP ratio remains on a declining trajectory over the forecast horizon. This is good news. A falling debt ratio implies that public finances can absorb some limited deterioration in fiscal or macroeconomic conditions. Nevertheless, the debt burden remains high and should still be considered a source of vulnerability. For example, a 50bp upward shift in the interest rate curve (with the 10-year BTP yield peaking at 5% in 2027-28 before gradually declining to 4.4% by 2035) would leave the debt ratio unchanged at around 140% until the end of the decade. A shock of 100bp will put the debt ratio on a divergent path. A growth shock (a stagnating GDP growth in 2027 rather than expanding by 0.8% as in our baseline) would also leave the debt ratio at uncomfortably high levels. ❑ Gross Financing Needs (GFN), which measure the amount of debt that must be refinanced each year and are therefore an important indicator of sovereign vulnerability, are projected to increase over the coming years. JGB: This Week in Review, The Week Ahead This note covers the accounting design of the investment-envelope bridge bonds set out in the 2026 Basic Policy (issuing law, special account, redemption rule and fiscal metrics), the ranking of redemption sources across the seven precedents, how the FY2027 issuance plan would absorb them, and the implications for the JGB curve and our trades. The Basic Policy states that the economic-security part of the new investment envelope will be managed separately in a special account and funded by "bridge bonds" backed by an earmarked redemption source. The Ministry of Finance's tally of FY2027 budget requests, released in early September, came to a record JPY143tn, with the envelope, which has no request ceiling, at about JPY12tn excluding open-ended items. The size of the bridge bonds, the special account that will hold them, and their redemption source and deadline will all be decided in the year-end budget and issuance plan. This note sets out how the market should read the phrase "not deficit bonds", from both the accounting and the issuance side. The conclusion is clear. Pension triple lock reform: Limited near-term savings The government announced an ambition to create a National Care Service- a social care system which would be free at the point of use at the next Parliament. To fund the new social care system, the government proposed to reform the pension triple lock system. The state pension could be adjusted to rise by the higher of inflation or 2.5% in April 2030, while state pension will also hold its value relative to earnings over time. Currently the pension triple lock adjusts the state pension to the larger of 2.5%, inflation or earnings. The pension triple lock is an expensive policy, and the IFS has noted that the government spent an additional £9bn per year by 2026-27 on state pensions since 2010 as a result of the triple lock vs this new modified triple lock system. The government noted that this pension change can save £15bn per year by 2040 (£11bn in today’s money), while IFS estimates it could be anywhere between £4-20bn per year by 2040. Overall, modifying the pension triple lock would be a welcome step to reduce long term fiscal pressures which would have built up otherwise. But these savings are likely to build gradually rather than appearing immediately. Near term savings are likely to be small from this change- the IFS estimates that this pension reform would save around £4bn a year in today’s number by 2035. A new social care system, on the other hand, is expected to cost around £18bn/year by 2035

records.text: Global Economic Weekly | 02 October 2026 5 US Aditya Bhave BofAS Revisions, risks, rate hikes • Revisions may have lowered the recent level of inflation. However, they do not change the story on underlying inflation. • It’s still at 2.5% and risks to inflation remain titled to the upside from AI demand, energy, the labor market, and strong consumer growth. • Therefore, even if inflation is a little softer after the revisions, we continue to think the Fed will take a risk management approach and tighten policy further this year. Complete report: US Economic Weekly: Revisions, risks, and rate hikes Inflation revisions were dovish, underlying inflation isn’t Inflation remains the key determinant of the Fed's near-term policy outlook. This week, the BEA revised inflation data following methodological changes to three categories that had proven particularly difficult to measure: portfolio management and investment advice, computer and software accessories, and legal services (Exhibit 1). As expected, the revisions lowered recent inflation readings, although by somewhat more than we anticipated. Core PCE inflation was revised down by 35bp in July to 3.0% y/y, and Sep printed at 3.0%. While these revisions reduced the level of measured inflation and may initially appear dovish, they do little to change our assessment of underlying inflation (Exhibit 2). We continue to estimate underlying inflation at 2.5% y/y, with little evidence that the trend has improved over the past 12 months.

records.text: US Economic Presentation2 October 2026 ab 29 Source: Haver, UBS • We estimate two sources of acceleration in the coming years. One: waning drag from population aging. Two: we estimate AI to drive a regime shift, accelerating structural productivity growth. • Immigration is unlikely to be slower in 2027 than in 2025 or 2026. Plus, although the weight of population aging is still negative, the second derivative is turning positive. The weight lessens in the years to come. Not only is structural labor supply poised to accelerate, we think productivity growth is too, thanks to AI. • We estimate structural US GDP growth is headed to more like 2-1/2% in the coming three to five years, compared to sub-2% FOMC and pre-Covid estimates. Although yields remain elevated, market expectations for the October FOMC meeting fell substantially with just ~5bp of hikes priced for later this month. Revisions lowered core PCE inflation by close to 40bp, with the 3-month pace now at 2%. Job growth in September slowed and was revised lower in previous months, while the unemployment rate rose modestly to 4.2%. Growth remains resilient, but strength is heavily focused in AI-related parts of the economy. Consumer/household data is much more modest. We do not see signs that pockets of strength are leading to any retightening in the broader economy as wage growth continues to slow. We think Fed officials will be increasingly uncomfortable weakening the broader economy further as the labor market is already not a source of inflationary pressure. The event intensified through the summer and fall of 1997 (about where we are now in the current El Niño), setting sea-surface temperature records and reaching peak strength around December 1997. During late 1997 and early 1998, El Niño contributed to severe drought and wildfires in Indonesia, flooding in Peru, Ecuador, and East Africa, suppressed Atlantic hurricane activity, and an unusually wet and stormy winter across California and the southeastern US. The 1997-98 El Niño winter was milder than typical in the northeastern US (link here). The event remained strong through early 1998 before stronger easterly winds returned, allowing more upwelling of cold ocean water and eventually starting La Niña by the end of the year — the opposite of El Niño, when the tropical Pacific is cooler than normal. NOAA's map (link here) shows the disparate climate impacts of El Niño by region, with the southern US likely to see cooler and wetter weather in the winter. The widely varying weather impacts suggest that impacts on the food supply chain could be equally varied, depending on the timing and location. NOAA's primary metric for tracking El Niño phases and intensity is tracking in line with other strong El Niño seasons.

Pathway to stability Ultimately, and most importantly and fundamentally, resolution of this episode of stress requires investor confidence in a credible and sustainable fiscal trajectory in France. The hurdle is that the divided parliament since 2024 has found it difficult to reduce the deficit much. The government expects the deficit in 2026 to be 5.4% of GDP a nd is targeting a deficit of 5.0% of GDP in the draft 2027 Budget. This might be somewhat ambitious and we think the deficit target could rise to 5.2-5.3% and with growth likely to underperform the government’s assumption, the 2027 deficit might be unchanged at 5.4% . In any case, the 2027 budget is only part of the uncertainty. There is also the 2027 election and the uncertainty of what an RN government means for the trajectory of French fiscal policy and France’s relations with the EU (for a deep-dive on what RN means for France, see our three -part note: Part 1 : The path to power , Part 2 : The policy agenda, and Part 3: Europe). records.text: Canada Economics Weekly 02 October 2026 Citi Research 3 Next Week’s Highlights Key events in Canadian markets next week Tuesday, October 6, 8:30am Int’l Merchandise Trade (Aug) Trade data will remain a very important driver of quarterly GDP growth, with falling real exports and rising real imports in July suggesting a somewhat softer start to Q3 GDP by expenditure than recent GDP by industry data. Of course, trade data over the next few months will be impacted by new US tariffs and Canadian counter tariffs. There is some possibility that exports rise in August due to some front- loading ahead of possible tariffs, although we think this impact would be small as expectations at the time were mostly that tariffs would ultimately not be implemented. Still, some already-released US trade data does suggest Canadian exports to the US could rise in August, likely reflecting exports of goods such as energy products or gold. Of course, tariffs could weigh on trade volumes starting in September. Survey data on exports fell modestly in September. While the direct impact of tariffs and counter tariffs should be small, uncertainty around trade policy could shift trade patterns in various ways. The effect of trade on quarterly GDP data is likely to remain volatile. Figure 3. Canadian exports to the US may rise in August Figure 4. records.text: Cayla Seder 01 October 2026 1 Insights Classification: Premium Material D M Inf lation In Focu s : Depth, not brea dth INFLATION TRENDS. Inflation has been elevated for long enough that policymakers are increasingly comfortable tightening policy. Over the past month, six major developed market central banks raised rates, and markets have taken this as a green light to price in more than 800bps of cumulative tightening over the coming year. Whether those hikes ultimately materialize will depend largely on whether higher commodity prices generate meaningful second-round effects. While headline inflation is at seasonal record highs (Figure 3), it is important to determine how much of this reflects a pure commodity price shock. The impact of fuel prices is eye-watering. As of September 28, online fuel prices rose 5.15% m/m, exceeding the September 2026 average increase of 3.51% and dwarfing the seasonal median gain of just 0.31%. Not only are fuel prices exceptionally strong, but momentum also accelerated into month -end as diesel prices continued to climb. There is, however, some encouraging news on broader pass-through effects. Food prices rose only 17bps on average in September, just 6bps above seasonal norms. In a world where fuel prices are rising by more than 500bps, a 6bp deviation suggests that, so far, the inflation shock remains concentrated rather than broadly embedded. US. The accounting of bridge bonds: four devices for stepping outside the Public Finance Act Article 4 of the Public Finance Act requires expenditure to be funded from revenue other than bonds, with a proviso permitting construction bonds for public works, capital contributions and loans. Any shortfall beyond that is funded by deficit bonds under the special deficit-bond act (the current act authorizes FY2026 to FY2030). Bridge bonds are neither; each rest on a dedicated law. Reconstruction bonds rest on the reconstruction funding act, GX transition bonds on the GX promotion act, child-support special bonds on the child-support act and semiconductor/AI bonds on the information-processing promotion act; the precedents include the Gulf War special bonds, the tax-cut special bonds that preceded the 1997 consumption-tax rise, and the pension special bonds for the state's half share of basic pensions. records.text: d a very benign move up On the surface, the u-rate rose from 4.1% to 4.2%. But on an unrounded basis, it only increased from 4.14% to 4.17%, a very benign move. Also, the move was for “good reasons”. HH employment was up a robust 406k (Aug: 569k), second consecutive large increase. Unemployment came in softer (78k vs Aug: 115k). However, the LFPR rose two-tenths to 61.8%. Other measures of labor market slack, U2 & U6 were down. Slower wages the most dovish part of Sep jobs report Unexpectedly, average hourly earnings slowed to 0.1% m/m from 0.3% while average weekly hours stayed unchanged. Index of aggregate weekly payrolls (income proxy) also slowed a tenth to 4.2% y/y. This was probably the most dovish aspect of the jobs report. Fed: This shouldn’t matter, but it might The Sep jobs report wasn’t soft enough to shift the Fed’s focus away from inflation. On a 12-month basis, u-rate is down, claims are benign and job growth is above breakeven. But given the slew of dovish Fedspeak this week, we aren’t surprised that markets viewed it as yet another reason to price out an Oct hike. Risks have clearly shifted away from our call for an Oct hike: we will revisit the call after the Sep inflation releases. 02 October 2026 Macro United States Shruti Mishra US Economist BofAS smishra44@bofa.com Mark Cabana, CFA Rates Strategist BofAS mark.cabana@bofa.com Alex Cohen, CFA FX Strategist BofAS alex.cohen2@bofa.com US Economics BofAS See Team Page for List of Analysts NFP: Non-farm Payroll

records.text: 3 Insights Information Classification: General About PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. records.text: US Economic Presentation2 October 2026 ab 31 Source: Challenger, Gray & Christmas, Haver, UBS • AI in 2025 was cited as the primary reason for 6% of job cuts in announced downsizings. Adoption has been rising quickly as we show on the next page, and less hiring may result outside of just layoffs. • Incoming data on job destruction that includes firms hiring less, remains quite low, and shows little change from pre-Covid rates. As we show on the next page, job creation and destruction runs between 7 and 8 million jobs per quarter. Those rates should rise if we hit our higher productivity regime that we project. • Recent college graduate unemployment rates are up 0.5 pp over the year. Is that all AI? Probably not. Labor demand has been weak, including sectors not yet impacted by AI. AI’s productivity boost likely to come with more disruption We can see AI is having an impact on the labor market, but right now it seems like people see AI in everything. We estimate the impact of AI on the labor market currently to be modest, but we also expect this is still early days for AI disruption. In other words, despite its limited direct bilateral exposure to the US for diesel, Europe is ultimately exposed to its global clearing price. If a US diesel export ban reduces global diesel supply, Europe would likely have to pay a higher price for its imports. The decomposition of supply-chains also highlights the central role of The Netherlands. Most European imports of crude and refined products arrive on the continent via Rotterdam, and the country is a key refining and distribution node. This shows very well in trade flows: direct US exports of diesel to the Netherlands amount to more than 3.5 times the combined US exports of diesel to Germany, France, Italy and Spain. From that, we need to dig further into the actual use of diesel in Europe to understand better the dependencies. Eurostat (here) provides us with a wealth of detailed data, albeit most of the time at an annual frequency (the last observed point we used below is 2024). Let´s start with the euro area as a whole. The use of diesel in 2024 in the economy amounted to ca 2% of GDP. This consumption is heavily dominated, ca 80%, by the transport sector. And transport seems to be broadly split between direct household use on one hand and the transport of goods and other services on the other. records.text: 701/10/2026 Broad agreement on diagnosis, if not cure Sources: Polity, Democratic Alliance, MK Party, EFF, IFP, ActionSA, BNP Paribas Striking convergence on diagnosis of local-government failure: Despite major ideological differences, virtually all candidates are campaigning on the same basic crisis: unreliable water and electricity, collapsing infrastructure, weak revenue collection, corruption, politicised appointments and dysfunctional administrations. The argument is increasingly about who can make municipalities work rather than about whether they are failing. MK clear constitutional outlier: Among the six largest parties, MK is the only one explicitly proposing a fundamental break with the existing constitutional order: it calls for moving away from constitutional supremacy to “unfettered parliamentary supremacy” (see MK manifesto). EFF’s local-government offer relatively pragmatic: The EFF’s 2026 manifesto retains familiar themes – redistribution of municipal land, extensive free basic services, insourcing and a larger developmental role for the municipality – but combines these with unusually granular delivery commitments on water leaks, infrastructure, tariffs, environmental management and municipal administration, which we consider noticeably more pragmatic than its national ideological brand might suggest. There would be an increasing probability of a wait-and-see stance if the yen appreciated to around ¥145/$, but this would be unlikely if there was a robust consensus that US rates will rise further. The policy rate would be expected to reach 175bp or 200bp by the end of the fiscal year, and while this would still be below the neutral interest rate the chance of impacting the real economy would rise. Some will likely warn of the risk of a policy error. Given the two opposing votes at the MPM, pushing ahead with rate hikes regardless would be a risk to the BoJ’s relationship with the government. There could even be expectations that government representatives at MPMs could exercise their right to demand delays to decisions. This would become even more likely if the new Policy Board members that replace Hajime Takata and Naoki Tamura hold strongly reflationary views. On the other hand, this would likely limit the rise in the terminal rate. We think pricing would likely be for the rate hike cycle to end in the first half of next year, and if the market factors in 2.25%–2.50% for the July meeting it would be appropriate for pricing to remain flat thereafter. In other words, the forward curve could twist flatten. Long-term interest rates will likely continue to outperform Treasuries. records.text: European Rates Weekly 01 October 2026 Citi Research 14 EGB supply outlook into year-end Q4 EGB supply should prove more benign in DV01 terms, with higher gross issuance but slightly lower DV01 than in 2025, leaving full-year 2026 DV01 issuance broadly unchanged versus 2025. Beneath the aggregate picture, however, supply pressures in Q4 reflect issuer-specific NCR dynamics rather than outright issuance volumes. Q4 EGB supply less duration heavy. This week's EGB supply marked the largest weekly EGB issuance in both gross and DV01 terms since June, and is expected to trend lower from here - Figure 13. Although October would remain a relatively busy issuance month in gross terms, DV01 supply is set to ease more noticeably, with subsequent funding concentrated more in the belly of the curve following September's heavier skew towards the 15-20yr sector. November should see a more meaningful decline in gross supply than in DV01 terms, ahead of a seasonally light December. Relative to 2025, while higher funding needs this year have lifted supply in both gross and DV01 terms through most of the year, Q4 should be an exception, with higher gross issuance but slightly lower DV01, leaving full-year DV01 broadly in line with 2025 - Figure 14. From a macro-funding perspective, the better news is that France does not have a very large external imbalance. The current account deficit has stayed close to or below 1% of GDP, and 0.5% of GDP on 1H26 average despite high energy costs. Since then, it has remained broadly stable around those levels. • 5Y and 10Y Basis: Since the announcement of the US-Japan investment initiative total- ing $550bn in September last year, concerns over future USD funding needs had driven persistent flattening of the 5s/10s basis curve, primarily through further widening of the 10Y negative basis. Our view was reflecting our detailed analysis (here) that a small numbers of items (IT products, lubricants and medicines) were responsible for increasing goods inflation since the start of the year, and that this should continue this month. Only the details will tell us whether the surprise was seasonal (eg clothing and footwear) or more "structural". Further up from here: In all cases, it suggests there is still so far no clear evidence of a broad-based transmission from energy costs into goods inflation. We note however that producer prices have edged up in the past months (Exhibit 18 ). Adding that to the idiosyncratic factors we mentioned above, we expect goods inflation to trend up further from here, with a peak potentially in Mar-27 around 2.1%Y (Exhibit 15 ). On average we expect core goods inflation at 1.0%Y in 2026 and 1.8%Y in 2027.

records.text: Elections in a snapshot: South Africa's local government elections on 4 November 2026 will determine the composition of 257 municipal councils (4,488 wards), including eight metropolitan municipalities and 44 district municipalities. Just over 500 parties will compete for some 27.67 million registered voters (see Electoral Commission of South Africa). Local government receives about 8–9% of nationally raised revenue and constitutes the primary service-delivery interface for most citizens. Municipalities are responsible for the services, infrastructure and local governance systems that underpin economic activity and daily life. The eight metropolitan municipalities alone account for more than half of national economic output and almost half of all households. Ballot structure: Voters in the eight metros receive two ballots – proportional- representation party lists and ward candidates. In the 205 local municipalities, a third ballot is added for the district council PR vote. Seat allocation uses the ‘Droop quota’ (largest remainder) – the key structural driver of coalition proliferation, as it does not favour larger parties and lowers entry barriers for smaller ones. New rules for 2026 election fail to pass in time: A proposed 2026 Municipal Structures Amendment Bill is before parliament, but attempts to get it over the line in time for 4 November seem to have been unsuccessful. This likely reflects the repeated movement of agricultural products, food ingredients, packaging materials, and finished goods through the supply chain before they reach consumers. Motor vehicles and parts and furnishings and durable household equipment follow at roughly 4-5%, while clothing and footwear, recreational goods and vehicles, other durable goods, and other nondurable goods also exhibit above-average freight exposure. The prominence of food in the rankings is consistent with evidence from the USDA's Food Dollar accounts. For 2024, USDA estimates attribute roughly 6.3 cents of every food-at-home dollar to transportation and storage activities. Our Leontief-based measure reaches a similar conclusion, suggesting that nearly 7 cents of freight services are embedded in every dollar of food consumed at home, highlighting the transportation-intensive nature of modern food supply chains. For core PCE, the rankings point to a broader set of vulnerable categories than suggested by transportation margins alone. Motor vehicles and household durables remain among the most exposed categories, but apparel, recreational goods, and selected nondurable goods also rank highly once upstream freight requirements are taken into account. This shows very well in trade flows: direct US exports of diesel to the Netherlands amount to more than 3.5 times the combined US exports of diesel to Germany, France, Italy and Spain. records.text: Japan Rates Weekly 02 October 2026 Citi Research 3 Rate hikes to counter yen weakness a big risk Upward pressure has remained in the yen interest rate market even after the latest BoJ rate hike. The short-term market in particular has been greatly impacted by growing expectations of consecutive rate hikes. Pricing of an October rate hike is at about 40%, and the market appears to be pushing for a hawkish response. We titled our September 18 Rates Weekly Yen weakness acceptable at effectively fastest rate hike pace? because pricing at that time was for roughly one rate hike each quarter and we did not think any more hawkish action was possible. In contrast, the Fed and the ECB have the option of consecutive rate hikes. A strengthening consensus that interest rate spreads will widen would put downward pressure on the yen, and we did not think that correcting for this using monetary policy is appropriate. There is no change to our view. If the BoJ does make consecutive hike along with the Fed and the ECB, we think it will put upward pressure on the yen and have a very significant impact on interest- rate markets. Firstly, the market would likely price in a December rate hike to a considerable degree. This is because monetary policy would in effect be seen as a tool to control forex rates, so pricing would be similar to that for the Fed and the ECB. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 35 Single Name Coverage: What’s Topical Of Late in IG TMT Our single-name technology credit work remains focused on AI implications, including financing structures, ecosystem support, and supply-demand dynamics. Despite lighter September issuance, off-cycle earnings and headline flow continue to drive elevated investor inbound. NVDA and ORCL, both within our current coverage, remain central to these discussions, from a funding and lease documentation perspective: • NVDA – funding update: We initiated NVDA credit coverage with a neutral view. Exceptional growth has turned the balance sheet into a strategic financing tool, but the potential tail risks of what we call "balance sheet-as-a-service" remain early-stage, opaque, and significant. The FY2Q27 print reinforced an expanding support toolkit that now includes shell lease guarantees, revenue-share/contract price-floor support, and potential RVS structures tied to the announced $500bn partnership. A key debate remains how markets absorb ~$1tn guided GPU/XPU- related financing, including the structures, ratings treatment, and investor bases. • NVDA – lease documentation development: With its FY2Q27 earnings, NVDA's disclosure of plans to reassign ~$20bn of future shell leases intensified investor scrutiny of powered-shell documentation. • ORCL – funding update: ORCL completed its $20bn equity ATM program in FY1Q27. records.text: European Rates Weekly 01 October 2026 Citi Research 2 OAT-Bund widening can no longer be ignored by policymakers, especially after this week’s contagion risk. ECB pricing is reacting, rightly so as ending hikes should be the first response. Should any contagion grow, the next step might be to revisit QT (which is doubling net supply on EGBs). Our fair value model residual for 10yr OAT- Bunds is about 50bp, suggesting the political/fiscal premium in OATs is already extremely elevated. Fading OATs seems perilous, however, given some kind of ECB intervention may be necessary for tightening, which is hard to time. While the bond sell-off is global, the widening in OATs merits special attention as contagion risk grows. The accelerating pace of OAT widening is nothing short of dramatic, only seen before in times of crisis – Figure 1. In the last week alone, the 10yr OAT-Bund spread has widened about 30bp to 140bp. The spread widening had been largely isolated to France, and Italy to a lesser extent. In the last few days, however, there has been growing signs of contagion which bubbled over on Thursday (for example, 10yr Spain-Germany is around 15bp wider this week having been largely unmoved previously). Figure 1. The re-pricing in OAT-Bunds since March – and especially since July - is a major historical event and yet it is yet to attract much comment by the ECB. Figure 2. records.text: US Economic Presentation2 October 2026 ab 4 Source: BEA, Haver, UBS Households: bifurcated…tariffs, energy prices and refunds Tariffs and energy prices are eroding the boost from OBBBA. The labor market slowdown has lowered income growth. Real spending growth continues to handily outpace income, as AI wealth supports financing spending from saving. • The US consumer continues to spend. Spending has slowed on net from the robust pace of 2024, but not nearly as much as real disposable income growth. • Households across all income groups expect to be more sensitive to future inflation now than in 2022. At the same time, households are less able to weather inflation. Households below the top 20% of the income distribution have relatively low levels of liquid assets. • Equity market wealth in Q2 was an all-time high share of household wealth (38%) and has accounted for all of the gains in wealth the last few years. The S&P 500 helps. • We have seen a ~$60 billion boost to tax refunds, thanks to the OBBBA, so we should be passing peak fiscal support for spending. The key question beyond that: Can spending keep outpacing income? Research DSA scenario analysis Scenario #1: 100 bp interest rate shock Clemente De Lucia | +39 -02 402-43012 | clem ente.delucia@db.com | September 2026 10 • Our DSA baseline projects a declining (stabilising) debt ratio. However, there is no room for complacency: the debt ratio remains high and vulnerable to shocks, as our scenario analysis shows, underlining the need for further consolidation. We conducted two scenario analysis: • Scenario #1 (Interest rate shock): A 100bp upward shock to the yield curve (with the 10-year BTP peaking at 5.5% in 2027 and 2028 before easing to 4.4% by 2035) would push the debt ratio at 143% by the end of the decade and up to 145% by the end of the forecast horizon. In other words, such a shock would put the debt ratio on a non-convergent path. We calculate that a shock of up to 50bp on the yield curve (BTP at 5% in 2027 and 2028) would keep the debt ratio at c.140% of GDP until the end of the decade, before it eases to 138% by 2025. A shock of 50bp, therefore, could be seen as a sort threshold between converging and diverging debt-ratio path. • Scenario #2 (Growth shock): Our baseline assumes real growth gradually stabilising at its potential rate of 0.75%. Growth is projected at 0.8% in 2026 and at a similar rate in 2027, before slowing in 2028 after the end of NGEU support and then returning to potential. But even then, the bar for action is high. The ECB has flagged its desire to keep the unwinding of the APP and PEPP portfolios at a measured and predictable pace, for as long as they don’t interfere with policy transmission. The ECB has also indicated that when the unwinding creates too tight liquidity in the system, it will introduce new tools, including new longer-term refinancing operations and asset purchases under a new structural securities portfolio. But the conditions do not seem to be in place for those new tools. Eventually (see details below), they could be designed flexibly enough to deal with some of the current issues, but with limitations, given their objective is to ensure enough reserves are in the system. Structural securities portfolio We see ECB purchases of EGBs through a structural securities portfolio as unlikely in the near term. But this is where we enter a grey area. First, because the move would need to be judged as disorderly by the ECB, and that’s where likely the bar is significantly higher than what market participants would consider disorderly. The reason the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) was created was exactly that, to deal with those disorderly moves unjustified by fundamentals. “In particular, as the Governing Council continues normalising monetary policy, the TPI will ensure that the monetary policy stance is transmitted smoothly across all euro area countries. The singleness of the Governing Council’s monetary policy is a precondition for the ECB to be able to deliver on its price stability mandate.” On our reading, it was created to make sure nothing broke when the ECB had to tighten aggressively in response to the last energy price shock. It was never used, though, and probably not even fully finalised. What’s a disorderly move? “A deterioration in financing conditions not warranted by country-specific fundamentals, to counter risks to the transmission mechanism to the extent necessary.” How would that be decided?

This may reflect this summer’s extreme weather and could be an important driver of the upside surprises relative to consensus. The near-term risk skew remains to the upside. (3) Energy prices rose sharply. While higher fuel prices should not have come as a surprise (and duty cuts will provide some relief in several countries in October), gas inflation also appears to be accelerating. Our bottom-up models suggest that October will be even stronger and could see the strongest monthly gas price increase since 2022 (Figure 27), despite Spain’s announced price cap, with further gains likely in subsequent months. records.text: 2 October 2026 Europe Blog Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 The concern is there are fundamental risks, too. There are public debt vulnerabilities in Europe. Public finances have not recovered from the pandemic shock. France ranks highest on our fiscal vulnerability indicator – defined as the distance from EU fiscal targets and recommendations – and has the added challenge of a weak NIIP. Fiscal vulnerability is a spectrum and others have to be careful about their public finances, too (see our recent note on Italy). The current situation is not like the debt crises 10 -15 years ago. That was preceded by a credit bubble which via a banking shock translated into increased fiscal pressures; the exception was Greece which was a genuine fiscal crisis. After a decade of rebuilding, the European banking system is much stronger in general and French banks are not significantly exposed to OATs . A sovereign -banking negative feedback loop should not be a primary driver of events – but should be watched as a potential secondary driver. Europe also has a much more developed and broad-based stability architecture today (e.g., ESM, SRM, TPI, etc). But there are differences , too. The combination of generally higher levels of deficit and debt post -pandemic, structural spending needs (strategic autonomy including defence) and rising global yields have narrowed the fiscal room for manoeuvre for many governments across Europe and made it harder to comply with the bloc’s fiscal rules. records.text: d inflation focuses on crude oil prices or broader energy shocks. Yet diesel has materially outperformed crude this year, raising a distinct question for inflation: how much does a diesel shock matter? Unlike gasoline, which is consumed directly by households and primarily affects inflation through energy-related CPI and PCE components, diesel is largely an intermediate input. It fuels the trucks, trains, ships, and delivery networks that move goods through the economy, and jet fuel prices also tend to be closely correlated to diesel prices. As a result, the effects of a diesel shock are unlikely to be confined to the energy line items of the inflation basket, and a spillover into core goods and services inflation appears almost inevitable. The key questions are how much of a diesel shock ultimately reaches consumer prices, which categories are most exposed, and whether the transmission is large enough to materially affect the broader inflation outlook. To answer those questions, we examine diesel exposure through two complementary lenses. The first measures transportation margins embedded in final consumer prices, while the second captures freight services used throughout the production chain. Together, the two measures provide a comprehensive view of which categories are most exposed to higher diesel costs and the likely magnitude of pass-through to inflation. records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 4 GDP revisions: what we learned What did we learn about the economy this week? The rich get richer and the expansion looks as reliant on AI as ever. The annual revisions to the National Economic Accounts made the economy look somewhat better on paper: cumulative GDP is higher, core PCE inflation is lower, nominal income is stronger, and the saving rate was revised up. But they did not change the underlying story. Growth remains unusually concentrated, labor is capturing less of national income, and most of the income upgrade reflects returns to assets rather than a broad improvement in household finances. GDP was revised up, but it remains narrow Real GDP in Q2 2026 was revised 0.6% higher, mainly because of business fixed investment (+0.4 pp) and government consumption and investment (+0.4 pp), partly offset by net exports (-0.1 pp), consumption (-0.2 pp), and less inventory building. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 Fairly steady labor demand, with a hint of softer Slower September and 3Q payrolls, with downward revision Payrolls at 29k and private payrolls at 46k were a little below our expectations. The slowdown was fairly broad; it appeared to reflect genuine slowing rather than the summertime volatility that had characterized recent months. Payrolls ran marginally slower in 3Q (61k per month average) than 2Q (81k) or 1Q (73k). September also included some slowing in aggregate hours worked and in payroll incomes. On net, the pattern in payrolls was about as we expected (slowing, but not because of payback for industry volatility), but at the margin, the payrolls data were a touch softer than we anticipated. Goods-related payrolls (manufacturing, retail, wholesale, transport) have rebounded this year, and their strength extended into September. After a slight pause initially reported in June and July, they resumed their rise in August and September—with strength in August and September reports and appear to be stabilizing at a decent rate of growth. The huge month-to-month summer time swings in leisure payrolls had seemed unlikely: they ran counter to the timing of the World Cup and appeared mostly to reflect swings in seasonals. In today's report, leisure payrolls stabliized at about the pace we had expected: the summertime seasonal swings appear to be over. The swings in government payrolls hid some underlying slowing. Verbal intervention is the first line of response. QT fine-tuning is unlikely, we think, at least in the very short run. Conditions are not there to create new longer-term refinancing operations, while asset purchases under a new structural securities portfolio to deal with excess reserves also appear unlikely. The dedicated law limits the purpose and period of issuance and sets the redemption source and deadline in its text. That is the first device. The second device is the account. Construction and deficit bonds are issued in the general account, but reconstruction bonds are issued in the reconstruction special account, GX and semiconductor/AI bonds in the energy special account, and child- support bonds in the child-support special account, with proceeds recorded as revenue of each. The Basic Policy's "separate management in a special account" means either a new account or a new sub-account in an existing one, the third such design after GX and AI/semiconductors. The third device is the redemption rule. Construction and deficit bonds follow the 60-year rule: 1.6% of the prior year's opening balance is transferred from the general account to the National Debt Consolidation Fund each year and the rest is refinanced. Bridge bonds are outside that fixed-rate transfer; each special account transfers the earmarked revenue it receives, that amount is redeemed in cash, and the excess is refinanced. The deadline is legislated: reconstruction bonds by FY2047, GX and semiconductor/AI bonds by FY2050 and child-support bonds by FY2051, including their refunding bonds. This week’s policy announcements on pension triple lock reform, social care and Brexit marked a potentially important long- term shift in direction, but don’t affect the near- term outlook materially and provided limited hints about the upcoming Budget. records.text: Surging hyperscaler capex will once again support EPS growth for the aggregate S&P 500 index this quarter. Consensus estimates show hyperscaler capex growing by 116% year/year in Q3 2026. This compares with 87% growth in Q2. We expect that hyperscaler capex spending will grow by more than 50% in 2027, surpassing current consensus estimates for spending of roughly $1.1 trillion next year, but also expect that the rate of both capex growth and upside surprises will diminish relative to recent quarters. Our recent conversations with investors about the outlook for AI capex have focused primarily on the uncertainty surrounding 2028 spending, but we do not expect companies will provide much clarity on capex beyond 2027 during this earnings season. In addition to the outlook for AI capex, evidence of return on AI investments will again be a key focus this earnings season. Last quarter, the hyperscalers reported accelerating cloud revenue growth and large revenue backlogs that signaled the monetization of their capex investments. ab 1 October 2026 Global Research Global Rates Strategy The Great French Rotation French risk is no longer a one-dimensional story. Budget 2027, pension reform, social- security financing and rating reviews are all back in focus. Investors are becoming more selective, within France as well as across EUR rates. The question is no longer whether France faces challenges, but where investors choose to position around them. Our answer remains: increasingly in EU bonds. Short 10y France vs EU: An alternative to OATs We continue to favour 10Y EU versus OATs and have raised our target on short 10y France vs EU to 85bp from 75bp, with a stop at 65 bps. The EU is increasingly the natural destination for investors cutting OAT exposure, benefiting from its high rating, predictable issuance profile and lower single-country risk. Growing liquidity matters too, with syndicated transactions increasingly pricing against the EU curve itself. Strong demand, rising APAC participation and a potentially lower 2027 funding requirement due to slower SAFE and Ukraine loan disbursements should continue to support EU valuations. By contrast, investor appetite for French credit remains weak and the easier the Budget 2027 process proves politically, the less fiscal consolidation is likely to be delivered. Power opportunism, not policy: Coalition formation is driven by position allocation – mayor, deputy mayor, speaker – rather than shared governance mandates. A stable coalition can be stably dysfunctional. The LGMSAA's 90-day framework and simultaneous no-confidence requirement are the legislative attempt to change this calculus; but the MISTRA Barometer II notes these provisions have not yet been tested under adversarial conditions. Paradox: Despite the ANC's national vote share collapsing to 40.2% in 2024, it reclaimed executive control across multiple coalition councils by 2024–25 – not through restored majorities, but through confidence-and-supply arrangements with the EFF and micro-parties, decoupling the national vote share and local executive power. Across countries, the data point to considerable heterogeneity (Figure 8). Among the largest economies, storage levels look more worryingly low in Germany (57.9%) and the Netherlands (58.5%) than in France (83.5%), Italy (87.1%) or Spain (74.6%). This partly reflects differences in national regulatory setups. For example, in France, suppliers must legally fill at least 85% of their booked capacity by 1 November, while in Germany, booking carries no corresponding injection obligation, leaving replenishment to commercial incentives. With the federal authorities so far reluctant to intervene and the curve structure blunting the incentive for capacity holders to refill over the spring, Germany now looks on track to miss its national target of 70% by 1 November. The UK has much less storage capacity, as 49% of its total gas use comes from domestic production, and 69% of gas imports come from Norway via a direct pipeline. As such, storage in the UK is used more for short-term volatility smoothing rather than to meet structural demand in the medium term, although low European storage levels affect the UK wholesale price due to the interconnected energy market. Some relief from El Niño? Historically, El Niño episodes have been associated with warmer winter conditions in

wo more rate hikes (vs. market pricing that is closer to four). Technical factors will likely dominate in the near term, especially around investor outflows. With IG down 3% in total return on the year and 4% on the quarter, the drawdown has reached a level where mutual funds/ETFs could see meaningful redemptions. But it is worth remembering that over the past five years, the credit market has seen multiple bouts of rate repricing, as the 10Y has gone from 1% to over 5%. While the rate-hiking cycle of 2021/2022 created a sustained drag on spreads and outflows, that was a case of much higher inflation and the Fed being behind the curve. Today it appears to be a case of inflation not coming down fast enough, coupled with robust growth driving a modest reset higher in policy rates. That said, we also cautiously think we are now at peak hawkishness, as higher energy commodity prices would erode domestic demand by lowering real wage (DM FX Weekly). Given this, we identified historical cases similar to the current episode based on the following criteria: (1) the upward trend in UST yields continued for more than 6 months, and (2) there was a ‘peak’ month of significant monetary policy repricing around the end of this rally, during which the expected short-term rate of both UST 2Y and 10Y rose by more than +35bp. records.text: We also think it is important to emphasise that liquidity demand is state-contingent. This is well illustrated throughout Euro area history. In particular, large swings in reserves have been associated with increased money market volatility even at relatively high levels of liquidity (Exhibit 7). Further, ECB research has also shown that reserve demand curves can shift meaningfully in periods of market stress, as was evidenced during the Euro area crisis. Whither QT? Given that reserves will be supplied via lending facilities, there is in theory no need to stop QT – the BoE’s recent QT plans point to quite low equilibrium Gilt holdings in the long run. At its operational framework review, the ECB stated an intention for the end of QT to come last in the balance sheet normalisation process. The rationale for this is that even as liquidity injections are supposed to be the marginal tool to provide liquidity, asset purchases force liquidity in the system whereas refinancing operations are dependent on bank behavior. One approach to think about what size of bond portfolio would be desirable is that of Vissing-Jorgensen, using a convenience yield framework to measure the impact of central bank bond holdings. Convenience yields are a measure of the financial system’s preference for sovereign bonds over other forms of duration. records.text: US Economics Weekly 02 October 2026 Citi Research 2 A substantial move higher in US Treasury yields over the last month took a pause this week, but despite numerous dovish developments, 2-year yields were less than 10bp lower over the week and 10-year yields were slightly higher. Yields remain sensitive to oil prices but were more reactive this week to global developments and dovish Fed speak. Yields were much less responsive to clearly dovish data, but we do not think Fed officials will be as dismissive. Most notably, both NY Fed President Williams and Fed Vice Chair Jefferson clearly pushed back on near-term market pricing for another rate hike. Pricing for the October meeting fell from ~16bp of a hike priced a week ago to about 5bp now. Data before each meeting will ultimately determine the path of policy rates, and our base case remains that this data will support leaving rates unchanged for the foreseeable future (until cuts resume in June 2027).
