records.text: ports. But the relevant comparator is no longer only another equity market. With gilt yields elevated and our economists expecting Bank Rate to reach 4.25%, UK equities are also competing against a higher domestic risk-free rate. That raises the proof required from long-duration equities, leveraged balance sheets and dividends without convincing cash cover. At the same time, the valuation pillar has weakened materially from August, HOLT market implied return spreads have narrowed and M&A premiums have normalised. The UK is still cheap, but less obviously mispriced once the cost of capital and earnings risk are considered. This sharpens the value case. Healthcare and selected defensives retain low relative valuation percentiles, while Consumer Discretionary, Materials and Industrials carry greater valuation risk against their own histories. The opportunity is not to buy the discount. It is to identify where the discount overcompensates for funding, policy and earnings risk. Sentiment: The macro has improved faster than conviction The missing ingredient remains sponsorship. UK funds continue to experience outflows, active and passive allocations lag Europe, and crowding remains elevated in parts of the market. Options volatility is subdued, but weak momentum and continued underperformance from conventional quality factors show that calm has not become conviction. Return dispersion has eased from last month’s extreme but remains elevated, sustaining the case for stock selection.

US Economics September employment: Back in orbit September payrolls surprised to the downside, following the exaggerated August strength. An increase in the labor force outpaced household employment gains, lifting the labor force (+0.2pp) and unemployment (+0.1pp) rates. The estimates reinforce signals that the FOMC will remain on hold in October. • September's employment estimates came in weaker than expected, downplaying earlier signs of reacceleration, with the BLS reporting a 29k gain in nonfarm payrolls (Barclays: 50k; consensus: 90k) on the heels of a cumulative 60k downward revision to the prior two months' data, which took August's spike down from +162k to +133k. Adjustments to seasonal factors played a big role in amplifying August job gains and depressing September's. Treasury’s expanded buybacks have n functioned similarly to previous liquidity support operations. The latest operations appear consistent with Treasury behaving in a price sensitive manner—purchasing off-the-runs at prices cheap to market mid at the time of the operation, consistent with patterns at prior buybacks (Exhibit 2). The latest operation saw much larger participation, with offer volumes 4x the size of the previous two expanded buybacks, potentially reflecting participants using the liquidity event as an opportunity to reduce risk amid Thursday’s rally. Prior to this, the expanded buybacks had seen significantly less participation than previous operations at the long end. So far, the larger buybacks have done little to encourage lower yields, but spreads have remained well-supported despite the increase in rate volatility since their announcement. Given buybacks’ limited impact on rate levels, growing attention has focused on other ways Treasury can ease pressures on duration, including reducing long-end auction sizes. The normalization of fuel tax on 1 September is behind the sharp uptick in headline, while imported inflation and public transport ticket reduction will exert downward pressure on core. UK | Fiscal & MPC speak: This week, Prime Minister Burnham announced the reform of the pension triple lock, from April 2030. The government's plan is to uprate pensions by the higher of inflation and 2.5%, while ensuring that the state pension keeps up with average earnings growth over time. Near-term savings are negligible - the OBR already assumes the triple lock guarantor is 2.5% into 2030 - and even the long-run savings depend on inflation and earnings growth. Any potential savings, it is important to stress, exist in relation to the counterfactual, where with the current triple lock, any major price shock boosts the state pension in a 2-step process, first as spot inflation rises, and then as wage growth adjusts with a lag. As such, it is important to look at this measure not as a spending cut, but rather as a major reduction in fiscal risks. Fiscal policy will remain in focus as the Budget nears (October 28). D

records.text: 12 Local government mandate on the ballot: The SRF/The Common Sense poll (March 2026) confirms that the issues South Africans consider most pressing combine national, provincial and municipal deliverables. Jobs and unemployment, the top priority for voters in the survey, are generally but not exclusively seen as the purview of national and provincial rather than municipal government. Of the other top concerns, water, roads, housing and electricity are the ones where municipalities are the primary delivery authority. Their combined weight among cited concerns is not a coincidence, in our view, but reflects the accumulated cost of two decades of municipal decay, which is now becoming more evident in failing levels of basic service delivery in even the largest metropolitan municipalities in core economic hubs of the country, namely Gauteng. General focus on practical delivery: The signature issues of the most vocal opposition parties, the EFF and MK, ranked at the bottom of the survey: racism and land reform. This suggests an electorate preferring service delivery rather than redistributive politics. However, illegal immigration ranked second in the poll with 23.3% – a level we have not seen in any comparable South African poll of the past decade. This concern appears to be concentrated in Gauteng and Cape Town metros, closely associated with Patriotic Alliance and ActionSA politics. records.text: EU—The Recovery Fund Ends With an Upside Surprise to 2026 EU Debt Supply Outlook The final funding applications under NextGenerationEU, commonly referred to as the European Recovery Fund (RF), were submitted by EU Member States by September 30. The European Commission is now assessing the related milestones and targets ahead of the final disbursements. With the application phase complete, the programme is drawing to a close, providing greater visibility on both its legacy and the scale of EU debt issuance in 2026. Final Recovery Fund Disbursements Fall Slightly Short of Expectations The original EUR 750bn Recovery Fund envelope announced in 2021, equivalent to around 3% of EU GDP , was subsequently revised down to EUR 573bn. Of this reduced envelope, less than EUR 10bn is likely to be forgone because some Member States did not deliver all previously agreed commitments. We therefore expect total disbursements to reach almost EUR 570bn, including EUR 55bn already paid in the first half of 2026. Full-year disbursements would consequently exceed EUR 170bn, well above our EUR 130bn forecast at the beginning of the year (Exhibit 1). The grant allocation will be almost entirely disbursed by year-end, but the programme’s loan component has been progressively reduced. With Southern European sovereign spreads remaining contained until recently, the funding-cost advantage of borrowing through EU-funded loans has narrowed. Fuel-surcharge mechanisms can transmit higher diesel prices into freight bills relatively quickly, but manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers need not immediately reprice their products in response. Existing inventories, margin absorption, contractual arrangements and operational adjustments can initially buffer the shock. If higher diesel prices persist, however, an increasing share of inventories will have been produced and transported at the higher cost, contracts will reset, and firms may become more willing to pass those costs through. In that sense, the duration of the diesel-price shock matters more for consumer inflation than its peak. Estimated inflation effects: Persistence is key Figure 12 reports the estimated cumulative price-level effects of an 80% sustained diesel-price shock under a range of operating-cost and pass-through assumptions. These should be viewed as conditional estimates of the potential price- level effect if higher diesel prices persist. They argue inflationary conditions are exhibiting the patterns of a typical supply shock, with a sharp increase in the price level (fuels, transportation, food); followed by normal, seasonally adjusted, monthly inflation rates; and low diffusion across the consumer basket (only 38% of goods and services are showing yoy inflation above 3%, while the historical average in the inflation-targeting period is 39%). Super core inflation – that is CPI excluding food, energy and transportation – is at 1.8%, below the BCRP’s 2% target. We expect two 25bp rate hikes, December and January During the more than 20 years of inflation targeting in Peru, every time 12-month inflation expectations have exceeded 3% (upper bound of the tolerance range) the Central Bank has always hiked rates. Although sometimes not immediately. Now, 12- month inflation expectations are slightly above 3%. It seems like the BCRP will be forced to hike before the end of the year. records.text: becomes vacant. This raises the possibility of a ‘two-centre’ arrangement – a new ANC leader shaping party strategy while Ramaphosa continues to lead the government. Having lost its parliamentary majority in 2024, the ANC can no longer determine the presidency alone; it will need partners to carry that in the legislature. One possibility is that the ANC initially attempts to govern through a minority arrangement after 2027. The Ramaphosa question: Ramaphosa's continuation as a stable anchor until 2029 has been less assured after May’s Constitutional Court ruling revived an impeachment process against him. Protracted litigation could leave the issue unresolved into the ANC's pre-conference period, complicating succession politics. Though the ANC would have enough seats to block his removal in the National Assembly, the immediate risk is prolonged leadership uncertainty and coalition strain, as Ramaphosa is the leader who has probably invested most personal political capital in building the GNU. Speaker Didiza's role in overseeing the parliamentary process adds a further political dimension, given her standing as a possible successor to Ramaphosa. records.text: M Global Idea Morgan Stanley Research 9 Looking ahead beyond 4Q26, however, we think that much of the hyperscaler decompression trade has played out. While a persistent basis to the broader index is warranted on elevated absolute and relative supply, spreads have widened a fair amount (similar to banks in the past). There is more (albeit not perfect) clarity on the cadence and frequency of issuance. Our analysts' estimates for ROIC also remain robust, with more evidence of that coming through over the next year. We also think that in 2027, capex will shift toward components such as chips, where financing is more tailored to short duration/asset-level/private capital. That doesn’t mean less IG issuance per se, but potentially a smaller y/y increase than we saw this year. Additionally, as rates stabilize, yield-based investors will likely continue to remain an anchor (despite low spreads) due to the moves on the Treasury benchmark. The story is arguably different for the big semiconductor names, in our view, as we've gotten little clarity so far on the magnitude and format of chip financing structures. A lot of the chip financing remains ahead of us, and what form it will take/which markets and investor pockets will be involved are all unknowns for now (see the recent credit initiation on NVDA for more thoughts). records.text: 2 October 2026 UK Weekly Digest Deutsche Bank AG Page 4 Whatever can’t be explained by a typical MPC surprise can also shed some light on recent curve movements. For example, if front -end rates have risen by less than would typically be expected following a policy surprise, it may suggest that markets are placing more weight on tightening over f uture meetings rather than on an immediate move. We highlight one caveat: t his method tells us how much the market move resembles policy tightening . I t does not mean its economic effects will match those of an actual Bank Rate change, because the two can have different drivers and work through different channels. What do our estimates show? First, we find that the market has delivered the equivalent of about 40bp of surprise tightening. That is close to the cumulative insurance hikes we expect the MPC to deliver in the upcoming meetings. Second, as seen in Figure 4, the fit isn’t perfect . However, it tells us something interesting. Compared with a typical MPC surprise, short-term rates have risen by less, and ten -year yields have risen by more, suggesting that markets may be pricing hikes for upcoming meetings rather than an immediate move. In other words, much of this tightening depends on the MPC eventually delivering, a point we come back to in the conclusion. records.text: Exhibit 3 highlights a few general conclusions. Oil screens well because oil implied volatilities are more subdued than in the earlier periods of the Iran War. Rates volatility has risen sharply and while the directional moves are clear in both scenarios, high implied volatilities combined with the offsetting effects on rates of growth and policy on rates in an oil shock mean that they do not screen as the best exposure to a move in oil prices. Europe’s exposure to energy prices means that Europe-linked assets across asset classes screen well to both a rise and fall in oil prices. Low FX-implied volatilities mean that European FX screens as well as, or better than, equities as an expression of either scenario. As always, there are limits to this sort of approach. The magnitudes of these scenarios could easily be different. The rise in oil prices in an adverse scenario that we show here is clearly not an upper bound and it is easy to imagine a larger shock. But if we have assumed the “right” mix of macro shocks (oil, policy, growth), then the rank ordering of assets in each scenario would remain the same, so this exercise is still helpful in informing the relative sensitivity of assets to each scenario. records.text: ab 1 October 2026 Global Research Global Strategy DM rates rout: Where are the weak links in EM? EM has outperformed through the DM rates rout. Is this now changing? Strong global growth and superior fiscal balance sheets have enabled EM outperformance through the DM rates rout thus far. Over the past week, however, strains from higher yields are evoking greater growth angst - global equity breadth and credit spreads have deteriorated quickly; the Mexican peso - a barometer of EM sentiment - relinquished its YTD gains in a week. Where are the asymmetric risks in EM from here if the rates selloff deepens? Who will likely stand tall despite the risks? Several FX weak links; equity & debt benchmarks better anchored than the past FX still has several weak links, in our view. Recall that large parts of EM struggled this year before the recent rise in volatility amid mediocre growth differentials vs the US, external health, and carry. Now, widening divergence in US-Europe real yields and France-Germany spreads are indicating further upside risks for the broad dollar, all else equal. Last month we recommended added long USD exposure via PHP; now we tactically add a 50% long USDZAR / 50% long MXNZAR basket targeting 3-5% gains - seeing ZAR as expensive relative to its terms of trade and vulnerable to any further tightening in global credit conditions. The market also expects that in the long run, higher productivity will contain price pressures. Lower realized and expected inflation should help compress breakevens across the curve, allowing the Fed to downshift from restrictive policy to neutral. The inflation breakeven curve, which is currently inverted, should normalize, with higher inflation expectations at the long end than at the front end. All else equal, this argues for marginally lower nominal rates and a steeper curve. However, faster productivity growth also raises expected returns on capital, which sustains high investment demand and reduces saving. records.text: European Rates Weekly 01 October 2026 Citi Research 12 We affirm our 2027 gross supply forecast of €125bn for the EU, whilst acknowledging the downside risks to it. In 2027, €40.1bn of EU bonds mature of which €3bn are EFSM/MFA bonds which we expect will not be refinanced. SAFE disbursements have started slow (only €12bn disbursed so far) and will be disbursed over five years in 2026-30. Assuming c. €20bn will be disbursed this year, this leaves c. €30bn/year for 2027-30. The disbursements under the Ukraine Loan Support (ULS) have also started slowly (€14.7bn disbursed according to EC data) and whilst the loan availability period is 2026-27, the ULS Regulation allows the disbursements to be made by 31 December 2028 suggesting that some of these loans and the funding for them might slip into 2028. Finally, the other EU programmes funded with joint EU debt (MFA, Western Balkans) make up a relatively small part of its funding needs. All told, we affirm our 2027 supply forecast of €125bn of gross supply and €90bn of NCR for the EU. However, the risks to our forecast, given EU’s expected liquidity surplus at the end of 2026, are to the downside. RV update Another volatile week – it is all about OATs. records.text: Marija Veitmane 01 October 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Europe an Banks – crowded, expensive and past the best Bond yields have surged over the past month, pushing rates to cycle highs. So far, equities have absorbed the rise reasonably well, largely thanks to exceptionally strong earnings from the Technology sector. Indeed, Technology and Communication Services were the only sectors to deliver positive returns over the month. Financials, by contrast, were among the weakest performers globally, with the sharpest selling concentrated in the US. European banks have held up better, but we believe they are increasingly vulnerable to underperformance due to a combination of crowded positioning, elevated valuations, and peaking fundamentals. • Positioning risk. Financials is the most crowded sector in Europe. Institutional investors built large positions there in 2024 when the yield curve has finally steepened, supporting profitability in the sector (Figure 1). Indeed, the shape of the yield curve has been one of the key drivers of institutional investors positioning making recent curve flattening potential catalyst for selling. • Valuation risk. Valuations are becoming more difficult to justify – while a Price / Book of 1.6 times is not particularly high, it is the highest level since 2008 (Figure 2). records.text: US Economics Weekly2 October 2026 ab 22 Soft September employment report Nonfarm payroll employment is estimated to have expanded just 29K in September, much more downside payback from the strength in August than we expected (UBS: 95K; Cons: 90K). Prior months were revised down -60K, but, smoothing through the ups and downs the general trend in job gains does not look much different to us now than it did at 8:29 am this morning. Private employment expanded 46K in September, short of our expectations and consensus (UBS: 90K; Cons: 81K) and in our preview about as low as we thought a reasonable range of possibilities would allow. Smoothing through the ups and downs, private employment has posted an acceptable 68K jobs over the past two months on average, which compares to a 3-month MA of 54K, a 4-month MA of 47K and a 6- month MA of 67K. Total NFP has averaged 66K per month over the last six months. If we thought the survey had 10K to 20K per month of average overstatement, that would put a fundamental pace of job gains around 50K to 60K per month as the trend. Not bad and not much different than we wrote in our preview last Friday. The August report in retrospect overstated the strength in the labor market, on top of a seasonal swing that supported August at the expense of September by more than we appreciated would unfold, and the residual net birth-death adjustment in September was less supportive than we anticipated. With the budget scheduled for October 28, we expect fiscal concerns to increasingly weigh on Sterling. Although PM Burnham and Chancellor Healey are generally viewed as fiscally conservative, much of the discussion at the Labour Party's annual conference focused on longer-term initiatives such as pension reform, electoral reform, and closer ties with the EU- all of which of have limited implications for the near term. The more immediate challenge is that the Office for Budget Responsibility's fiscal headroom is narrowing for several reasons. First, government spending remains elevated. Between April and August, borrowing exceeded expectations by £8.1bn, reflecting, in part, both the Defence Investment Plan and growth challenges. Notably, the growth outlook has become more challenging relative to the OBR's March projections. While the government forecast 1.6% growth in 2027, consensus expectations have fallen to 1.2% from 1.4%, widening the gap between official and market forecasts. At the same time, higher borrowing costs are steadily eroding fiscal headroom. When the OBR estimated headroom at a relatively comfortable £23.6bn in March, more than double the £9.9bn projected a year earlier, 10-year gilt yields were around 4.2%; today they are roughly 120bp higher. Similarly, instances in which the FOMC left policy unchanged near elections can largely be explained by the broader macroeconomic and policy backdrop. We do not find evidence that the FOMC has "skipped" a rate hike or cut ahead of an election, or otherwise interrupted the policy cycle. The Committee's decision to remain on hold in October 2006 reflected a pause following an extended tightening cycle. Election- adjacent meetings in 2012 and 2014 occurred while the federal funds rate was pinned at the zero lower bound, making a hold the expected outcome. Likewise, the decision to leave rates unchanged ahead of the 2016 election was consistent with the prolonged pause following the December 2015 liftoff, rather than an apparent reluctance to act during an election period. The historical record of rate cuts near elections points to a similar conclusion. The election-period easings in 1990 and 2008 occurred amid active easing cycles and reflected deteriorating economic conditions. In particular, the cumulative 100 bps of rate cuts in October 2008 took place as the FOMC moved aggressively toward the zero lower bound. Taken together, these episodes provide little evidence that the FOMC delays or avoids warranted policy actions ahead of federal elections. Open short 10y Italy vs Germany with 150 bps target (entry: 119, stop: 100) A cycle like no other with resilient growth, energy price risks and a broadening demand for capital will put segments of the rate complex under pressure while demand for safety could increase. records.text: What can stop OAT-Bund spread widening? We see three possible routes to n stabilisation. First, inflation relief from global energy prices. The connection between energy prices and global yields, and the heightened correlation of OAT-bund spreads to 10y USTs recently, suggests that a stabilisation in global duration and/or less acute energy risks would be beneficial for OATs too. Second, signs of successful negotiations for the 2027 budget - keeping the deficit as close as possible to the government objective of 5.0% - or evidence of increased fiscal caution by presidential contenders could offer support. Third, financial conditions tighten sufficiently to warrant a shift in growth and inflation expectations, and thus a policy response from the ECB. As above, the hurdle for a significant policy shift – especially using the ECB’s balance sheet – is likely relatively high, especially given both resilient Euro area growth and also underlying fiscal risks in France. However, the rapidity of the sell-off vs fundamentals, and the increasing spillover to other EGB markets is building the case for some shift in policy messaging, with the first step likely to be the ECB reiterating that its tools are available should market conditions be deemed disorderly and challenge the transmission of monetary policy. Governance deficit amplified in coalitions: Coalition municipalities suffer additional distraction: councillors and administrators are diverted by the continuous work of constructing, defending or dismantling governing majorities. Motions of no-confidence and by-elections accumulate without producing measurable improvements in service delivery. Johannesburg changed mayors five times in 2021–24, with each change consuming administrative bandwidth that could otherwise have been directed at service delivery. records.text: 2 Europe Economic Weekly | 02 October 2026 Weekly view The pushback has started Bond market moves continue to capture attention. Yes, France gets (and, to some extent, deserves) particular attention, but the moves are broad-based. Euro area AAA 30- year yields are at their highest level in more than 10 years. The 10-year real yield is higher than it was during peak policy tightening in 2023. And the nominal effective exchange rate may have come off 1.4% since its summer-25 peak, but it is still much closer to that peak than to its long-term average (+8.5% vs 2019-24, for instance). Our rates colleagues highlight ECB pricing as a key ingredient in the rise in long-term yields. The market sees close to another 100bp of rate hikes by next summer (on top of the 50bp already delivered), without any tangible correction lower thereafter. We view that as too much, and expect one more hike in December, with risks of a second, but not more. What can the ECB do? In our main piece today, we discuss options for the central bank to push back. Our thoughts run along two lines: first, for generalised tightening in financial conditions, verbal interventions and guidance on the policy rate cycle would be arguably its preferred tool. The ECB seems to have become nervous now too on the general tightening of financing conditions. The pushback has started – not only– by President Lagarde. Morgan France Italy TPI announced The above discussion shows some ambiguity around TPI. No one knows the ECB’s threshold for intervening in terms of yield and spread levels. It is likely that the ECB does not know this either and may never have discussed it. The mere existence of TPI does, however, reduce the risk of very disor- derly market moves. At the same time, the ambiguity allows some widening in spreads that keeps the country under pres- sure to make necessary adjustments. The spirit of the EU Treaty provisions on monetary financing and no-bailouts is that problems need to be tackled at their source and that mon- etary policy must face constraints in intervening. To contain moral hazard in a monetary union with 21 fiscal authorities, market pressure is a mechanism to bring about necessary fis- cal/structural changes that the EU Treaty endorses. The ECB is allowed to intervene to protect the singleness and the trans- mission of its monetary policy, but it must strike a balance so as not to undermine the market mechanism that other EU Treaty provisions seek to protect. The question for the ECB will be whether there has been a fundamental change in fiscal outlook. Reserve manager decisions tend to offset valuation effects, i.e. they would buy EUR into weakness and sell into strength to keep holdings steady. If this historical trend was all that lay behind the Q2 numbers, then the necessary valuation adjustments imply reserve managers would have bought USD21bn EUR. With buying at more than 4x that figure, we conclude there was a meaningful active effort to boost EUR holdings . While the EUR is the largest beneficiary of this apparent trend , we note that the same also applies (to a smaller degree) for the GBP, AUD, CHF and CNY. The JPY stands out as a target of reserve managers ’ active sales. The JPY weakened in Q2, with valuations contributing to a USD16bn fall in reserve holdings. But rather than buying into weakness, reserve managers actively sold USD46bn of JPY , taking the JPY share of reserves from 5.4% to 5%. This was the second consecutive quarter where JPY selling occurred alongside a valuation -driven drop. Why are our public finances projections more pessimistic than the government's? Even if our baseline is that a budget will ultimately be adopted, we maintain our forecast for a 2027 deficit of 5.5% of GDP , above the government's 5.0% target. We project the public-to-GDP ratio to reach 121% next year (Figure 4 and Figure 5). Our view reflects the interplay of three key factors: • First, in line with the assessment of the High Council of Public Finances, we believe the government's 2027 growth assumptions remain optimistic (Figure 6). The government projects real GDP growth of 1.0% next year (Barclays: 0.8%) while at the same time estimating that its fiscal consolidation package, which entails a structural primary adjustment of 0.8pp of GDP , will exert a negative fiscal impulse of 0.5pp of GDP on activity. This implies that, absent fiscal consolidation, the French economy would be set to grow significantly above potential. We view this as unrealistic given the drag from higher energy prices, which has so far been more pronounced in France than elsewhere, as well as the dampening effects of political uncertainty and higher interest rates. • Second, the government's fiscal projections do not incorporate the latest rise in long-term yields. See “ Italy vs France: Assessing sovereign risk dynamics ”, 3 July 2025 • Markets and rating agencies closely monitor countries’ external positions. An improving current account (CA) has consistently supported credit-rating upgrades. Since the sovereign-debt crisis, Italy’s external position has strengthened steadily, with the CA moving into surplus. • As Italy is a net energy importer, the CA may have moved into deficit in Q2. Based on the usual relationship between the CA’s energy component and oil prices, we estimate that the balance may have shifted from around 1.3% of GDP in Q1 2026 to around -0.6% in Q2 2026. • During the 2022 energy crisis, Italy’s CA also moved into deficit before rebounding. While the CA is a flow measure, the Net International Investment Position (NIIP) provides a broader view of a country’s external position by capturing the cumulative effect of current-account balances. It shows whether a country is a net creditor or debtor to the rest of the world. As the right-hand chart shows, Italy has a positive NIIP and is expected to retain it even if the CA remains negative for several quarters. records.text: serve policy continuity An early departure would be more likely to preserve than disrupt ECB policy continuity. If Lagarde chooses to leave early and triggers a process that chooses successors for the ECB president, chief economist and head of markets as a block in the next few months, some of the most influential positions at the ECB will be set for the next 8 years. This could lock in the type of monetary policymaking the current European Council (heads of state and government) wants to preserve before the various European elections over the next year potentially challenge the status quo. Our baseline assumes the ECB hikes once more to 2.75% at the December meeting. The risk is that the ECB hikes to 3%. At the current pace of tightening once per quarter, a decision to hike to 3% could be faced in March. By preserving the current ECB approach to monetary policy with an early agreement on personnel, EU leaders would make it easier for a new ECB President to hike at their first meeting in March, if that emerges as the appropriate course of action. The ECB has a well -established strategy and reaction function, and ECB Chief Economist Lane – whose role is to propose the appropriate policy stance – will be in office until May. This h elps preserve a sense of continuity, not disruption, should Lagarde leave early. More than 85% of municipalities’ end-2025 bad debt book consisted of debts more than 90 days in arrears, of which more than 70% owed by households. The ZAR470bn consumer debt figure counts only what was billed and unpaid. Actual uncaptured revenue is larger still, we believe, with an estimated ZAR23.2bn in combined revenue losses from services municipalities distributed but could not bill. Non-payment not merely delinquent: Metro municipalities alone have written down 70% of their ZAR169bn debtors’ book as amounts they do not expect to recover, according to the latest Auditor-General report. This bolsters our assessment that non-payment is a logical outcome of a mix of structural poverty and weak enforcement. In our view, grant-dependent households rationally calculate that paying municipal bills does not improve their access to the nationally controlled social grants, housing lists and equitable share distribution (i.e. transfers from central to municipal government). In Mangaung and Buffalo City, more than half of households depend on such grants. Why an early departure has become more likely President Lagarde’s language on an early departure has shifted from saying she expects to finish her term (20 February 2026) to more recently saying that she will depart the ECB “in 2027”. When pressed on whether that means at the end of her term in October 2027, she only said “we’ll see”. The forthcoming French presidential election is a potential catalyst for Lagarde’s early departure. In July, Lagarde told the French newspaper Les Échos that it was “certainly possible” she ends her tenure at the ECB early to play a role in the upcoming French presidential elections. She has ruled out standing as a candidate but did not rule out being involved with campaigning and advocating for pro-European values “in whichever capacity” she deemed most efficient. The first round of the French presidential election is on 18 April 2027 . The candidates need to be formalised by 12 March 2027 , with official candidate debates likely to follow soon after . records.text: Who Would Be Exposed to a Ban on US Diesel Exports? Refined product margins have widened significantly since March. Diesel has been especially affected, reflecting highly inelastic demand due to its importance in industrial supply chains and ongoing strikes on refineries in the Middle East and Russia. Wholesale prices have increased by over 90% in Europe and over 80% in the US and Asia since the start of the war in Iran (Exhibit 1). The threat of a US diesel export ban raises further upside price risks and shortage risks in the most exposed economies. In this Global Economics Comment, we leverage our commodities’ team’s recent analysis to assess how a ban would likely affect growth and inflation across global economies. In the very near term, a US diesel ban would put downward pressure on prices in the US, with our commodities team estimating a $0.25/gallon price reduction (or just under 4% of the current price) per week of export bans, implying a modest 2-3bp drag on headline US inflation after a month and a 4-5bp drag after two months. But this small decline in inflation would likely reverse and ultimately turn inflationary after roughly two months, since our commodity strategists estimate that each week of a diesel export ban would raise US retail gasoline prices by $0.3/gallon per week once diesel storage capacity is exhausted after 9-10 weeks. records.text: 2 Global Economic Weekly | 02 October 2026 Global Letter Claudio Irigoyen Global Economist BofAS claudio.irigoyen@bofa.com Antonio Gabriel Global Economist BofAS antonio.gabriel@bofa.com The fog of war Markets always struggle to trade more than one theme at a time. And this week showed that the macroeconomic outlook is being driven by a multiplicity of themes that can create significant mispricing. US inflation came in softer than expected and in line with dovish comments from Fed officials, leading the market to think the Fed may wait until December to hike. But the underlying fundamentals still point towards higher rates. A new narrative argues that oil flows are normalizing in the Middle East, but Brent keeps trading above $100 per barrel. Consumer spending remains strong, but consumer sentiment is weakening. Something does not add up. Most likely, (1) higher global real rates is still the path of least resistance, (2) without fiscal consolidation on the horizon, government intervention in financial markets is increasingly likely, (3) the Middle East conflict is far from coming to an end, and (4) consumption and investment in the US will remain strong as long as the AI trade doesn't break. What is really driving real rates? There is a debate on what drives long-term real rates. records.text: M Idea 2 Headline and Core Up What happened | Headline jumps (3.8%Y) and core increases a touch (2.5%Y): EA headline inflation increased to 3.8%Y in September, from 3.2%Y the previous month. The print was 10bp above consensus but in line with our updated forecast after the countries releases earlier this week (here). Core inflation increased to 2.5%Y from 2.4%Y, in line with consensus, but a touch less than we thought. The uptick in headline came primarily from energy (18.8% from 14.3%) with a jump of 3.9%M on the month. Food inflation rebounded to 1.4%Y from 1.1%Y, with a sharp increase of non-processed food inflation (4.0%Y from 2.7%Y). We suspect this reflects adverse weather conditions this summer. Services inflation increased to 3.2%Y from 3.0%Y, we think mostly because of the correction of a soft August print for tourism. Goods inflation eased a touch (1.1%Y from 1.2%Y). This is a surprise, as we thought it would continue to be lifted by IT products and lubricants. All in all, we continue to stress that EA inflation does not show strong evidence of a broad- based transmission from higher energy costs to core or food inflation. The adjustment in inflation targeting from 3% to 2.5% is itself a step towards greater alignment with euro -area convergence benchmarks . This adds credibility to policy across both government and central bank, but it remains a distant target: Hungary is not in ERMII (the mechanism that precedes EUR adoption) and no official date has been established between the European and Hungarian authorities. Hungary appears set to converge towards Eurozone macro standards , but the actual process of EUR adoption – by no means a guarantee – remains some way off. HUF OUTLOOK Tailwinds for the HUF have slowly receded in recent months. Post-election exuberance, high real rates and beta -asset outperformance collide with the realities of rising energy prices, higher global yields, and a less supportive risk backdrop. The outlook f or the HUF seems to pit a trio of supportive domestic factors – low inflation and high real rates, policy credibility of EUR convergence and a more modest positioning profile – against the vagaries of external risk profile.
